You are a clinical information extraction system. Read ONE outpatient consultation transcript (lines like "[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): text") and return ONE JSON object with the clinical information it contains, in the trained clinical-extraction format. Return only the JSON.

Rules
- Use only what is said. Never invent or infer. Leave out every field and section that has no information.
- Record who said it (doctor, patient, nurse, caregiver, family_member, clinical_staff, unknown), in lower case.
- A denied finding goes in negative_findings, never in symptoms. A doctor's question is not a fact: use the answer.
- A medicine the patient takes is not an allergy. A stopped medicine is not current. Dose, frequency, route and indication belong only to the medicine they were said for.
- Doctor impressions are provisional or differential, and only if the doctor stated one. Do not add a diagnosis the doctor declined to give.
- Use the right status for plan items (planned, completed, recommended, conditional). Do not add a follow-up that was not arranged.
- If speakers disagree or a detail is unclear (dose, date, allergy, name), keep both statements and describe the real doubt in clinical_uncertainties.
- Cite one or two segment ids per item in evidence_ids. clinical_evidence is []. All confidence fields are null.

Transcript (encounter 03690)
[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hello, sorry about the delay, do sit.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, you know, hello, thanks for fitting me in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): how are things, what's been happening?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Actually, mainly a dry cough. There's a couple of other things, but that's the main one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it it been?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been going on for two months. I thought it would sort itself out, but it hasn't.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): tell me a bit more about it: how bad it gets, how often, and whether anything makes it better or worse
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Honestly, every other day. Mild, really. I've also had sore ankles.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): can I check a few measurements before we carry on?
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, this won't take long...
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay: blood pressure 128 over 81, respiratory rate 18, temp 36.7 degrees. And SpO2 97 percent on room air, heart rate 69.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay, time for me to examine you
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): sure thing
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, look straight ahead.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): There are tender raised red nodules on both shins and your ankles are puffy.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the examination finished. Did you get fever, coughing up blood, night sweats or weight loss?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): None of those, you know, no.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): has your heart given you any trouble?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I've never touched a cigarette.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): what about alcohol?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing, I'm teetotal.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your job?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in accounts at a hospital.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you live by yourself?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I share a house with my brother.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): how are your meals?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I have eczema.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah. Which medicines do you take at the moment?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Hydrocortisone cream. I take it when needed for the eczema.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have you been on it?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): About two years.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you react to any medicines or foods? Any allergies?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I mean, I don't think I have any, no
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, here's what I'm thinking. I don't have a clear answer today: possible sarcoidosis is possible, and so is tuberculosis.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood tests is what I'd like next, for possible sarcoidosis.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fine with me.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to order a chest X-ray, for cough and erythema nodosum. Rest and elevate the legs, and I'm arranging a chest clinic review. Don't skip meals, and try to eat smaller portions more often through the day. The respiratory clinic would be the right next step, I'll refer you. Let's plan a check after the tests. That's all from me. Any questions?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): take care now

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Keane, before the doctor comes in, I've your blood pressure at one thirty eight over eighty two, and the pulse is 76. You can stay where you are.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm seventy four and I'm wrecked, so the sooner this is done the better.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Dr Brennan. Come on in, the pair of ye. What's been troubling you, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The legs. At night they seize up in desperate cramps, and stretching or walking it off only helps a small bit. Next day I'm like a wet rag.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's roaring the house down some nights. Mam, tell her how long it's been.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, two months, maybe longer, I haven't a notion exactly. Both calves, the right is worse, and I'm too tired to be counting.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is it just the calf, or does it run up into the thigh as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the calf. I get up and stamp around the kitchen and—
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she won't drink. I put a glass by the chair and it sits there all day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Will you let me finish. Then I can't get back to sleep, and I'm fit to be tied.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): The sleep is broken after them, I hear you. How much are you actually drinking in the day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, I don't... uh, the tea goes cold half the time.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Go on, Mam.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup of tea in the morning and a sup of water with the tablet. That's the height of it.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles, pain in the chest, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Don't be adding things on me.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand, I won't pile on. What tablets are you taking at the minute?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. I call it frusamide, forty milligrams every morning, years now, for the blood pressure I think. And I got magnesium in the chemist for the cramps.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty milligrams each morning for the blood pressure, yes. The magnesium, what strength, and how often?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): One at night. The dose, err, I haven't a notion, the bottle's at home.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She doesn't always take that magnesium either. And Auntie Brid keeps pushing her biotin, the hair tablets, as if that'd fix cramps. Brid's the one on the biotin, not Mam.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it most nights. I can't hear myself think with the two of ye going on. Brid's tablets are her own business.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else, even now and again?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Two paracetamol, the 500 ones, if the legs are sore after a bad night. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to medicines at all? Anything that didn't suit you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not... look, I'm wrecked, can we not—
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has to ask, Mam.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I've taken penicillin and everything, the amoxacillin one years back, and not a bother.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good, so nothing that disagreed with you. I'll have a look at the calves. They're soft, there's no heat, no swelling, and the pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): They feel grand sitting here. It's only in the bed they go mad.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Apart from the legs and the tiredness, any bother with the tummy or the waterworks?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's all grand. It's the cramps and being wrecked, nothing else.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think these night cramps may well be tied to the water tablet and you drinking so little, but I won't change the frusemide until we see the salts. I'll book bloods for the potassium, and the kidney numbers with them.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): More bloods. Brilliant. That's all I need.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I know it's a nuisance. Stretch the calves before you get into bed, and try for more than that one cup of tea, even a glass with the dinner. We'll see you back in a fortnight with the results.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods for tomorrow morning at the desk, and the review for two weeks. Mind yourselves.

Transcript (encounter 01355)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi, uh, is it okay to come in now?
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, sit down. Tell me why you came.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I wanted to get a sore ankle looked at.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has this been bothering you?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, it's been like this since Monday.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sure. Okay, give me more detail on it, whatever comes to mind.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Walking definitely sets it off. It's a few times a day. Moderate, I'd say.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been a little swelling too?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, that too.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any pain in the foot?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain in the foot, thankfully.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you noticed crack or pop or numbness?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing to report there.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your urine normal, no changes?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No changes there.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you been to theatre before?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Just part of my thyroid removed, years back.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take any prescribed or over-the-counter medicines?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Allopurinol, 100 milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you start it?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Six months now.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, right.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Bisoprolol, 2.5 milligrams, maybe, once a day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have the packet or the prescription with you?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not with me. I'll bring it next time. Erm, I take ibuprofen gel, three times a day.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anything ever caused you a reaction? I mean any allergies.

[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm irritable. Snapping at my little boy, snapping at everyone. That's new, and I hate it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding from down below?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain in the tummy, or tightenings?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath on the stairs?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll leave that. Any fever, feeling shivery?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waterworks and bowels, all alright?

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams once a day. Any iron, or aspirin?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just the follik acid. I said. I'm too tired for this.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No drug allergies.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family, then. Parents or siblings with thalasemia, sickle cell, serious anaemia? And his leaflet, alpha or beta? Sorry, I need you to repeat that, the computer ate it.

I'll book bloods with the nurse Thursday morning, full blood count and a haemoglobinopathy screen. No need to fast. Come before 10, and bring his leaflet if it's still on the seat.

Rules

Transcript (encounter 00510)
[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right, Dana, the booking note says insulin review, and then in brackets, lows at night. Is that the headline?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the headline. Okay, so, you know I got that new sensor in the fall? The one that beeps? It woke my husband up before it woke me, which tells you something about how deeply I sleep through my own lows.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's actually useful information. How often is it going off in the night?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): About twice a week. Usually around three in the morning. I wake up drenched, my pajamas are soaked, and I have to go eat jelly beans in the dark like a raccoon.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Jelly beans at three a.m. Mm-hm. And is it a low every time the sensor beeps, or sometimes a false alarm?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly real. The sensor says fifty-something, and my finger stick agrees, within a few points. Last Tuesday it said forty-four, and I just sat on the kitchen floor eating a banana, honestly feeling kind of silly.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not silly. Anything else different lately, besides the nights?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm wiped out in the afternoons. Like around two, three o'clock I hit a wall. I thought it was the lows messing with my sleep, but maybe it's something else.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Could be both. Let me ask about some other things. Any blurry vision lately?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes are fine, I had my eye exam last month, and they gave me the thumbs up.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Numbness or tingling in your feet?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. My feet are the one part of me that behaves.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any vomiting or stomach upset, because that can throw the sugars off.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Nope, no vomiting. Stomach's been good. Which is a relief, since I'm not allowed gluten anyway, so I'm cautious.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, the celiac. Let's make sure I have all your insulin and other medicines right. Walk me through a day.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): So at bedtime, I take glargine, 20 units. Then with meals I take lispro, usually about 6 units, depending on what I'm eating and what the sensor says. And then lisinopril, 5 mg every morning, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your other conditions, I have type 1 diabetes of course, high blood pressure, and celiac disease. Anything else?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the list. Oh, and my appendix came out when I was fifteen. It's in my chart somewhere, I think. Does that count?
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): It counts, we like complete records. Tell me about exercise, it matters for the nighttime lows.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I run three mornings a week, about five miles. And on Saturdays I have the 5K group, which is more of a social hour with some jogging.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): There it is. Think of your body like a car in a cold garage. A hard run uses up the fuel in your muscles, and then overnight your body keeps pulling sugar in to refill the tank. If your long-acting insulin is still pushing hard at three a.m., you hit empty.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. That actually explains why it happens after my Friday run and not after rest days.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Exactly. Okay, let me get your numbers. Arm out, please. Blood pressure is 122 over 76.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse is 70, oxygen saturation is 99 percent, temperature 36.7, and you weigh 176 pounds on our scale.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Good, I was 180 at Thanksgiving, thanks to my mother-in-law's pie.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those are all good. Here's what I think. The overnight lows look most likely like too much of the long-acting insulin at bedtime, particularly after exercise.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So I turn it down? I've been scared to touch it, honestly. Last time I changed a dose on my own, I overcorrected and went high for three days.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): A small step, not a big one. I'd like you to cut the glargine from 20 units down to 18 units at bedtime, and keep everything else the same.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Eighteen. Okay. And if I still go low?
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then text the clinic, and we'll adjust again by another two. Meanwhile, have a small snack at bedtime on the days after you run.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): A snack I'm allowed to have! Peanut butter on gluten-free toast, it is.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I also want a fresh HbA1c blood test before I see you, so we can see the longer picture.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I can do that on my way to work, the lab's right by my office.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Perfect. And I'd like to see you in three months to review how the nights are going.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Three months, okay. Thank you, doctor. I'll go home and tell my husband the jelly bean raccoon retires soon.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's hope. Take care, Dana.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab your vitals before he comes in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, go ahead. We were stuck on the highway forever, some fender bender by the exit, whole mess.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Blood pressure is one thirty-two over eighty-four. Pulse 78. Oxygen sat 97 percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. That cuff bites every time. Anyway.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): You're good. He'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi. What brings you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough. Every morning I wake up hacking, and the stuff that comes up is brown. That's the reason I came.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, years. About ten years, maybe longer. It was already going when I was still smoking.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every single morning, doctor. I hear him from the kitchen, twenty minutes easy.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, she's right. Thick brown phlegm. Not yellow, brown.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still smoking?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Quit last year. Before that, err, a pack a day, uh, forty years.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He really did quit. I'm still proud of that.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Weight up or down?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Stable. Hasn't budged.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I don't really know. I get warm sometimes after lunch, but I never checked it, so maybe that's nothing. Hard to say.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicines?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not prescription ones. I take Mucinex, the gaifenesin, six hundred milligrams, when the phlegm gets bad. Couple times a week.
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Box is in the bathroom cabinet. He does use it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, before I forget, our granddaughter Maya had a softball game Saturday. They were down by four, then this little kid, not even ours, hit a triple and the whole place went nuts.
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She wouldn't take the glove off in the car. Still had dirt on her knees at dinner.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety degrees in those bleachers, we were melting. Got mint chip after, and the coach says next week they play Riverside if the heat breaks. Wild.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sounds fun. Cough worse any time besides the morning?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly just the morning. Rest of the day, err, I'm alright. Garage, errands, all fine.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything help it?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Hot coffee takes the edge off. The Mucinex too, I think. Then it just kind of burns itself out.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Deep breath. Lungs are clear. No wheeze, no crackles.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Huh. Feels rattly when I first get up though.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not hearing that now. I think this is chronic bronchitis from the smoking years. Working impression, not a locked-in diagnosis.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Chronic bronchitis. My uncle ended up on oxygen down in Florida, different deal, I don't want that road.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm booking spirometry, the breathing test, for this cough. Front desk will put it on the schedule.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the tube you blow in, right?
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. We might do a chest scan if it does not settle after that. Not ordering the scan today.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should we be scared?
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. I do want him to get a flu shot and the pneumonia vaccine. Pharmacy can do both.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I had a flu shot a couple years back, I think. Pneumonia one, I don't remember that at all.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Get both this season anyway. Come back in three weeks and we'll go over the spirometry.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks, ok. Can I still mow? The yard is a jungle and the neighbor kid wants twenty bucks now.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Mow the lawn. No restrictions.
[SEG0044] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll stick the vaccines on the fridge calendar so it actually happens.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): She'll nag. She already nags about the trash cans. It's fine.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. That's it for today.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk you out. Front desk will book that breathing test.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): The N3 was a car park this morning. Was it as bad coming in from your side?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I wasn't counting the cars. I'm on my lunch, can we start.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Go on then. What's brought you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The hand goes dead on me at night. And I dropped a cup this morning, smashed it all over the kitchen. That's the reason I'm here.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dead, as in numb, or is it sore?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Numb. Umm, pins and needles in the thumb, the index and the middle finger, right hand mostly, and the left only if I lie on it. It's been about four months, since February.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking you from sleep?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night nearly, two or three in the morning. I have to shake the hand to get it going again. I barely sleep and I'm wrecked the next day, so don't tell me I look tired.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't. The cup, is the grip going in the daytime as well?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Well actually the phone as well, a mug at the desk yesterday, and the cup this morning. The grip just goes and the thing is on the floor.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the hand with it, or only the numb feeling?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain. Just dead and tingly. I already said numb.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry. Pain in the neck, or does it shoot down from the neck?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's grand.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness in the feet?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Short of breath, or chest tightness when you're walking about?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I'm not here about my chest.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Give me the ordinary life in one go, would you, the job, the hours, the food, exercise, drink.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm in the office at the furniture factory in Navan, accounts, on the computer the whole day, hours half seven till half four, five days, and the odd Saturday if the invoices pile up. Diet is sandwiches at the desk and a takeaway most evenings, and a fry on the Sunday, and I don't exercise, the walk from the car park is the height of it. Four or five pints of a Friday, well actually it's four, and I don't smoke. There, happy?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'll do. In the family, diabetes, blood pressure, heart trouble, any of that?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my other sister is grand, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. I haven't got sugar myself, if that's the next question. Can you look at the hand.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): In a second. What tablets are you on?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two tablets, if the hand is at me in the morning, not every morning. I was on naproxin five hundred milligrams twice a day for the hand and I stopped it in March, it did nothing and it turned my stomach. Amitriptaline got mentioned and I never took it, not once.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol when you need it, naproxen stopped since March, amitriptyline never started. Any vitamin or blood pressure tablet hiding in the press?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's the lot. Are we examining or chatting.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Examining. Both hands on the desk.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): They're there. The right is the one, obviously.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thenar bulk is preserved both sides, no wasting. Grip is a little weaker on the right than the left.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): What's thenar even mean.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Err, pad of muscle under the thumb. It's not shrunk, that's the good bit. Tell me what you feel when I tap the right wrist.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's the buzz, yeah. Don't keep doing it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Positive Tinel's on the right. Left wrist, no tingle when I tap. Light touch is duller on the right thumb, index and middle finger than on the ring finger.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. I could have told you the fingers. Are you done.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Done with the hands, err, let me think this out loud. Little finger is spared so I'm not chasing the ulnar nerve, but night waking, the three fingers and the positive tap, my leading thought is the median nerve squeezed at the wrist, carpal tunnel, and I am not concluding it today. A root in the neck could still do this, and off sugars or a lazy thyroid can copy the whole picture. I will not put a final name on it yet.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): After all the poking you still don't know. For god's sake.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know what leads the list and what I won't cross off. Let's see what the tests say before anyone stamps it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. So what do I actually do.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Get a neutral wrist splint off the chemist and wear it on the right hand at night for the next two weeks. It stops the wrist folding up in your sleep. You can still shake it out if it goes dead, but the splint is the thing that might settle it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A splint in the bed. I'll look an eejit. The invoices won't do themselves either if I'm messing about with appointments.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): The lads don't need to see it, it's for the night. Bloods are booked, not a maybe. The nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, fasting glucose and a thyroid test. Nothing but water from midnight, in at half 8, and you eat straight after.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday, half 8, fasting. I'll tell them at the office. This is eating my week.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, the B12. I'm not booking that unless they come back borderline.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): And the nerve test, is that today or what. Someone said nerves.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it does not settle with the splint, then we do nerve conduction studies. Conditional, not arranged.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's the neck you were on about?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it does not settle, a scan of the neck, only in that case. I'll see you in two weeks with the bloods either way, that visit is booked.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): The itch. Between me fingers and around me waist. It's fierce, worse at night, and I can't sleep with it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The waist, say that bit again. I was half looking at this yoke.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Around me waist, where the elastic sits. And in between the fingers. I'm scratching the skin off nearly. It's doing me head in.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long is it going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. About two weeks. Well, actually I can't pin the day, it just sort of crept up.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No, it's three weeks. She was at it before the bank holiday, I mind the Monday.

[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, 4 milligrams or 10? Screen jumped. Say the Piriton again.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Four milligrams, at night, and I stopped it. I already said that.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. Hands out for me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeh. Scratch marks between the fingers, and a couple of little burrows. Let's see the waist.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Here, this side. Don't poke it, it's sore.

[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hold on. It's not only her. The partner is scratching the same, and the small lad. Nights, mostly.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Say that again? The child as well?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yes. The little boy and her fella. Both of them itching.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): It's me, himself and the child in the house. And yes they're at it too. I was too tired to start into all that.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll send the script for the permethrin now. If it's not settled two weeks after the second treatment, come back to me.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit down, you're very welcome. What brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm grand, I nearly talked myself out of coming. It's probably a waste of your time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not a waste at all. Tell me what's been happening, however you want to put it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a small bit of a pain, up here on the right under the ribs. Comes on after the fry or cheese, anything greasy.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right side, under the ribs, after the greasy food. What does it feel like when it's there?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): A deep ache, more than a sharp thing. I'm grand between times, so I don't know why I'm fussing.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And once it starts, how long before it lets go?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was going to say all evening. Umm, well actually no, two or three hours and then it eases. It's been about three months, an antacid takes the edge off, and I was sick with it the once. I'm making it sound worse than it is.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three months is worth a look, even if you're playing it down. Anything else you notice when the pain is on you?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I just wait it out. Put the kettle on, that sort of thing.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said you were sick the once. Was that vomiting, and did it happen again?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Vomited, yeah, err, just the once, a couple of weeks back after a roast. Nothing since. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you been taking anything for it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): That gaviscn from the chemist. I thought it was two spoons, well actually it's one spoon, the 10 ml, when the pain starts. My sister keeps pushing her omeprozole on me but that's hers, I don't take it.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So gaviscon, 10 ml, when the pain starts, and not your sister's tablet. Does it do much?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Takes the edge off, that's all. I'm not looking for a miracle.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family had trouble like this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had her gallbladder out, years ago. She was far worse than me. That's the only one.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Your mother had the gallbladder removed. Anyone else?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband John is on metformin for his diabetes, two tablets a day, but that's his sugar, not mine. I don't take a thing of his.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave his metformin well alone. Now, any fever with these pains, or do you feel shivery?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm not shivery either.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And chest wise, any cough, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. I can walk the length of the town.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed at all?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah no. Well, the jeans feel a small bit loose, or maybe they just stretched, umm I haven't been on the scales. No, I'm the same weight I've always been.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no weight loss, then?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): The thing that actually annoyed me today was the bus. Forty minutes from Salthill in the rain, and the radio hurling cutting out.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was the rain that bad on the coast road?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Sheets of it. And I missed the last ten minutes of the match stuck at the lights. Galway were doing tidy enough before that.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah that's frustrating. Who were they playing?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't even catch the name properly, the reception was desperate. My neighbour's lad is on the under sixteens, he was practising in the garden in all that wet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Practising in that? Fair play to him.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): His nan knitted him a scarf in the wrong colours entirely. We were in stitches over it. Purple and orange, if you can imagine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Purple and orange, lord. Did he wear it anyway?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): He did, to please her. He's a good kid. Anyway, that's me rambling, sorry.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't be sorry, it's nice to hear. Let me come back to your tummy, if I may. Lie back and I'll have a feel.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on. It's only a bit sore, I'm not going to leap off the bed.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tummy is soft. Tender under the right ribs, and sore when you breathe in there. No guarding, and nothing rigid.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. That's the spot. Still only mild, though.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely biliary colic, the gallbladder acting up after fatty food. I wouldn't call it certain until we see the tests.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder. Sure I'm nothing like my mother was. She couldn't keep a cup of tea down.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): You can be milder and it still be the same sort of thing. I'd like a full blood count, liver blood tests, and an ultrasound of the tummy.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound for this? It feels like a lot of fuss.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the bloods and the ultrasound. Bloods can be done downstairs today, and the scan as soon as there's a slot. Not a fuss, just a proper look.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Grand, so. If you say so.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease off the fry and the cheese in the meantime. Stick with the gaviscon, 10 ml, when it niggles.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): I can leave the rashers. I'll miss them, but I can.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the pain turns severe, or you can't keep fluids down with vomiting, or you get a fever, or the whites of the eyes go yellow, go to the emergency department and don't wait for me.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Yellow eyes. I hear you. I doubt it'll come to that.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks and we'll go through the results together.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I'll be grand, I'm sure of it. I'll bring a brolly next time.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do. Mind yourself on the way out, it's still pouring.

[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright, thanks, take care.

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the ankles first, in your own words.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Not sore, no. Just puffy and tight, the shoes won't go on. I had to wear the old slip-ons in.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And would you say the swelling stays the whole day?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Depends if I've been mooching about the shops.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. And the passing water, what's that been like?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm up twice a night at least, and during the day I'm in and out. I blame the tea, I drink a fierce amount, six mugs easy. My sister says I'm a teapot with legs.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain when you pass water, or any blood?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain and no blood. It's just often, that's all.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The amlodopine, ten milligrams, once a day, for the blood pressure. And the water tablet, uh, frusimide, forty milligrams in the morning. I've been on the blood pressure tablets for years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty, every morning. Are you getting that one in every morning?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok, we'll leave that as not certain so. And the readings at home, have you been checking them?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I've the little machine from the chemist. This morning it said 128 over 76. Most days it's around one thirty over eighty. My grandson set the cuff up, he's great with phones, he put an app on it I never open.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's handy to have. Let me take it here. There we are, today in the clinic it's 162 over 94, and the pulse is 74.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): 162? God almighty. It was grand at home this morning. I had a coffee on the bus, maybe that did it, and some fella's shopping bag was on my foot the whole way in.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Different places can give you different numbers, you're not imagining it. Can I have a look at the ankles?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Fire ahead. The right one is the fatter, I think. Or maybe they're the same, I can't see past the belly half the time.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are pitting, soft swelling up as far as the lower shin. I'm not hearing anything odd in the chest either.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's a relief. I was watching some thing on the telly about hearts and I had myself buried, so I did.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or tightness with all this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Breathing is grand too, if you're wondering. I walked from the bus stop no bother.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, right so. Will I get that from the chemist on the corner? They were out of the other yoke last month and I had to traipse all the way into town.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send the script over and you can collect the ramipril today. The nurse takes your bloods Thursday morning, a kidney test and a fasting sugar, so we know where we are with the new tablet. Nothing to eat from midnight, and hold the morning tablets till after.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning, fasting, grand. I'll get the early bus so. Do I still take the water tablet that morning or leave it?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold all the morning tablets until the bloods are done, the frusemide as well. If the kidney test or the sugar is borderline we'll do a urine protein. If the ankle swelling hasn't settled we'll organise a scan of the legs. I'll see you back here in two weeks anyway.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mr Brennan. I'll take your readings before the doctor sees you. Sleeve up there.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressure is 138 over 82. Pulse 74. Oxygen is 96 percent on room air.

[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All done. Doctor will call you in a second. Have a seat.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr Brennan. What brought you in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cough, doctor. Well, actually it's every morning. I wake up coughing. The wife said I was to stop ignoring it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been there.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Years. Five years easy, maybe longer. I couldn't put a date on when it actually started, to be honest.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Phlegm.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Brown phlegm. Well, actually it's a dirty brown, not bright or anything. Most mornings, and not a lot of it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood in it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I'd have come in a lot sooner if there was.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. None.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): A wee bit if I'm hurrying on the stairs. Not when I'm sitting. I can still walk the dog grand.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Weight's been steady. Same belt hole as last year. The good trousers still fit.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever or night sweats.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neither of those.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Not anymore. I quit last year, around Paddy's day, so March. Twenty a day before that, for about thirty years. The lads gave me fierce stick over quitting.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah sure speaking of the lads, the grandson had a hurling match on Sunday out in Kilmacud.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The weather was wicked. Horizontal rain. We were soaked on the sideline, the whole lot of us.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the M50 on the way home was a car park. An hour, easy. He's only seven and he still got a score. Chips after, the car all steamed up, and he was delighted with himself.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): The cough.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. I do go on. Yeah, the cough.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, 5 milligrams, one tablet every morning, for the blood pressure. Been on it a few years. And I had the brown inhaler, beclamethasone, two puffs twice a day, but I stopped it in March.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Beclometasone. Stopped in March. Not using it now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not a puff since. Once I was off the cigarettes I thought I was grand. Oh, the chemist handed me amoxicillin last winter for a cold. I never took it, the box is still in the press.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit of a wheeze in the morning, yeah, with the cough. It eases once I'm up and moving.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bowels or waterworks.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, they're grand. No trouble there at all.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to the chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Your hands are freezing, doctor, I'll tell you that for nothing.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Expansion is equal. Breath sounds reduced at both bases. A few crackles, they clear when you cough. No wheeze just now.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Crackles. That sounds worse than it feels, to be honest.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm calling it chronic bronchitis for now. COPD is still possible with that smoking history. Spirometry will sort which.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): COPD. God. That's what the neighbour has, and he's forever at the clinic.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm booking spirometry for Thursday week, to see if this is COPD.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday week. Do I have to do anything special for it.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): No inhaler the morning of the test. Get the flu vaccine and the pneumococcal vaccine. Stay off the cigarettes. Come back in three weeks.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): The jabs. I keep putting them off. The chemist on the corner does the flu one anyway. Three weeks, right.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Three weeks. We'll go through the result then.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I have the spirometry down for Thursday week, and your review in three weeks. Thursday morning for the test, is that alright.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday morning is grand. Nothing else on, unless there's hurling, and I'll shift that.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's everything from me.
[SEG0051] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're booked in. The slip will be at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely. Mind yourselves. That rain is not letting up.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for hanging on. What has you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): It's nothing, really. A bit of an itch on the hands. I nearly didn't come.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't mind him. He's been clawing his fingers and his waist half the night, and we're all in the one house.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where exactly is it itchy?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Between the fingers, and a small bit at the waistband. Only a nuisance.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): When is it worst?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Night time, I'd say. In the day I'm grand.
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The little fella scratches his tummy in the bed too, and my wrists are at me as well.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Two days. A couple of days, maybe. Nothing at all.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two days my eye. It's three weeks, since before the Easter break at school.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't pin the start today. Let me look at the hands and the waist.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. There are little tracks between the fingers, and a few raised bumps along the waist. It doesn't look infected.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No fever. Not a bit sick.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Maybe a pound, maybe I haven't. No scales in the house. I'm grand.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's the tummy? Any upset?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No, stomach's fine. Eating away.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on, so I know what we're working around?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodopine, five milligrams, in the morning for the pressure. The cholesterol one at night, twenty milligrams. Sugar tablets, two of them with the breakfast, err, I forget the name of them. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, from the health shop.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That helps. With the night-time itch, the webs of the fingers, and the whole house scratching, I'd say this is scabies. I wouldn't fully rule out eczema, but I won't park it as eczema and leave it. We don't need blood tests for this.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll use permethrin cream, five percent. Spread it from the neck down to the toes, in between the fingers, under the nails, over the waist and the soles. Leave it eight to twelve hours, wash it off, and do the same again in seven days.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): The same night, everyone in the house gets it, you and your partner and the child, even if you think the itch is small. Hot wash the sheets, towels and clothes at 60 degrees, and bag whatever won't wash for three days.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print those steps out for ye before you go, so you've them in the hand.
[SEG0029] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he actually uses the cream. He'd skip it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in a fortnight and we'll have another look at the skin.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Right so. Seems a lot of fuss, but grand.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. You're a bit early, the doctor's still busy. I'll take your blood pressure while you wait.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, whatever. This is a fuss over nothing.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): One forty eight over eighty six. Pulse seventy eight, regular. Your daughter phoned the desk as well. She says one morning last week you were confused, couldn't find the kettle, talking all over the show.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish. I was half asleep. I was not confused. She dramatises everything.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in. Sit. What's the problem today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter made the booking. She fusses. I told her it's nothing.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): What is the nothing?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): In the mornings I get a bit clammy, sweaty, and my hands go shaky. Before I eat. It's minor.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. A few weeks. Maybe a month. I don't count.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings, ja. Not if I sleep late and I actually eat. So, nothing really.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not dizzy.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, tight chest, or short of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mmm. Hard to say. Maybe. The trousers still fit, so no, not really. I don't know.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're diabetic. Still on the tablets?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The gliklazide and the metforman.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Gliclazide, what dose?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighty milligram. One tablet in the morning when I get up.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): With food?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): With rooibos. I skip breakfast. Porridge sits too heavy, so I eat later, a pie at the shop.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Metformin, dose and how often?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams, twice a day. Morning, and with supper. I do eat supper, so that one I don't miss.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Vitamins from the chemist, sitting in the cupboard. I never take them.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Last blood test, what did they tell you?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): At the day hospital, a good while back. They said the H B A one C was borderline. I don't remember a number, I threw the paper out. So I'm fine, hey.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long diabetic?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve years, about. From when I retired off the railways.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Living alone?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Flat in the complex. My girl is in Alberton, she pitches up uninvited. Load shedding killed the gate motor last week, that's the actual problem.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): When the sweats come, hungry or just shaky?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Hungry, not really. Shaky, and sweaty on the chest and the back of the neck. Tea and a biscuit, I sit, it eases.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blacked out?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): She reported confusion. Did that happen?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag no. I found the kettle, I was just tired and slow. Not confused. I'm seventy two, not ninety.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pouring the tea, hands steady?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, well, actually, no. The kitchen goes swimmy and I grab the counter, the cup spills. So ja, dizzy, a little, seconds only, and something sweet and it's gone. I didn't reckon that counted.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): It counts. Arms forward, steady now, skin dry and not clammy. Pulse regular, no extra beats. Chest clear.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning sweats and the shakes, on gliclazide, no breakfast. Sounds like a low blood sugar. Working idea only, not confirmed.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Low sugar. Ag, I doubt it. I feel lekker right now.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Doses stay as they are. Gliclazide eighty milligrams every morning, metformin five hundred twice a day. Eat something proper before the gliclazide, not just the rooibos.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you get shaky, take sugar or juice, sit, and don't drive until it has settled.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bloods are booked. HbA1c, a glucose, and kidney function because of the metformin. Come back in two weeks for the results, that visit is booked as well.
[SEG0051] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sharp. I'll put the bloods on for Thursday morning at the lab, and the review in two weeks.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Thursday for the bloods, review in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. She's still making a big thing of a small thing.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about fever or coughing up blood?

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is your chest okay generally?

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. How are you going with all this?

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It won't be quick. I've been a mess since that letter.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me what's been on your mind. What made you book in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, the camp reckons I've got thalassaemia trait. She's pregnant, so they want her to have bloods. That's why we're here, nothing dramatic.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm sixteen weeks... sorry, fifteen weeks and a bit, sixteen on Thursday. And I keep thinking about the baby.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): She's spiralling. I'm not. They said trait, not the disease. Big difference.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you remember them saying on the day?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, it was six weeks back... no, three weeks. Community camp at the town hall, finger prick, then a letter. Carrier, see your GP if your partner's pregnant. That's all.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks of me googling at midnight. He pretends it's fine.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah nah. I can't hear myself think in our flat with those podcasts going half the night. Doesn't make me a patient.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. And in yourself, day to day, how have you been feeling?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm alright. I feel like a wet rag when I get home, but I've overdone it. Long shifts, that's all.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's not alright. His feet have been going numb for a couple of months and he just waves it off.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): They have not. My feet feel dead at the end of a shift, last few days, not months. It's nothing.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So between you I'm hearing a few days up to a couple of months, and you don't quite land in the same place. I'll note it as roughly that span.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): And there's a frog in my throat some mornings. Aircon at the warehouse. Hardly a thing.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aside from the feet and the throat, any chest pain, or getting puffed when you walk?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking these days? Just so I've got the list.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodopine for the pressure, in the morning. I was on five milligrams... no, they bumped me, it's ten. The cholesterol one at night, atorvastaton, eighty... no, forty milligrams. Sugar tablets, metforman, five hundred twice a day, and only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, a teaspoon stirred in water.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks. I wouldn't stop any of those off the back of a camp letter.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Even that shop powder? I keep saying it's not real medicine.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just powder. Leave it. My auntie uses the same stuff.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in your family with thalassaemia, or anaemia that needed transfusions?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nobody. Mum's side are all fine.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the worry side, how has that been sitting with you?
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's anxious. He checks that letter every night, he just won't admit it.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not anxious. She's the anxious one. I glance at it, that's all.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. My working impression is this is the trait, the carrier state, not thalassaemia disease. That fits the camp letter and what you've told me. It only really matters for the bub if your wife carries it as well.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Storm in a teacup. We could've sorted this over the phone.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I still want her tested properly. I'll order a full blood count and a haemoglobin electrophoresis, the proper screen, not another finger prick.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can we do it tomorrow? I don't want to sit on this.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yep, no worries. I'll send the request now and reception can book you tomorrow morning.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): And if hers comes back normal we just drop it, right?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): If hers is normal, this doesn't put the bub at risk of the severe illness. If she comes back as a carrier too, I'll refer you both for genetic counselling so you can talk the options through with someone who does this every day.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Counselling. More talking. Brilliant.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's worth doing if we land there. Either way I'll see you both back here in two weeks, once the results are in.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll come. Thank you, really.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Fine. Still reckon it's a fuss.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep on the morning blood pressure tablet, the night one, the sugar tablets and that powder, just as you are. If the feet get worse, or you get chest pain, don't wait for me, get seen sooner.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. Of. See you in a fortnight.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Alright, I weighed him just now. Seven point six pounds, heart rate a hundred and forty-two. He stayed pretty calm.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. That was very smooth, he usually objects to the scale.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): How was the drive? I was stuck past the mall forever, rain coming sideways, and my defroster is basically decorative.
[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Quite slow, I'm afraid. We sat at the river bridge nearly twenty minutes with the windshield completely fogged. I apologize if that put us behind.
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My husband argued for the back roads, and I overruled him, which was foolish. He is home with the dog, who has taken up residence in the laundry basket.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, the laundry basket always wins. I'm Dr. Ellison, by the way. This rain is meant to sit all weekend, just gray and heavy.
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. My mother will not stop texting about her tomato plants drowning. I told her the tomatoes can wait.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): They can. So, what brought you in with him today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His skin has gone yellow. That is why we came.
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yellow. When did you first notice it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. I cannot really date it. It crept up on us, maybe a few days, but I am not certain.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. A lot of this age is hard to date. How have the feeds been?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes the breast, and we give formula too. I nearly said every three hours, well, actually it is every four. The nursery doctor also said he has eczema on his cheeks.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eczema, okay, noted. Is he hard to wake for a feed?
[SEG0016] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He wakes quite reliably on his own.
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Ah.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not really.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): And diarrhea?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Never.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): With the eczema, does the skin weep or ooze?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not that either.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does he seem itchy? Scratching at the cheeks?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No... well, sometimes he rubs his cheek against my shoulder.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sometimes, then. Any cough, or breathing that seems too fast?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Not the cough, and not the fast breathing either.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does his belly hurt him, do you think?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, he is not in pain.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Looking at digestion more broadly, anything else with his belly that worries you?
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing else there.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have the wet diapers dropped off?
[SEG0035] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. My sister's boy was yellow last spring, and she still texts me at odd hours about those blue lights. He's chubby now, so, uh, that's her story, not advice.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Of course. Thank you, that is kind to mention.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medicines at home?
[SEG0039] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, Doctor. We give d-vysol, vitamin d drops, four hundred units once a day by mouth. Err, I think we missed yesterday. The bottle stayed in the other bag.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Four hundred units a day, and yesterday is a maybe. Any allergies?
[SEG0041] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look him over. You can keep a hand on him.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): The eyes are yellow, and the color comes down across his chest and belly. Belly is soft, and I don't feel an enlarged liver.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): The soft spot is flat. He seems comfortable enough.
[SEG0045] person_4 (PATIENT): Uh.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): That yellow is bilirubin. At ten days the liver is still maturing, so pigment from old red cells builds up and stains the skin. Breast milk can slow the clearing a little. I think this is ordinary newborn jaundice.
[SEG0047] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I understand. I appreciate you explaining it plainly.
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd like a blood test for bilirubin today, before you leave. The lab down the hall can draw it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Today is quite alright with us.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the level is high, we might start phototherapy. I won't decide that until we see the number.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Either way, I want to see him back in three days. We'll call you this afternoon with the result.
[SEG0052] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will be by the phone. Should feeding change at all?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the breast milk and the formula, and try not to go much past four hours. Wake him if you have to. Call or come sooner if he's hard to wake, if the yellow reaches his legs, or if the wet diapers thin out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Right, Mr Hale, quick check before you go in. Blood pressure is one thirty eight over eighty two, pulse 76, sats ninety six percent on air.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Took long enough. I've been sat in that corridor since half eight.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry about the wait. On the repeat list I've got ramapril five milligrams once a day for the blood pressure.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's ramipril, and it's ten, not five. Chemist upped it. Five was donkey's years ago. Still once a day, yeah, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll flag that. And atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night for the cholesterol, that's current?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Twenty. Don't miss that one.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Lovely. Doctor's free, I'll pop you through.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr Hale, thanks for waiting. I'm Dr Shah. What's brought you down today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): The cough. Every single morning I'm coughing up this brown muck. I'm tired of it, and I'm tired full stop, so can we not drag this out.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Brown stuff in the mornings. How long's that been going on, do you reckon?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): umm. Years. err, honestly I couldn't tell you when it started. Well before I packed the fags in, anyway.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you stop smoking?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Last year. March. Just stopped. Still fancy one when the van's playing up, but I haven't had one.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): You still driving for work?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Vans. Early starts, which is when this cough is worst, sat in the cab hacking away. Parking here was a nightmare as well, don't get me started.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain in the chest. Just the cough and what comes up.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, temperatures?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't get fevers. I'm just irritable 'cause I've been hanging about, that's all.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Same. Same belt hole. Wife would've noticed, she notices everything.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): And when you walk, up a slope or carrying stuff, how is the breathing?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit. I don't know. well, actually maybe on the stairs, but I'm sixty four and I don't sprint. Not gasping. Hard to say.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll leave that open. Have you been given anything for the cough?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): They tried that mucus one, I always say it wrong, carbo, carbocisteine. Two capsules three times a day. I stopped it in March. Did nothing except make us feel sick.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March, ok. And the brown inhaler on the old letter?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Never took it. Never even picked it up from the chemist. So that doesn't count.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your chest. Deep breath... and out. Again.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest expansion is fine. Few crackles at the right base, no wheeze. Heart sounds are normal. Ankles aren't swollen.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it bad?
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Long morning cough, brown phlegm, you quit last year, and the chest is mostly quiet apart from those crackles. My working impression is chronic bronchitis. Could be early COPD, I can't say that properly without numbers. Doesn't look like a chest infection today, no fever, weight steady.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): COPD. Great. My brother had that and he was on oxygen. Don't tell me I'm heading there.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying that. Different people, different lungs. We measure first, that's the whole point.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. What are you actually going to do, then.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book spirometry for Tuesday morning, nine o'clock, with the respiratory nurse. That's the blowing test, shows if the airways are narrowed. No fasting for that one, just turn up.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Tuesday. That's my early round. Ugh. Alright.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): And uh bloods Thursday morning here, fasting, water only. Full blood count and kidney function, because of the ramipril. Take the ramipril after the bloods, not before.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday as well. Two trips. Brilliant.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the spirometry comes back borderline, then we do a CT of the chest. I'm not booking that now. Only if the numbers sit in the middle.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And if they're fine?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If they're clearly normal or clearly obstructed we may not need the scan at all. I'll see you back in two weeks with the results either way.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. More waiting.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): One more thing. With the smoking history I'd like you to get the flu jab and the pneumococcal one at your practice, this autumn is fine. And please don't go back to the cigarettes, even when the van's playing up.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): The jabs I can do. The fags, yeah, I hear you. Can I go?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can. Reception will have the Tuesday and Thursday times on a slip.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): On the roof of my mouth, and on the gums at the front.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been eating only soft things for a few weeks.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do the dentures still fit well? ~
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): They've been loose since the winter. ~
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She had them made years ago. Her face has changed since then. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take them out at night? ~

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): That can make the sores worse. How long have you had the sores?

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or sore throat? ~

[SEG0019] person_4 (CLINICAL_STAFF): No, I'll be very gentle. Open wide, Mrs Rao.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): What is it, doctor? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): It looks like denture stomatitis, with thrush on top, and the dry mouth makes it more likely. ~
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): What causes the dry mouth? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Often tablets, or not drinking enough, or other things. I'd like to look at her medicines list and arrange some blood tests.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I've brought her list. ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. In the meantime, she should take the dentures out at night, and keep them in a cup of water.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try to remember. ~
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll remind her every evening. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Brush the gums with a soft brush, and sip water through the day. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll also refer you to the dentist to have the dentures checked or remade.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thank you, doctor. ~

Transcript (encounter 00591)
[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, Sam, the booking note says you've swallowed a bit of Lego. Is that right?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... yeah. I swallowed a bit of Lego. A little one. A flat grey piece.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Tell me what happened, from the start.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): I was... um... holding it in my mouth. While I was building a spaceship. And then I sort of... gulped.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, that happens more than you'd think. When was this?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Yesterday. After tea. Or... no, it was before tea, actually.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yesterday, before tea. Did it go down easily, or did it get stuck anywhere?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It just went down. Straight away. It was a bit... um, weird.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble breathing once it had gone down?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No. It was fine.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any being sick or vomiting afterwards?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No... um, no. I wasn't sick.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And how is your tummy feeling now?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): It's... a bit achy. Not horrible. Just a tummy ache.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Would you call it mild, moderate or severe?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Mild. I think. Um... yeah, mild.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did the ache start?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): This morning.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you point to where it is for me?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Here. Um. Round my belly button, like.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anything make it better or worse? Think about eating, or moving around.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... it's a bit worse when I run around. And lying down helps.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sensible. Now let's check your regular medicines. Do you take anything every day?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. A puffer, I think. And... something for my... um...
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take your time. What's the puffer for?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): For my asthma. The blue one. Salbutamol.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. How much of it, and how often do you use it?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... 100 micrograms. When I need it. Mum says it's written on the side.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's right, I can see that on your record. What else is there?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): A cream, for my eczema. Hydrocortisone. Once a day, on my elbows.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the last one?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Um... Movicol. The sachets. For my constipation. Mum makes me have it in orange juice. One sachet a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): That one's useful today. Keeping it going helps things move along.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it help the Lego come out?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It'll certainly not hurt. Hop up on the couch, and I'll have a feel of your tummy.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it going to be cold? Last time the doctor's hands were freezing.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've warmed them up, promise. Tell me if anything hurts when I press.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft, which is what I wanted to feel. You can sit up again.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): So what's going to happen to the Lego?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here's what I think. It's small, smooth plastic, so most likely it will pass through on its own.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): When?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually within a few days. It comes out with your poo, and you won't feel a thing.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I have to look in the toilet for it? That's gross.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): A quick look each day, please, with mum or dad helping. Just so we know it has gone.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Um. Okay. I'll make my brother do it.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, nice try. Now, here's what you can do while you wait. Eat normally, with lots of fruit and veg.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): And chips?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sometimes. Drink plenty of water too, and keep taking your Movicol every day.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Can I still build stuff?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, but not in your mouth. Lego goes in the box and nowhere else.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Okay. Um, I won't.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the ache gets bad, or you're sick, or you feel hot and unwell, tell mum and come straight in.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. I'll tell her. She'll probably tell me anyway.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in three days, to check how things are going.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, can it be after school?
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll ask reception to find you an afternoon slot. Off you go, Sam, and well done for being so brave.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. Bye.
