[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, doctor. The Luas sat at Charlemont for ages and then the car park was full, I was pure mortified coming in the door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. Sit down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Desperate rain as well. Left the umbrella on the bus, typical.
[SEG0004] person_4 (NURSE): Notes are here. I did her blood pressure outside.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm I had a whole list in my notebook and then I forgot the notebook on the kitchen table, which is just like me, but anyway that's not why we're here.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Why are you here?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Err I'm pregnant, about sixteen weeks, and I'm worried the baby could have thalasemia. Himself was told at a blood camp that he carries the trait, and I've been sick with the worry.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was the camp?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh I cannot pin the date. It was last summer, or maybe after the October bank holiday, I go over it and I still haven't a clue.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The letter said beta thalassaemia trait. It came to the house after the GAA club session.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No bleeding. Not a spot, I've been checking every day since the positive test, probably more than any sensible person would, sorry.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. There is a heavy tiredness though, and uh I couldn't tell you when that began, last winter or the one before, it all runs together.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sleeping?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Sleep's been rotten. I lie there going through the what-ifs since the letter came.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's awake half the night. I'm anxious too, but sure I'm not the patient.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medicines?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I take folick acid by mouth every morning for the pregnancy. I told the midwife five milligrams, that was wrong, it's the 400 microgram bit inside the pregnicare tablet from the chemist.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No drug allergies and no food allergies.
[SEG0023] person_4 (NURSE): My own sister was told she was a carrier and her little lad is in senior infants now and flying it. I only say that so people don't panic in the corridor.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I never smoked. I used to have a glass of wine on a Friday and that's stopped since the test turned positive, not a drop.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The trait means one haemoglobin gene is altered. The red cells come out smaller. It doesn't make him ill by itself. If both of ye carry it there's a one in four chance of the full condition in the child.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So he's not sick? I read three websites, they contradicted each other, and my cousin went on about a neighbour's child who needs transfusions, and I spiralled, which I do.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. He's not sick from the trait. Working impression is a possible risk to the baby only if you carry it too. Not confirmed.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): They mentioned my haemoglobin was low, something like 12, but that was my old result.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): We won't use his figure. Nurse, today's numbers?
[SEG0031] person_4 (NURSE): Blood pressure 118 over 74, pulse 86, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft. No pallor. The womb feels about right for sixteen weeks.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I say sixteen weeks because it's tidy, but the twelve-week scan was fifteen plus a few days and I always round it up, my mother says I over-explain everything.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your mother's health?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Mam has high blood pressure. Nothing like thalassaemia on my side, that anyone ever said.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book a full blood count and a haemoglobin electrophoresis for you today. That's the screen.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Today, even though I had toast and tea? I always get in a knot about fasting rules and then I end up describing my breakfast, which nobody needs.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): No fasting needed. If the bloods show you carry it as well, we might refer ye to genetic counselling. I'm not booking that now.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if she's clear?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then this doesn't put the baby at risk of the major illness. I'll see ye back in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stay on the pregnicare?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, stay on it. If you get bleeding or bad pain, come straight in, don't wait.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. The notebook had about twenty questions, half of them daft, but the baby was the only one that mattered.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll come back. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0045] person_4 (NURSE): Reception will send ye to phlebotomy on the way out. I'm off at four, so it won't be me.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks a million. Sorry again for landing in late.

[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's pain under my right ribs after fatty meals, doctor. She didn't want to come, but I insisted.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days or weeks has it been? These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been going on for about a week.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, fatty meals. That makes it worse. Only lying still, and it's not much. Honestly, a couple of times a week. I've been feeling sick too. I mean, as for feeling sick, it's mild, honestly. It comes and goes. I had pain going to my right shoulder before. That's settled now, though.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any dark urine, yellow eyes or pale stools?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't had dark urine, yellow eyes or pale stools, no.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, go on. Did you notice any fever?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Definitely no fever.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Actually, doctor, I did notice fever. She doesn't always say.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think I did. Maybe a little, I'm not sure.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note both what you've said and what you've noticed. Neurologically, anything strange?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your breathing, any trouble there?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's talk a little about your daily life and habits.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I do a yoga class on Thursdays. Lots of rice, lentils and some fruit. My partner and our baby.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any health conditions I should have on record?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I have anxiety, for about a year. I've had high blood pressure for five years now.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, any other things?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I have heart failure.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so anxiety and high blood pressure are already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): My son has asthma.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's on your current medicine list? These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She is on escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day for the anxiety, I give it to her. She is on lisinopril, 10 milligrams, once a day for my pressure, I give it to her. She takes metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm-hmm.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's an antacid, 10 ml, when needed, doctor.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had any previous surgeries?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, no, I've never been operated on.
[SEG0034] person_4 (NURSE): Doctor, I've got the readings for you. BP is 126 over 78, saturation 97 percent, pulse is 82 beats a minute, temperature 36.5.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, let's have a proper look at you.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fine.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll listen to your chest now.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is tender under the right ribs and you stop breathing in when I press.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fine.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, based on the history and the examination, this looks most like gallstone-related pain. That's my thinking for now, and it may change as we learn more. A stomach ulcer is also on my list.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm scared it's something bad. Is it?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like gallstone-related pain, but I'd like to confirm. Let's book liver blood tests to look into biliary pain. I'd like to arrange an ultrasound of the abdomen for biliary pain. I'll start you on paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day when needed, one week. That's for pain. Avoid fatty and fried foods until the scan. Please take the tablets with food so they don't upset your stomach.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's get you seen by the surgical clinic, I'll arrange the letter. Let's plan a check after the scan. I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, thanks, I'll see you then.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late. The luas was a pure disaster and then the rain started, I nearly turned around and went home.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're here. Sit. What's the problem.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, umm, my auntie was told last month she has lymphoma and I've been in bits ever since, not sleeping, googling at three in the morning.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been pacing the flat all week, doctor. I had to nearly drag him down here.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the aunt why you're in, or is there something on you.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the lump. I've a painless lump in my neck. I'm after having it two weeks, uh, no, three weeks.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): The right, just under the jaw. It doesn't hurt one bit, and that's what frightens me. Painless is bad, isn't it?
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bigger since you noticed it.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Like a marble, maybe. Umm, I spotted it the night of the hurling, so yeah, three weeks.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Night sweats.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Once. Just the one night I woke drenched. Not since, thank God.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever now.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I felt grand this morning. No temperature that I could tell.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight loss. Cough. Sore throat.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No weight loss. No cough. Throat's been fine. Err, I did get a scratch off the cat though, about two weeks back, on the left hand. It's nearly healed.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The cat's mine, she sleeps on my bed. My sister's allergic so she won't come near the place. She takes biotin for her hair, swears by it. Would biotin shrink his lump?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Biotin does nothing for a node. A lymph node swells when the body is fighting an infection. A cat scratch is a common reason.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): So is it cancer then? My aunt's started in the neck. Will I need a biopsy? How fast would you know?
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling it cancer. Most likely a reactive node. I can't fully rule out lymphoma from the chair, so we'll get a scan.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok. Ok. Umm, last year in student health they did bloods and said the white cells were borderline. They never repeated it. Does that change things?
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll note it. Any tablets.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing regular. I don't even take paracetemol.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I take sertaline myself, fifty milligrams, but that's for me. He won't go near it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0027] person_4 (NURSE): Err, I'll grab his obs. Temperature 36.7, pulse 88, blood pressure 118 over 76, sats 99 percent.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, on exam there's a right neck node just below the angle of the jaw, about 2 centimetres, mobile and non-tender. No other nodes. Throat clear, ears clear.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Two centimetres, is that huge? What if the scan is bad? Should I be getting rid of the cat? I'm really not able for this.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): No surgery today. Bloods today, full blood count and CRP, and an ultrasound of the neck. Back here in two weeks for the results.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks is ages. What if it grows, or I get a fever before that? Does the ultrasound hurt?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scan doesn't hurt. If the lump grows quickly, or you spike a fever, or the sweats come every night, come back sooner or go to emergency. Stay off the lymphoma pages tonight.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll watch him. I mind my own mother as well so I'm well used to checking for fevers. We'll be here in two weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, you know, hi, doctor, I came as soon as they called me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, come in and sit down. What brings you here today?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, it's my throat closing up. I thought I'd wait, but it hasn't gone.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll just record a few vital signs.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's it, just a little longer...
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: pulse is 108 beats a minute, pressure 92 over 62, oxygen saturation is 99 percent. And temperature 36.6, respiratory rate 16.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that normal?
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll interpret them after the examination. Since when exactly?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): It started yesterday.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more about it: how bad it gets, how often, and whether anything makes it better or worse.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): It comes and goes. I'd give it a four, out of ten. I mean, and I've been feeling faint as well, since yesterday.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain or recent illness at all?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not a single one.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, go on. Any rashes or skin problems otherwise?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No rashes.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any medical conditions I should know about?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I've always been fairly healthy.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): What line of work are you in?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a bus driver, so I sit for long hours.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who lives with you?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My partner and our baby.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me ask about allergies, anything at all?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Nickel. I come out in... well, a rash on my skin.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, do you take any regular medication?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing regular, um, no.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll need to examine you for this, it won't take long.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your lips are swollen, you have hives, you are wheezing and your pressure is low.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed. Right, here's what I'm thinking. I don't have a clear answer today: anaphylaxis is possible, and so is a severe allergic reaction.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with anaphylaxis do well once it's treated properly. Let me repeat that back to make sure. You've had your throat closing up, yesterday, and no chest pain or recent illness.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Correct.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I want monitoring done, that's for anaphylaxis. The result will help us decide whether anything more is needed. The treatment will be adrenaline, 0.5 milligrams, once now, single dose. It's for anaphylaxis. Lie flat with your legs raised, I am giving the injection now.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow. I'll also refer you to the emergency team.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the symptoms return, that's the point to come in urgently.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I, I understand.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, that's the plan. Do you want to ask me anything?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, I'll do that. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): All the best.

[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja, thank you, sister. Shame, she's been a bit miserable.

[SEG0004] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The school is fussing for a letter, but we've really come because her eye is red and sticky after the cold.
[SEG0005] person_4 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. My eye has been sticky.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sticky, right. Is it the one eye or both?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It began in the left, and then the right joined. Both are red now.
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): It feels horrid. I feel like a wet rag. I think I have overdone it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): A wet rag, so you're tired. Since the cold, hey?
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. And excuse me, I have a frog in my throat.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): That frog. Is the voice actually husky, or just a tickle?
[SEG0012] person_4 (PATIENT): It is husky, thank you.
[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had a cold last week. Runny nose, and that has finished. Err, I can't tell you the exact day the eye started. Maybe Wednesday, maybe Thursday.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the start date is foggy. Does the eye hurt her?
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): No. It is not painful.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does bright light bother her?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not that either.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever today? Hot, or shivery?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not really. She was warm while the cold was on her, not today.
[SEG0020] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, doctor. The file says Asthavant, two puffs of two hundred micrograms when she wheezes.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, sister, that's not what the box says. The pump from the chemist is a hundred micrograms. Still two puffs when she wheezes.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hmm. The file and the box don't agree on the strength, so I'm not going to lock a dose in. She's got asthma, ja?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ja. Asthma since she was small. We only use the pump for the wheeze, not every day.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And with the asthma, is she wheezing now?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No... well, sometimes. At night, a little.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sometimes at night, noted. Any blurred vision, or spots? And has she ever been in hospital with the asthma?
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): No. I can see quite well. At school I cannot hear myself think. The classroom is very loud. Also, my feet feel dead when I sit still.
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Never. No hospital for the asthma.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): The noise is just the classroom, I'm not calling that a hearing problem. I'll leave the feet for another day. Both conjunctivae are red, the left a bit more than the right, the lashes are crusted and sticky, the corneas look clear, and she doesn't flinch at the light.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, thinking it through. Sticky red eyes after a cold, no pain, clear corneas. This is most likely a viral conjunctivitis. An antibiotic is not going to hurry it.
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no drops?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): No antibiotic drops. Clean the lids with cooled boiled water and cotton wool, give her her own face cloth, wash hands, and don't share the towel. It may stay sticky a few days.
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The school won't take her without a note.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll write the letter for the school just now. She can go back tomorrow if she's up to it, as long as you keep the hygiene going.
[SEG0035] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We gave Panado, five mils, when the cold made her hot, but we stopped once that settled. Nothing in the eye.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good, leave the Panado stopped. If the eye turns painful, or the vision goes fuzzy, or it's not settling in four days, come back and I'll look again.
[SEG0037] person_4 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall tell my teacher.
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks. We'll do the cloth and the hands.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): I'll have the letter ready at the desk.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Off you go, don't fret.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Obs are done, I'll stay a tick in case the numbers come up.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. What's brought you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, it's this cough. Every morning. And I'm, I'm frightened it's something really bad.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. How long have you had it?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Years, honestly. Years. Err, worse when I get up, with this brown phlegm. Not loads.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's been clearing it into the sink since I started last spring. Same brown stuff.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I quit the fags last year, in the March. Twenty a day before that. Why's the cough still here if I stopped?
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quitting doesn't undo it overnight, I'm afraid. Any chest pain when you cough?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I keep checking with my hand, which is silly.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not silly. Weight, has that dropped?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No, steady. I was 78 kilos last time. And I put the little finger machine on at home, it said 93. Do I need hospital for 93?
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Those home ones drift. Just now on ours, oxygen saturation 97 percent, pulse 78, weight 78.4 kilograms.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): 97. Oh. So not hospital. Sorry, I spiral a bit.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Long smoking history, stopped last March, morning cough, brown phlegm, weight steady, no pain, clinic oxygen fine. That pattern is chronic bronchitis far more than anything nasty.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Is bronchitis COPD? Is COPD cancer? I know that's a daft question.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cancer. Err, COPD is narrowed airways after years of smoke, and the cough and phlegm is the bronchitis side. I won't call it COPD until we've measured you. I'm booking spirometry.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): What actually happens? Does the tube hurt?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): You blow hard down a tube, a few tries. No pain. They'll send you a slot.
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Can I add what I've noticed? Cut on his shin healed in five days, nice and clean. But he sleeps badly, up and pacing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Healed in five days means no slow-healing wounds, that's fine. Sleep I want to hear about.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't sleep badly. I sleep fine. She's, um, fussing. Once for the loo and I'm gone again.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Also the water tablet. He doesn't take it on Sundays. Blister pack doesn't lie.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No, not Sundays. Saturdays. I miss Saturdays at my daughter's. Sunday I always take it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Saturdays then, not Sundays. What strength is the water tablet?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): 2.5 milligrams every morning. They call it bendrofluazide. White, tiny. Except the Saturday.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bendroflumethiazide, yes, 2.5 mg once a morning, for the blood pressure. And the purple inhaler, still on that?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Two puffs, morning and night. I call it seratide, might be saying it wrong.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Seretide. Purple inhaler, fluticasone with salmeterol, two puffs twice daily. What about the blue one?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Salbutamol, the blue inhaler, when I'm wheezy. Maybe twice a week. Is that too much? Be straight with me.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twice a week's modest. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): My brother's on metformin, he's diabetic. My sister takes biotin for her hair and she wants me on it for the cough. Would it help, even a bit?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Biotin's hers, metformin's his. Not yours, and biotin won't shift this cough, so leave it. I'll note your brother's diabetes in the family history only.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I take a statin for my cholesterol. Nearly got written on his repeat once, so I'm saying it out loud.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stays off his list. The blood pressure, still ongoing?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, years. That's why the water tablet. You didn't check the pressure today, did you? Should you?
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): No blood pressure this morning. Weight, pulse and oxygen only.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Another day for that. Any fever?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood in the phlegm, ever?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Brown, not red. Brown isn't secret blood, is it? I need you to say.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It isn't. Old tarry phlegm looks brown. Fresh blood looks red or pink. Are you breathless?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit, on hills. Flat ground I'm okay if I go steady. That's the bad sign, isn't it?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): It fits, it doesn't prove disaster. Working impression, provisional, chronic bronchitis, and I can't exclude early COPD till the spirometry. If the numbers are down we might do a chest x-ray. Not ordering it today.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): So x-ray is only if. Spirometry is actually booked? What if there's a shadow and we've waited?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Spirometry is booked. I'm not expecting a shadow. No blood, steady weight, no pain. This is not how a lung cancer story usually starts.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Chemist said a pneumonia jab, and flu, because I smoked. Do I need both? When?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd advise both, pneumococcal and the yearly flu jab. You arrange them at the nurse clinic, I'm not injecting you now. Come back in three weeks for the spirometry result, the slot will be sent.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): And if something changes before that? And Saturdays, do I keep skipping the water tablet? Purple inhaler stays the same?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you cough blood, get much more breathless, or the phlegm changes sharply, come sooner, don't sit on it. Seretide stays two puffs twice a day. Take the 2.5 mg water tablet when you get to your daughter's, so Saturday isn't a miss.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. Uh, thanks. I'll try not to google it all night.

[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Does he go to school tomorrow?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly, yes. Milk, ice cream for sure, curd sometimes. Not with rice or chapati.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I weighed myself this morning, 62 kilos. Same as before, no loss.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No vomiting.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She sleeps badly, doctor. Half the night she is awake.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not true. I sleep fine. She worries more than I do.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any wound slow to heal?
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No. She cut her thumb last month, it healed in five days only. Normal.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, it closed up quick. Why, you are thinking sugar?
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which medicines?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Pantaprazole, 40 mg, every morning on empty stomach, for the acidity. Two years now.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does not take the tablet on Sundays. I have seen the strip.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, not Sunday. Sunday I take it, we have family lunch. It is Saturday I miss, when I go to the market. Sorry.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other tablet?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No other tablet. I left dairy for one week and the bloating was much less, then ice cream at my cousin's engagement brought it back the same evening. My cousin has coeliac, can I get that? Should I stop wheat?

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep a diet diary for two weeks. Write each meal and if bloating or loose motion came that day. Limit the milk and ice cream. Do not cut gluten.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks feels long. Can I come sooner if I get frightened? Any new tablet?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks, bring the diary and the blood report. No new tablet. Continue the pantaprazole and take the Saturday dose also.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The test is today itself? Do I fast? The needle is very painful, no?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): No fasting. Reception will book the blood test today. Small needle, few seconds.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok doctor. I will write the diary properly. Please make sure it is the coeliac test, I have been so worried.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I will sit with her and fill the diary.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Reception is just outside.

[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): CVS on Western. I'm not standing in a long line, just so you know.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): I'll flag it. And nobody's changing the Metformine, that stays.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. If you get swelling or you can't breathe after the cream, stop it and get seen, that would be a reaction. Otherwise I will see you in two weeks.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just get me the cream. I need to sleep.

Transcript (encounter 00523)
[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hi. Sorry, I'm a few minutes late, the lot out front was full.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oh, don't worry, that lot is a nightmare on Thursdays. And this rain, it was sunny an hour ago. Did you end up parking on the street?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Garage across the road. Eleven dollars.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ouch. Well, you're here now. Your chart says it's your diabetes check, the sugars have been creeping up. Is that how you see it?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. The numbers on my meter are higher lately.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How high are we talking, roughly? What do you see in the morning?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Around one-sixty. Used to be one-ten.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's a real change. Have you noticed anything in yourself, anything that feels different?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm thirsty a lot. More than normal.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thirstier than normal. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): About one month.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what about the bathroom, are you going more often?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Up at night to pee. Twice, sometimes three times.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twice or three times a night. Is that new as well, or have you always been a night-time person?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): New. I used to sleep straight through.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Got it. Any blurry vision, like you can't quite focus on the page?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Eyes are fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Remind me, when were you diagnosed with the type 2 diabetes?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Three years ago. And high cholesterol, same time.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, type 2 diabetes for three years, plus the high cholesterol. And you're managing with diet alone, no pills so far?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Just diet. The walks stopped when it got cold, though.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the diet. I'm always curious what people actually eat, not what they think they should say.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Lots of rice. Bread. My wife makes banana bread on Sundays.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Banana bread, I love banana bread, I won't hold that against you. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And alcohol, do you drink?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of beers on the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's moderate. Okay, let me check a few numbers. I'll take your blood pressure, then we'll put you on the scale.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure comes out at 134 over 82. A touch high, but I'd want it again before I worry. Step up here for me, please.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight is 94 kilograms. Last year you were 90, so a few kilos have crept on over the winter. Now, take your sock off, I want to look at your feet.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Which one?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Left first. I'm touching a few spots with this thin little thread, tell me when you feel it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Yep. Yep. Yeah, I feel that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, sensation in both feet is normal. And the pulses at the ankles are strong, so the circulation looks fine.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): That's good, right?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Very good. So here's my thinking. It looks like your blood sugar control is slipping, mostly from the winter routine, the extra rice and bread, and the walks stopping.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): So I need pills?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not yet. Let's get an accurate picture first. I'd like to order an HbA1c, which tells us the average of the last three months. We'll draw it today at the lab downstairs.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Is that all?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd also like a urine test for protein, since diabetes can affect the kidneys over the years. You can give that sample on your way out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, go back to walking, even twenty minutes after dinner, and try swapping half the rice for vegetables. Banana bread, one slice, not three.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): My wife won't like that.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell her it's doctor's orders. Let's meet again in two weeks, when the results are back, and talk about whether medicine makes sense.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Great. Take care of yourself, and if the rain stops, maybe skip the garage next time.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Thanks, doc.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Hello, doctor. I'm sorry, this is rather embarrassing. I've been leaking urine. Mainly when I cough or sneeze, but also when I can't get to the toilet in time.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please don't be embarrassed, it's very common, and very treatable. How long has this been happening?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I really couldn't say. It's crept up. A year? Two? I only noticed when I had to start wearing pads.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you leak?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Most days. A few drops on a cough. And if I get the urge, I have to run, and sometimes I don't make it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you pass urine in a day, and at night?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Eight, nine times in the day. And twice at night.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any burning, or blood in the urine? ~
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None of that. ~
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you taking?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Furosemide, 40 mg, in the morning, for my ankles. A blood pressure tablet, I couldn't tell you the name, it's a little pink one. And a vitamin.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the water tablet is 40 mg in the morning, and the pink blood-pressure tablet you can't name. What's the vitamin?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Vitamin D, I think, 800 units, once a day.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Any other conditions?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, and I've had four children.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink a lot of tea or coffee, or take any fizzy drinks? ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Four cups of tea in the morning, and I like a fizzy orange. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): That could be adding to it. Let me ask a few more questions. Do you ever feel that your bladder hasn't emptied? ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Sometimes. I'm up and down. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any constipation? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Now and then. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to check your urine today with a dipstick, to rule out infection. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd say what you describe, leaking on coughing and sneezing, and also an urgent need to go that you sometimes can't hold, is a mixture of stress and urge incontinence.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Two kinds? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's very common to have both, especially after childbirth and with age. ~
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): What can be done? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): First, pelvic floor exercises, squeezing the muscles you'd use to stop passing wind or urine, ten squeezes, three times a day.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I've heard of those. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): They work for most people if done regularly for three months. I'll also refer you to the continence physiotherapist, who will teach you properly.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cut down the tea, coffee and fizzy drinks, and don't drink too much in the evening. Keep a bladder diary for three days.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): What do I write? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): When you drink, what, how much, and when you pass urine, and any leaks. ~
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I can do that. ~
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in six weeks, with the diary.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_3 (NURSE): Hello, I'm Pat, the practice nurse. I'll weigh the baby and take her temperature before you see the doctor. ~
[SEG0002] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. She's been so unsettled. ~
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): Temperature 36.9, weight 8.4 kilos, heart rate 128.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Walsh. Who's this? ~
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Evie, she's ten months. It's her nappy rash, doctor. It won't clear, and nothing's working.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Waaah. ~
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has it been going on?
[SEG0008] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nearly three weeks, I'd say. It's red and raw, and now there are little spots round the edge.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where is it exactly?
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The whole nappy area, in the folds, and between her legs.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or has she seemed unwell?
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. She's feeding well, but she's grizzly when I change her.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blisters, or weeping?
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No blisters. A bit weepy in the creases.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you been putting on? ~
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Barrier cream, every change, and I've switched nappies twice. And I leave her bare for a bit each day. ~
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, as far as you know?
[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No allergies. She's had no reactions to anything.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has she had eczema, or any other skin conditions?
[SEG0020] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A little eczema on her cheeks.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has she had antibiotics recently? ~
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, for an ear infection, a fortnight ago. ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Lay her on the couch.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Waaah! ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a bright red rash across the groin and buttocks, with satellite red spots around the edges, and the skin folds are involved.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Is it thrush? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's what it looks like, a fungal nappy rash, but I can't rule out a bacterial infection on top.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What can I do? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to take a swab from the rash, to check, and I'd like to start an anti-fungal cream, clotrimazole, apply it three times a day for a week, after cleaning.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the barrier cream? ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep using it over the top, but not before the anti-fungal cream. ~
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Change her nappy often, clean with water and cotton wool, no wipes, and let the skin air dry.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the rash spreads, blisters, or she gets a fever, or if it's not better in a week, come back and see me.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Obs are done. Blood pressure's 148 over 86, heart rate 76. He wouldn't stand for a weight.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Creatinine's 168, eGFR's 38. He wasn't fasting. I'll hang about, it's quiet. My little one's got a cold so I swapped onto an early.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Can we just get on with it. I'm only here for the kidney check and I'm bloody tired.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yep. Type 2 diabetes and the kidney disease, that's the review. The tiredness —
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah I know. Tired for months. I nod off after lunch. And the knee, that's what's actually doing my head in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's the knee been?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Few weeks. I don't really...
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer than that. Two months, easy, he was limping before Easter. I've been staying at his place since then, so I see it.
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Was I? Anyway it aches. Worse at night.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): You getting something from the chemist for it?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Just the shop ibuprofin. Two tablets when it's bad. Not every day.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): What strength are they?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm the box says...
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): 200 each. He takes two, so 400, and some days he does that again at night. My sister's mad on biotin for her nails, keeps posting me bottles, but that's her thing not his.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so some days that's 400 twice, 800 all up. Any swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Oh, the parking ticket, it —
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I'm not puffed. Wee's fine too, no burning, before you go there.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any medicines?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry. He didn't eat. I took my own perindopril at six, not his, mine, and then we were running late.
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Don't start on breakfast. I'm not hungry mornings.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ramipril, still 5 milligrams every morning?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. The rampril. I don't miss that one.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): And metformin?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): 500 twice a day. With food, when there is food.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The evening one gets skipped. Three nights a week, easy.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Not three. One or two. I'm not counting them.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll call the metformin 500 milligrams twice a day and note we're not sure every dose goes in. Thinking it through, ibuprofen clamps the artery going into the kidney, the ramipril opens the one leaving, the filter pressure drops and the creatinine climbs. That's your 168 and the eGFR of 38, I reckon, not the diabetes suddenly chewing more filter. Diabetes does dull the nerves in the feet over the years, but that's a separate story and your feet aren't the problem today.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): So the rampril stays.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stays. Continue ramipril 5 milligrams each morning. Ibuprofen stops today, full stop. I'll put paracetamol on a script, one gram up to four times a day, for the knee.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Panadol. Fine.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nurse, can you take repeat bloods Thursday morning, creatinine and eGFR again. Ramipril after the test, not before.
[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning, yep. I'll book him at 8. No fasting needed.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If those numbers come back borderline we'll add a urine albumin creatinine ratio. Not ordering that today.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): More tests. Great.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if the knee hasn't settled in a fortnight, then a knee x-ray. Only if it hasn't.
[SEG0042] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He won't ice it. I've said.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ice it, and keep the knee moving gently, don't rest it the whole time. Still no nurofen.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a fortnight with the Thursday results. That's booked.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Fortnight. If I'm still standing.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Knee's not red and it's not hot. The bend's a bit short of full. That's enough for today.
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put Thursday at 8 in the book on the way out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Lord, the rain. The car park is a lake entirely. Anyway, it's the legs has me in, doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): The legs. What are they doing?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Cramps. Fierce ones in the calves, both of them, the left worse. Two months now. Of a night, nearly every night, and they wake me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long, did you say? And does anything ease them?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months, yeah. If I get up and stamp about, or stretch the foot up, they ease, but sure then the night is gone.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): And the terrier next door starts up then. White little yoke, barks at his own shadow.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's up on the landing with it most nights. I stay over a few nights in the spare room, so I hear her.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any swelling of the ankles or the calves?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. Grand in the daytime.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Redness or heat in either calf?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not red, not hot.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I'm not short of breath either.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waterworks or bowels, any trouble there?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Bowels grand, waterworks grand.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Operations in the past?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never had one. Of.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what tablets you're on.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Err. The water tablet, Mizartan for the pressure. I've high blood pressure this years. Metformine for me diabetes, and Omprazole for the acid.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The water tablet is Frusemide. Forty milligram, one in the morning, for the ankles. Every day, she doesn't miss it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): And Mizartan, the strength?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Eighty, I think. White box.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mizartan is eighty milligram, once in the morning. She's spot on with that.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformine dose?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformine, 500 milligram twice a day, with breakfast and with the tea.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the Omprazole?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Omprazole, twenty milligram, mornings. Five-ish years I've been on that one.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything from the shop besides?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Magnesium tablets. The girl in the shop said they're for cramps. I like that shop, they still say hello, not like the big place in town.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The magnesium is maybe four hundred milligram. I wouldn't swear to it. She takes it at night, most nights, though she misses the odd one.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly drink water. Three or four teas a day and a small glass with the tablets. My sister would drink a lake and be in the bathroom for it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Any alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked in me life. A small sherry at Christmas, that's all.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I used to walk miles in the post office. I'm retired out of that now. Don't walk much at all these days.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me read what the nurse wrote. Blood pressure one forty over seventy-seven. Pulse sixty-eight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I misread that. The pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. The sixty-eight was the pulse last time in March. Today's pulse is seventy-four.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your last pressure was one-forty, that was March too. Weight today is fifty-two kilograms.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Fifty-two. I was a stone heavier in the post office days. There was a canteen bun every Friday, that didn't help anyone.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've had a look at them. Soft both sides. No swelling, no redness. Pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, two months of fierce cramps in both calves at night, the left worse, they wake you, and walking or stretching eases them. No swelling, no redness, no chest pain, no shortness of breath. Frusemide 40 milligram, Mizartan 80, Metformine 500 twice a day, Omprazole 20, plus the shop magnesium. Very little water.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I was going to stop the water tablet today. Often that's what sets night cramps off.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The ankles come up fierce if she misses even a couple of days. The heart doctor told her to stay on it. And in March they said the potassium was a bit low.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. That changes it. We'll keep the Frusemide going. I won't stop it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I had thought of a magnesium blood level and an ECG on top. There's no chest pain, and the shop magnesium would muddy a level, so we'll leave those. Blood tests for the potassium this week. That's the plan.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I stay on the magnesium from the shop?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay on that one, but don't double it. And every night before bed, stretch the calves, the foot up towards you, hold it, both sides.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): And drink a bit more water. A glass with each meal, on top of the tea. Not a flood.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage a glass with the meal. My cousin swears by bananas, two a day, and she's still driving at eighty-six, fair play to her.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bananas are fine if you fancy them. I'm not starting a potassium tablet. My impression is the cramps are coming from the water tablet and not drinking enough, and the potassium may be low. That's provisional, mind, until we see the bloods.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will you want to see her after the bloods?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book back in with me in two weeks, when the results are in. They'll have the blood form for you outside.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand so. Two weeks, and I'll do the stretches. Mind yourself in that rain, doctor.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in. What is the problem.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, my right heel is paining badly. Since two months the first step in the morning is like a nail going in, and if I walk a little it eases itself. I think I've overdone it with the jogging.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which heel.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I got new shoes also, from our own shop, very stiff, and the shop is so noisy I can't hear myself think half the day.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left or right. Answer that.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Right side. Only the right heel. Sorry, when I get nervous I talk all around.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only the first steps, or the whole day.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): First steps are the worst, especially in these new stiff shoes. If I stand long in the shop it comes back a bit, not the whole day.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swelling or redness.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling, no redness. I checked every morning.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fall or twist.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No no, nothing like that. I run three to four km most mornings, then I am standing the whole day, I work in a footwear shop.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Night pain, yes or no.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Will this need an operation? My neighbour had some heel surgery and she was in plaster, I am really frightened.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I asked about night pain.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No. It does not wake me. Only the morning, and a little after long standing.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any tablets.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine 5 mg morning for the pressure, atorvastin 10 at night for the cholesterol, metformin 500 morning and night for the sugar. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, my mother sends it from Pune.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): You miss any of them.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, the night one, the cholesterol tablet, sometimes I forget. The others I take properly. Is that dangerous, doctor?
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take it every night. Do not skip. I will book a heel x-ray today, and you stop all running for six weeks.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): X-ray? Is it a crack? These shoes I started the same week the pain started, two months back, sole like a board. And if I stop running fully I will put on weight with the sugar, no?
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Same week as the stiff shoes, pain settles after a few steps, no injury, so I am cancelling the x-ray. No test, and no need to stop running fully.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me press. Tender just on the inner side of the right heel. I don't see any swelling.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yes, that exact spot. Is it something bad inside the bone?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is plantar fasciitis. Morning first-step pain, stiff new shoes, that tender spot. Not a fracture.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Plantar fasciitis, ok ok. What should I actually do? Kindly tell me the steps, I will forget, and can I still jog?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Calf and plantar stretches, morning and evening, hold twenty seconds, three times. Silicone heel insoles in the shoes. Jog on alternate days, keep it shorter than 4 km.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the stretch tear the heel? Our shop has gel insoles, are those ok? And should I stop the Ayurvedic powder?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): It will not tear. Gel heel cups are fine. Continue the powder and your usual tablets, they are not for this pain.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, my feet feel dead after standing, is that the nerve? I feel like a wet rag by closing time.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numb, pins and needles, or just tired.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Not numb. No pins. Just dead tired, like a wet rag. Sorry.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is fatigue from standing, not a nerve problem. Do the stretches and use the insoles. If it has not eased in three weeks, come back.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks, ok. If it gets worse before that, what to do? I saw ice on the internet and now I am more scared.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ice after standing is fine, ten minutes. If it gets worse, come earlier. Otherwise only if it has not eased in three weeks. No scan, no injection.

[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand so.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, have a seat. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I have had pain in the jaw when I chew, and I felt I ought to have it seen to.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Which side is it, and how long has it been bothering you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right side. It has been three weeks, umm, no, closer to five weeks. After a chewy meal I feel as though I have overdone it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the jaw click, or lock, or is it only an ache?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It clicks when I open wide. It does not lock, I am pleased to say.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to cut in. I live with him, we are partners. I have heard him grinding his teeth most nights for weeks.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not aware of that myself. I am sorry if it has been a nuisance at night.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think it through out loud. Pain on chewing, a click, and night grinding fits the jaw joint and the chewing muscles, and a cracked tooth can imitate it. I am not going to conclude this is arthritis today.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I would rather you did not rush to a label.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. I have felt quite well in myself, apart from being tired.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired how?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): By the evening I feel like a wet rag, if you will forgive the phrase. The days are rather long.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the click with every bite, or only when you open wide?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly with a wide opening, or with crusty bread. Not with every mouthful.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The grinding gets louder when work has been grim. Nearly every night lately, I would say.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does stress make the pain worse, or only the grinding?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The pain is worse when I am under pressure. At the open-plan office I cannot hear myself think, though that is the building noise and not my hearing.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. I will not treat that as an ear symptom. Any ear pain, or any swelling you have seen?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No ear pain, and no swelling that I have noticed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the ache?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Neurofen. I thought the tablets were two hundred milligrams, uh, but I checked the packet and they are four hundred. I take one by mouth when it is bad, perhaps twice a day.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else regular?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will have a feel. Open slowly. There is a click on the right as you open, and the muscle just in front of the ear is tender. There is no swelling, and you open about three fingers, which is acceptable.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a little tender there, yes. Some mornings I have a frog in my throat, though it clears once I have had tea.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): A rough voice, or pain in the throat?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a rough voice, for a few minutes. Nothing more than that.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also says his feet feel dead after standing about. I am not sure he means it medically.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I would not wish to mislead you. They are not numb. They are simply weary after a long day on my feet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that is fatigue rather than numbness. Any cough, wheeze, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): What is the work, in that open-plan office?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a conveyancing solicitor. The hours have been heavy this quarter, I am afraid.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We share a flat in Carlton, so I hear the night grinding more than he realises.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or, err, take a drink in the evenings?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I have a glass of wine with dinner, perhaps four nights a week.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is temporomandibular joint dysfunction driven by the night grinding. A dental cause is still possible, so I would like a dentist to exclude a tooth problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall arrange to see one. What should I do in the meantime?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): A soft diet for the next fortnight, no crusty bread and no steak, and a boil-and-bite mouth guard from the chemist at night until the dentist advises. Keep the neurofen at four hundred milligrams, up to twice a day, with food.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. That is very clear.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it has not eased in a fortnight, come back and see me. If the jaw locks or you develop a fever, do not wait, and reception can give you a dentist's name on the way out.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Must be two years. My cousin's wedding in Durban, there was this huge cake, and the DJ kept playing...
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, err, say that again? I was on the wrong tab.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): About two years for the pimples and the periods. And these dark hairs on my chin, shame.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you just run late, or do you miss whole months?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I miss them. Sometimes nothing for three months, then it comes heavy and the sheets are a write-off.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): The hair on the chin, when did that start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, my mum won't drop it. She's got sugar, been on insulin for years, she says I'm headed the same way. Even the parking marshal was...
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, I'm rambling. The hairs, I can't tell you when they started. They're just dark, and at the clothing shop where I work people stare.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. I can see a few coarse hairs on the chin, and comedones on both cheeks. Has the weight gone up?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, same two years, eight-ish kilos I reckon. They weighed me in the passage just now, 79.4. My varsity jeans are a whole story, hey.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the tummy, or have the bowels changed?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain, bowels are fine.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, no. Breathing is fine. I walk to the shop most days.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on? This list looks ancient.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine 5 milligrams in the morning, that's for the pressure. The cholesterol one at night, atorvastin 20. Sugar tablets, metforman 500 twice a day, for the sugar. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, half a teaspoon, my neighbour at the spice shop says it...
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on. Screen jumped. The cholesterol one, dose again?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): 20 milligrams at night. Amlodipine stays 5 in the morning. Nothing else from the chemist.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to butt in, doctor. Her mum's outside. She says the cut on the shin healed in five days, that she sleeps badly, and that she doesn't take the tablets on Sundays.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): That cut. Did it heal normally, or was it slow?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Normal, hey, five days and done, not slow. It's not Sundays, it's Saturdays I skip the cholesterol one, when I go through to my sister in Pietermaritzburg. The sleeping, mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saturdays then. I'm not putting the sleep down as a clear yes.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): For the note, the weight before she came through was 79.4 kilograms. Blood pressure today is 122 over 78, and the pulse was 76.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): 122 over 78, got it. Thanks, you can go.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Ok, I'll leave the file.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, spots, missed periods, chin hair, the weight. I'm thinking polycystic ovarian syndrome, provisional, not confirmed.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that serious? My friend had something and she couldn't...
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling it confirmed. I'm booking bloods, the hormones and a glucose, and a pelvic scan. I am not starting a contraceptive pill today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): The pill? I've never been on one. Umm, my friend says it helps the skin, but with the sugar tablets I don't know.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might look at a contraceptive pill if the bloods and the scan fit. Only then. Keep that Ayurvedic powder exactly as it is, and don't add anything new.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The powder's just in the morning. I don't know the real name, the writing's all faded.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the packet next time if you find it. Come back in six weeks and we'll go through the results. Reception will have the blood form and the scan date.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, ja. Parking out there took me round the block twice, the machine wouldn't take the card...
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks it is. Packet if you find it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, I'll try. Thanks, hey.

[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, have you had any drowsiness?

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing else aches.

[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take any prescribed or over-the-counter medicines?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm, I'm on Seretide inhaler, twice a day for my asthma. I mean, um, I'm on something called warf... warfarin, 3 milligrams, maybe, in the evening.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got the box or the prescription on you?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Actually, no, it's at home. Oral rehydration solution, after each loose stool.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the dose?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): It's 1 sachet. Hmm, I'd been on bisoprolol, not any more though, I stopped.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any inherited conditions that you know of in the family?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): My father has Parkinson's disease.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Hmm, I think I reacted to some antibiotic once, years ago. I don't remember which one, or what happened exactly.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about smoking?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): I have about eight cigarettes in a day.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing, I'm teetotal.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): How active are you?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about your eating.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): I drink a lot of tea and snack through the day.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything in your past medical history I should know?

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I can see asthma in your file as well. Have you had any surgical procedures?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, yes, I had an operation for a hernia, last spring.
[SEG0046] person_3 (NURSE): Here are the numbers, doctor. Temperature is 36.9 degrees, pressure 125 over 81, pulse 70, saturation 97 percent.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shall I start the examination?
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure thing.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Raise your arm for me.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): He is alert, drinking, with moist lips and a soft tummy.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed. So, based on the history and the examination, the most likely explanation is a mild stomach bug.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, is it dangerous, doctor?
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand the worry. At the moment I'd say it's a mild stomach bug, and we'll watch how it goes. So, to recap quickly. You've had vomiting once or twice for six months, moderate, and no no wet nappies or drowsiness.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, you know, yes, you've got it.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small, frequent sips of fluid and keep him off nursery for two days after it stops. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose. The thing that would worry me is if he stops drinking or becomes drowsy. If that happens, go to emergency.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): I know what to watch for.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again if he is not drinking.
[SEG0059] person_4 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Come by reception afterwards and I'll fix the appointment.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think we're done unless you have questions.
[SEG0061] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, I'll do that. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, look after yourself.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Madam, before you go in, vitals. Blood pressure is one thirty eight over eighty six, pulse seventy eight, temperature thirty six point seven, saturation ninety eight percent.

[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, come, sit. What is the problem today.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Lower back is paining, and the pain shoots down my left leg. It is there from 3 weeks.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Only while sitting, or all the time.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sitting only it gets worse. If I stand for a bit it eases. I think I've overdone it, that is all.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Please, I am not in the mood for a lecture.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Numbness or weakness in the legs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, not weak. But my feet feel dead, both feet, from about a week. And the whole day I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right leg paining?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Left only.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Trouble passing urine? Any change in motions?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough, chest pain, breathlessness?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Since yesterday there is a frog in my throat, that is separate. And that drilling outside, uh, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The throat started yesterday morning only. Back pain is why we came.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Current tablets. Names and doses.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipin five milligram in the morning for the pressure. Metformine 500 milligram morning and night, those are the sugar tablets.

[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, that powder she bought from the shop near the temple. I don't know what is in it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. So pressure, sugar, cholesterol, all ongoing. No new tablet from me today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank god. I am fed up.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): On the couch please. Straight leg raise.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh, slowly.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Left side, pain starts around 40 degrees. Right leg lifts fully, no pain. Tenderness on the left lower lumbar side. Ankle power is normal, no foot drop.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That was enough, it is hurting.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heels and toes. Walk.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Like this?
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heel and toe walking is normal.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She sits the whole day, accounts desk, hardly gets up.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, accounts, what to do, the work is like that.

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): No MRI now. Err, let's see, I am not concluding the exact cause without more. If it has not settled after physiotherapy, then we might think of a scan.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My colleague already gave exercises and I got worse.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stop those. Do not follow colleague exercises. I am booking physiotherapy, they will show you what to do.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. When.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Reception will fix the physio slot. Meanwhile get up every thirty minutes, do not sit for long stretches. Continue ibuprofin 400 milligram twice a day with food for one more week, then stop if the pain allows.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): One more week, fine. I just want to lie down.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And review?
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks. If the leg becomes weak, or if urine is not passing, come earlier, do not wait for six weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Can we go now.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Take the physio note from the nurse on your way out.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I will give you the physiotherapy request. Kindly wait two minutes at the desk.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right so, blood pressure is 118 over 74, and the pulse is 82. You're grand there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that high? I'm all over the place, I hardly slept with the scratching.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not high. Tell me about the scratching, in your own words.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this itch between my fingers, and around my waist where the jeans sit. I can't stop at it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And I'm at it too, and the small fella—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): He's three. Sorry, I talk over people when I'm nervous. He wakes clawing at his tummy.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright. How long has the itch been going on for you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Well I blamed a new washing powder at first. It didn't ease though.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And roughly how long?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): About three weeks. Maybe a bit more. It's desperate at night, I'm still going at two.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with it, or feeling fluish in yourself?
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was eating away, grand in herself. My da is on metforman for his sugar, I thought maybe this was a sugar rash.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. And I haven't diabetes. I'm not on any of that.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand. That metforman is his da's, not yours. Any allergy to creams or tablets?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0016] person_1 (NURSE): I'll say, when my own little fella had a dose of this last winter I was up to my eyes in washing. Fierce altogether.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itchy rash between the fingers and at the waist, worse at night, and the people at home itching with you, I'd say this is scabies. The mite burrows into the very top of the skin, and the itch is your body reacting to it, not the creature biting you all night.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh God. Are we dirty? I hoover every day. How did we get it?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): It is nothing to do with being dirty. It passes by close skin contact, it's very ordinary, and it does not mean the house is filthy.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): And the burrowing, does that mean it's in my blood? I'm sorry, I just keep asking.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): It stays in the surface of the skin. It does not get into the blood. The finger webs and the waistband are simply where it likes to sit.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): My wrists have been itchy maybe a fortnight. Not a patch on hers.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back to you. Itchy rash between the fingers and round the waist for about three weeks, worse at night, no fever, no allergies, and your partner and the three year old are scratching as well. That is the scabies pattern.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do we actually do? Do myself, my partner, and the small fella all need the cream? We're all in the one house. And do I ring the creche?
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, for you, your partner, and the child, all on the same night. I'll take you through it step by step.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Is five percent not very strong? I saw a one percent bottle online, permetrin or something.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): That one percent is a different product, not for this. You want the five percent cream. Lyclear is the name you'll see on the box.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): I can show you the putting on of it after, if that settles the nerves.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have a shower first and let the skin cool and dry. Then the cream goes on every inch from the jawline down, between the fingers, under the nails, the waist, the belly button, the soles of the feet, and the genitals. Don't skip the skin under rings.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not the face? What about him, he's only three, what about his face and hair?
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): He's three, so he gets the same as the two of you, jawline down. We only do the scalp and the face in babies under two, or if the head is itchy. Keep it out of the eyes and the mouth.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the face is grand on me anyway. How long does it stay on before a wash?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eight to twelve hours. Overnight is the handy way, then wash it off in the morning. You do the very same again seven days later, even if the itch is easing.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the duvet, she was half saying we should bin—
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say bin it. I said I didn't know. I trail off when I panic.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't bin a thing. Hot wash the clothes, the towels and the bedclothes from the last three days, at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, seal it in a bag for three days. The mite dies quickly once it's off the skin.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty. Right. What about the couch? And can I work tomorrow? I'm on the till in a cafe.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): No spray for the couch. Hoover it if you like, that's plenty. You can go to work the morning after the first treatment, once the cream is washed off. Ring the creche and let them know, and he can go back the day after he's treated.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been taking a ceterizine, ten milligrams, in the morning, from the chemist, for the itch. Do I stop that?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the cetirizine. It only dulls the itch, it does not kill the mite. The itch can hang on for two or three weeks after the cream has done its job, because the skin is still reacting.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two or three weeks after? What if it's still as bad? I won't cope.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the itch is still as bad three weeks after the second treatment, come back and I'll look again. No blood tests today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): And you're sure it's not eczema? My cousin had eczema something fierce. Sorry, more questions.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your cousin's eczema is not yours. Looking at the skin, it's dry and scratched between the fingers, with a few tiny burrow marks, and there's a faint rash along the waistband. No weeping, and no sign of cellulitis.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, do we do two nights together or do we wait the week? I get muddled.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): One night now, and once more in seven days. Not two nights running. The prescription will be at reception, enough permethrin for the three of you, two applications each. You'll be grand.
