[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. Mom, cane. Watch the rug.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. And thanks for not rushing me on the scale, my balance is still a whole project. We'll be out front if the desk wants the insurance card, it's the blue one, not the expired one.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, it's this itching. Between me fingers and around the waist. It's driving me mad.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's worse at night, I can't get a wink, and I'm not sure of the date, maybe after the holiday or...
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. How long.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): About three weeks, between the fingers and round the waist. Started as a small patch and then it spread.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Worse at night. Yes or no.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Fierce at night. I'm scratching till all hours.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone else in the house itching?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I got Eurax from the chemist, tried it a few days and stopped, did nothing, and I'm worried it's...
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone else. Partner. Children.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. Sorry. My partner's scratching as well, and the little fella, he's 4, itching at night too.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): I'll grab your readings. Blood pressure one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse seventy six, temperature thirty six point six.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Shivers?

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Face itchy? Scalp?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not the face or the scalp. Just the hands and the waist.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hands out. Waistband.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burrows between the fingers. Scratch marks along the waist. Face is clear.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it serious? I was googling at half four and I proper frightened myself.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looks like scabies. Common. We can clear it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Scabies, God. Will the child be scarred, is it in the mattress for...
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): No scarring. Mites die off the body in a couple of days.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So what do I put on? Is it safe? I've a hundred questions, sorry.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Permethrin five percent cream. Neck to toes, between the fingers, under the nails, waist, soles. Bedtime on, leave it 8 to 12 hours, wash off in the morning. Repeat in 7 days.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): If I put it on at nine, shower at seven, is that enough? I've to be in the creche early and I'm mortified.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's enough. Bedtime on, morning off.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. And, um, will it clash with me tablets? I'm on amlodopine five milligrams in the morning for the pressure, atorvastatin 20 at night for the cholesterol, and only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning from the health shop.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): No clash. Allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Partner and the four year old, same cream, same night. Neck down. Keep it out of the eyes and the mouth.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Even if they're not as bad as me? He won't sit still, he hates when I...
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Everyone. Same night. Or it circles back.
[SEG0037] person_3 (NURSE): I'll go through the washing, if you want.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Please, yeah. I'll mess it up otherwise.
[SEG0039] person_3 (NURSE): Hot wash sheets, towels, clothes from the last three days, 60 degrees. What won't wash, bag it 72 hours. Don't fumigate the sofa.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): And the teddy? He sleeps with it, I can't just...
[SEG0041] person_3 (NURSE): Bag the toys three days. Hot wash if they'll take it. No sharing towels.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Work after the first treatment, yes. Itch can linger 2 to 4 weeks. Don't use the cream every day.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): 2 to 4 weeks? I won't cope, is there a tablet for the night that won't...
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the itch hasn't eased in two weeks, come back. Chemist today for the permethrin.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh gosh, sorry we're late. I went to the wrong building and the parking garage was full, I circled forever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're here. Sit.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's him, not you. Why are you here?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Um. I wake up sweaty and shaky. It scares me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Pretty much. About three weeks now.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breakfast?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I skip it. Just coffee. I'm never hungry that early and then the morning's gone and...
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm her daughter, I stay with her. She takes the diabetes pills and goes right to the coffee. I've tried.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which pills?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformin and, uh, gliklazide. The gliklazide is 80 milligrams in the morning. I've had the type 2 about twelve years.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin dose?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I thought it was 500 twice a day. Wait, no, sorry, it's the thousand milligram tablets, twice a day.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Morning and dinner for that one. Gliklazide just once, before the coffee.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other diabetes medicine now?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped the Jardience in March. Ten milligrams. It had me up peeing all night.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): They talked about insulin and I never took it. I won't do needles. Is that bad? Are you going to make me?
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Chest pain with the shakes?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ever pass out?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She did get confused once. Last Tuesday morning she couldn't tell me the day. It passed after I got some juice in her.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't remember that. Was it a stroke? Am I going to get Parkinson's like her husband?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): One episode, cleared with juice. Fits a low sugar. Not a stroke.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): So the sugar's crashing? Do I stop metformin? Is gliklazide the problem? Should I throw it out?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Likely a low from the gliklazide on an empty stomach. Metformin stays.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): What if I'm at the store? What if I'm driving the car?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit down. Juice or glucose tabs. Don't drive till it settles.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I should check a number when she's sweaty?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Before the juice if you can.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pressure today is 136 over 74. Pulse 82.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): No tremor right now. Heart is regular. Skin's dry.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Is 136 awful? Is that a heart attack starting? Do I need a pressure pill?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not awful. No new pill.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering an A1c and a fasting glucose. Lab tomorrow morning, before you eat.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the needle big? Will it hurt? Do I have to fast for both of them?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small needle. Water only after midnight. Pills after the draw, with breakfast.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): What if I forget and drink coffee? I always drink coffee. I don't even think about it.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we move the fasting test. Don't drink it.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there. She walks right past the toast. Every single morning.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breakfast every day. Gliclazide with food. Not on an empty stomach.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Are you cutting the dose today? What if the shakes don't stop? When do I see you again?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cutting it today. Back in two weeks with the results. If a morning sugar is under 70, call sooner.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's only a wee lump. Left breast. I found it in the shower and it's not sore, so I doubt it's much.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The screen just jumped.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): A lump, left side. Couple of weeks back, in the shower. No pain in it. I wouldn't be losing sleep.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Desperate. The M50 was stopped dead and the hurling was on the radio, Limerick, and I only heard bits of it. My brother was texting the whole time, delighted.

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Tiny, like I said.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Often enough a lump like that is the breast tissue thickening where the hormones act on the little ducts, and they get a bit clogged. That's the body doing its ordinary work. It still has to be checked.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're saying it's nothing.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not. I can't rule out something more serious, painless or not. I'm referring you urgently to the breast clinic.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): They'll see you within two weeks, and they'll do the mammogram and the ultrasound up there. If the skin starts dimpling or you see blood from the nipple, don't sit on it, ring us the same day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is grand. Am I needing tablets?
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): No tablets from me. Any reactions to medicines before? A rash, swelling, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Maybe. Years back I came out in a rash. Could've been the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, once more? It flashed up a warning there.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): A rash. I never found out if it was the antibiotic or the painkiller. That's the height of it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): I'll send the referral through from the desk now so you're not waiting. Mind that rain on the way home.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, doctor. The number 19 sat behind a bin lorry and then I came in the wrong door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, Mr Hale. Have a seat. Were you rushing?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit. I was up the allotment at half six staking beans, and next door's cat was in the compost again. Filthy animal.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite a start. What did you come in for, though?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. Right. It's the waterworks. I'm up three or four times a night for a wee, the stream's gone weak, and I dribble after.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): So night-time trips, a poor stream, and dribbling at the end.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I stand there and it just trickles. Takes forever, and then there's a little bit more in the pants.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, did I even lock the shed. I keep seeing that fork left out in the rain, and if it rusts...
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry. Umm, I couldn't put a date on it, it's been months but it crept up, and I really don't know when it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. No clear start, then. Is the dribbling the same, or newer?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): The dribbling's the newer bit. Last few weeks. The getting up and the weak stream, that's the one that's been months.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Blood? God no. My brother, he had a thing with his...
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay with you a second, sorry. No blood that you've actually seen?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): None. Not once. I would have noticed, I'm sure.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burning or pain when you pass water?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No burning, no pain. It's just slow.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Through the day, are you rushing, or is it mainly the nights?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Mainly the nights. I do go more in the day than I used to, but I'm not dashing for it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the evening?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Tea. Always a pot while the news is on, 2 or 3 mugs, and another if the football's on. Can't drop the evening brew.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): That late fluid will keep waking you. It isn't the whole reason for a weak stream, but it piles on the night trips. Think of the bladder as a tank you're topping up at bedtime.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I did wonder. My dad was the same, ended up having the prostate out when he was about seventy. I sit there at night and I think of him.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, thank you. Medicines, what are you on just now?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Ramipril. Five milligrams, mornings, for the blood pressure. Been on it years. Nothing else, uh, far as I remember.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ever had a PSA, the prostate blood test?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): They did one at the hospital, three-ish years ago. They said it was borderline. I never got a number, and nobody chased me, so I let it lie.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline, and no figure. Alright. Thinking it through, weak stream, dribbling, up at night, in a chap your age, this is most likely the prostate enlarging in the ordinary benign way.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't properly exclude a cancer from the story alone, so I don't want to call it that, but it isn't what the pattern is shouting.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the bit I didn't want to say out loud. The cancer word.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. What I am going to do is book a PSA blood test and a urine sample, today. The urine is to look for blood we haven't seen and for infection. The PSA is the fresh prostate check.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I fill the pot here?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, before you go, if you can. Reception will hand you the bottle. I'll put both requests in now, so they're arranged, not a maybe.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the PSA's up?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we talk about what it means. It isn't a diagnosis on its own. There's also a tablet I want to start, called tamsulosin.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Never heard of it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four hundred micrograms, one capsule by mouth at night. It eases the muscle at the neck of the bladder so the stream often picks up. First few doses can make you light-headed if you stand up fast, more so with ramipril on board, so take it once you're in for the night.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Tamsolosin, right. Will it fight with the ramipril?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tamsulosin. Not a fight, but both can drop the pressure a little, so if you feel faint you sit down and you tell me. I'd like you on it starting tonight if the chemist has it. I'll send the prescription.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Alright. I'll try it. Nights are grim enough already.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): And ease off that evening tea. Half a mug, earlier if you can. Don't stop the ramipril.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Half a mug. The football will feel all wrong, but fine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels been alright, any change?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine. Clockwork. Sorry, I do rattle on about nothing.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright. I've felt your tummy, it's soft, and I can't feel the bladder. I'm leaving the prostate examination today, the blood test is the useful bit first.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Soft is good, is it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is. Come back and see me in about four weeks, results in hand, and we'll see if the tamsulosin suits you. Put it on the calendar so it doesn't drift.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, sorry we're late, doctor. The robot by the Spar packed up and the traffic was hectic.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come in. On the bed.
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Parking was a proper mission as well. I nearly left the car on the yellow line.
[SEG0004] person_3 (NURSE): Obs are done, doctor, if you want them.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Go ahead.
[SEG0006] person_3 (NURSE): Blood pressure one oh eight over sixty eight, pulse 88, temperature 36.8, oxygen 99 percent, respiratory rate 18.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. Why are you here.
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The coach at practice was going on about—
[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): My ankle's sore.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side.
[SEG0011] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right one. He twisted it yesterday at soccer practice.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): When exactly.
[SEG0014] person_4 (PATIENT): Um... I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yesterday afternoon. After school. He's twelve, grade seven.
[SEG0016] person_4 (PATIENT): It's uh heavy like a brick, and puffed up like a balloon, and then it just...
[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Swollen since last night. Quite puffy on the outside of the right ankle.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you stand on it.
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): Ja. But it bites when I put it down. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four steps on the right foot. I watched you. You managed.
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He limped from the car on that right foot, but he did walk. He walked off the field yesterday too.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Numb toes.
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ag, his spare sock is still in the— sorry.
[SEG0024] person_4 (PATIENT): No. Not numb. I don't think so.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever or shivers.
[SEG0026] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the knee sore. The shin.
[SEG0028] person_4 (PATIENT): No. Only the ankle.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): A pop when it went.
[SEG0030] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He didn't say anything about a pop. He just sat down.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicines. Any drug allergies.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No allergies at all. I gave him one Pannado this morning, five hundred milligrams, for the pain.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Asthma. Old fractures. Operations.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No asthma, no old breaks. He's never had an operation. Healthy child.
[SEG0036] person_3 (NURSE): Ice pack's ready when you want it, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): In a minute. Swelling over the lateral right ankle. No bruise.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tender just in front of the right lateral malleolus, not on the posterior edge. Medial side is not tender. Pulses in the right foot are fine, toes are pink and he moves them.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ottawa rules, out loud. Ankle pain, but he took weight yesterday and here, and there's no posterior malleolar tenderness either side. No x-ray today.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am not calling this a break. Working impression is a lateral ankle sprain. A small avulsion is not fully excluded, so it stays possible, but I will not conclude that now.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): No x-ray unless it worsens. If he cannot walk, or the swelling increases a lot, then an x-ray.
[SEG0042] person_4 (PATIENT): Saturday's game. Do I play. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): No soccer this week. Rest the ankle. Elevate it on a cushion. Ice wrapped in a cloth, ten minutes at a time, a few times today.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Pannado again tonight?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): If he needs it, another 500 mg this evening, with a bit of food. Maximum four doses in the day.
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if it's still fat on Monday?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back if it's not settling in three days. Earlier if he stops taking weight on it.

[SEG0001] person_3 (NURSE): Mr Hartley, I'm Chloe, the nurse. You came in with a wrist injury. Let me get your pulse and blood pressure. ~
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, my dear. I'm afraid I've been rather foolish. I fell off a ladder, cleaning the gutters.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): Pulse 88, blood pressure 144 over 86, temperature 36.7.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning, Mr Hartley. I'm Dr Naylor. Tell me what happened. ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was about eight feet up, and the ladder slipped, and I came down on my left hand, with my arm out.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was that?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): About two hours ago. And my wrist has swollen up, rather alarmingly.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How bad is the pain?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Severe when I move it. I can hardly turn my hand over.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you hit your head, or hurt anywhere else?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no head injury. My right knee is a bit sore, but nothing much.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): A little tingling in my thumb and index finger.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any medical problems?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure and an underactive thyroid.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And do you do anything which might affect healing, do you smoke?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up thirty years ago.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your wrist. Tell me when it hurts.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow! There. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): The wrist is swollen, with a visible bump, a deformity, on the back of it, it's very tender over the end of the radius, and the fingers are warm with a good pulse.
[SEG0021] person_3 (NURSE): His capillary refill is normal, doctor. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Chloe. Mr Hartley, this looks like a broken wrist, a fracture of the radius, called a Colles' fracture.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, bother. ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't be certain without an X-ray, and it could also involve a small bone in the wrist, so I'd like an X-ray of the wrist, and one of the knee.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I have something for the pain? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will give you something strong right away. ~
[SEG0027] person_3 (NURSE): I'll bring it now. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please keep the arm raised on a pillow, and don't eat or drink anything until the X-rays are done, in case you need it set.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need to be put back? ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly. If the bone has shifted, we'll set it under local anaesthetic, in the department. ~
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): How very modern. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chloe will take you through to radiology. If your fingers go cold, blue or numb, tell her at once.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I shall. Thank you. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hello, come in. Mind the step.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you for fitting us in, doctor.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course, please stay. It's helpful to have you here. Busy day out there?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): I mean, always is. The traffic coming in was terrible.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Start wherever you like, I'm listening.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): I've been dealing with a sudden painful cold leg.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has it been like this?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Around about a month, I think.
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): hm, I'd say more like about two months
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, so roughly one to two months. Is that right?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Uh, uh, I suppose so, yes.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, carry on. Is it there all the time or does it come and go?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): it happens a few times a day
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there anything else with it?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): It, It usually comes with not being able to move the foot. Oh, and numbness in the foot. That's been about the same, three weeks. The not being able to move the foot? That's been for one week.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, a few quick ones: fever, chest pain or recent injury?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing to to report there.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): How's your breathing otherwise?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Breathing's normal.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your bowels, any trouble?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Nothing unusual, you know, no.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, diclofenac. I get swelling of my lips.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about any past illnesses or ongoing conditions.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, an irregular heartbeat.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, right.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): I have acid reflux, for nearly five years
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so an irregular heartbeat is already on your record. We'll keep that in mind today. A few questions about your lifestyle now.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm a bus driver, so I sit for long hours. Not much, I mostly stay in these days. My partner and our baby.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): what's on your current medicine list?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day
[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, I think the last prescription for the metoprolol was 100 milligrams. We changed it at the last visit.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hm. Do you have the latest prescription with you?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I left it at home. I take omeprazole, once a day for the reflux.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what strength is that?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): 20 milligrams.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, did you ever have any procedures done?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Just my appendix taken out, when I was in my twenties.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's start with the basic checks.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, bear with me while this finishes...
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): okay: temperature 36.7, blood pressure 133 over 76, SpO2 99 percent on room air, heart rate 122.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): May I examine you now?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay, doctor.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): nearly finished here
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): The right leg is cold, pale and mottled, with no pulses at the groin or below.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's enough for me. From what you've told me and what I found, I think we're dealing with an acutely ischaemic leg at this stage. I can't rule out a deep vein thrombosis yet.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Is this permanent?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't promise yet, but most people with an acutely ischaemic leg do well once it's treated properly.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange an urgent CT angiogram for acute limb ischaemia. Let's use heparin, 5000 units, bolus now, single dose. That's for limb ischaemia. You need the vascular surgeons now, this is time critical. I think the vascular team should see you too. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose. I'll want another look straight away.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): good, thanks, I'll see you then
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): goodbye for now

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. I was told to come back, because my throat swab came back positive. The nurse phoned me yesterday.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, I've got the result here. Group A strep, a bacterial throat infection. How are you feeling now? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit better than at the weekend, but my throat is still very sore. And my glands are swollen. ~
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did it start? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Five days ago. Fever, headache, and a terrible throat. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any rash, or difficulty swallowing your saliva?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash. I can swallow, it just hurts.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Just paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your throat. Open wide. ~
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Ahh.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tonsils are red and swollen with white spots on both, and there are tender swollen glands under your jaw.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): It looks bad? ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's typical. I'd say this is strep throat, bacterial tonsillitis, as the swab confirms.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Can you give me something? ~
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'll prescribe penicillin V, 500 mg, four times a day, for ten days.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days? My friend had five. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): For strep throat, ten days is the full course, to clear it and prevent complications. Finish it all, even if you feel better in two. ~
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything about the antibiotic you'd like me to explain before we go on? ~
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's clear enough. ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pulse 82, temperature 37.6, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine. A mild temperature, as expected. Rest, drink plenty, and use paracetamol for the pain. Salt-water gargles help too.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I go to work? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay off until you've had two days of the antibiotic, and your fever has gone.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't swallow, drool, have a very stiff neck, or a one-sided swollen throat, come back at once.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in a week, if you're not completely better.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0006] person_4 (NURSE): Sister here. I did his vitals just now. Blood pressure one thirty eight over eighty four, pulse seventy two.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Seventy two, okay. Umm, how many times a night? Say it again, I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Three... no, four. Well, three to four times, mostly four, every night. It's been five months... ag, no, six months.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm his carer from the agency, I come evenings. I hear him up and down. Ag, and the load shedding last night was hectic, my shift got moved.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Six months. Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I've looked, hey, nothing red in the pan.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And burning, or pain, when you pass water?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No burning and no pain. But Doc, is this cancer? Am I going to need an operation? I lie there worrying half the night.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't call it cancer from sitting here. Err, hold on, the cursor jumped. Which tablets are you actually on?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): I've got high blood pressure. I take enalapril, ten milligrams every morning. I was on doxazosin too, two milligrams... no, four milligrams at night, but I stopped it in March. I was dizzy on it, but that's gone since I stopped.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He drinks tea in the evening as well, two or three mugs after supper. I keep telling him.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Two or three? Say that again, I was typing.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two or three mugs of tea, after supper, every evening.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, that late tea will have you up. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, no, no allergies. They offered me oxybutynin at the chemist but I never took it. I tried saw palmetto from the health shop, for a week... no, two weeks, then I stopped. It did nothing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): So you never started the oxybutynin. Is the stream weak in the daytime as well? Any leaking when you cough or laugh?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, it's weak in the day too, and I dribble in my underpants. No leaking when I cough. None of that.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): This sounds like an enlarged prostate slowing the flow. That's only provisional until the tests come back. I'm sending a PSA blood test and a urine test, you can do both at the lab today.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): If the PSA is high, does that mean cancer? Will I need a biopsy? How long do the results take? I'm really frightened, hey.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): A high PSA is not cancer on its own. We'll go through the number when it's back. I want to start you on tamsulosin, four hundred micrograms at night, for the stream.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Tamsolusin? Will I get dizzy and fall in the passage, like with the doxazosin? And must I give the tea up for good?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can drop the blood pressure a bit, so stand up slowly the first few nights. Cut the evening tea right down, you don't have to bin it forever. If you feel faint, skip the dose and phone the rooms.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll sort the tea, he forgets. Must I give that tablet with supper or at bedtime?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bedtime is fine. Sorry, the prescription screen is slow again. Come back in six weeks and we'll go over the results. Reception will book you.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks feels long. What if I can't pass water at all before then, or I see blood? Must I just wait? And will six weeks even show if the tablet works?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't pass water, or there's blood, or you get a fever, come straight in, don't wait. Otherwise we'll see you in six weeks. The tamsulosin usually needs a few weeks to settle in.
[SEG0032] person_4 (NURSE): I'll walk you to the lab just now for the blood and the urine bottle. The forms are printing.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, sister. Oh, Doc, my father had prostate trouble as well, not cancer, just the enlargement. Does that run in the family?

[SEG0001] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Doctor, it's my mother's legs. They've swollen up again, and she sits in the wheelchair all day now.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, I'm glad you came together. Mrs Pillai, can you tell me about the swelling?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Both my legs are swollen, from the feet to the knees.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you first notice it?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't remember. My daughter noticed it first.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I think it was around the festival, but I can't be sure. It might have been earlier.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is it worse at any time of day?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): In the evenings. By the morning it is a bit less.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there pain, redness or any warmth in the legs?
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, no redness. She says it just feels heavy.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does she have any health problems that we should know about?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has had heart failure for years, and high blood pressure.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is she taking her water tablet regularly?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I take the water tablet.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She does, mostly, but I only see her in the evenings. Her carer gives the morning ones, and she sometimes refuses.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And which water tablet is that, and what dose?
[SEG0017] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Furosemide, 40 milligrams, once in the morning.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any allergies to medicines, Mrs Pillai?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Penicillin. It gave me a rash once.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I'll note that. Is she short of breath lying flat?
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, she sleeps with two pillows as she always has.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to look at her legs and listen to her chest. Could you help me lift the footrest? ~
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, of course.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is pitting swelling of both lower legs up to the knees, and no redness.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it bad, doctor? ~
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's a fluid build-up. With her heart condition and sitting all day, that's the usual cause.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should we change her tablets? ~
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I would like to increase the furosemide to 40 milligrams twice a day, morning and early afternoon, and I'll prescribe that.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll make sure the carer knows. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please keep her legs raised when she is resting, and encourage her to take the tablets.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I would also like a blood test to check her kidneys and salts, since we are changing the dose.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When should we do that? ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Within the week. Then I'll see her again once the results are in. ~
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, come sit. I'll just do your vitals. Temperature is 37.8, blood pressure 132 over 84, pulse 86.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Shame, not bad hey. We sat at that robot by the mall forever, the N1 was crawling, I thought we'd miss you completely.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ja, traffic is hectic. My sister had a molar pulled in June and she sat in this same queue moaning the whole morning, proper drama.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he talked Proteas the whole drive. They collapsed again last night.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, don't start me. That bowling was rubbish. We were going to braai, then loadshedding hit, and the weather guy says it only cools down by Thursday.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, err, this screen has frozen on me again. Right. What's brought you in?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Doc, my cheek is swollen and the tooth is throbbing. It's been three days, since they put the crown on.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, uh, say that again? I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Throbbing toothache, right hand side, and the cheek has blown up. Three days now.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The dentist did the crown on Friday and then the rooms shut. He's away till next week, no locum, we phoned.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did the pain actually start? Same day as the crown?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, the receptionist said he's in Ballito with his family. The emergency dentist in town is fully booked, we tried twice this morning already.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): I heard that. I asked when the pain started. Friday, or later? Just say it again.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Sorry. Friday evening, same day as the crown, the top right one. Three days of this throb.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish? Hot, or shivery?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit warm, ja. Mild. Not shivery.
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature was 37.8 when I checked just now.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): How bad is the throb, out of ten?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The right one, about a seven. Worse at night, and if I chew on that side. I've been taking two Panados, the 500s, every six hours, and it just takes the edge off.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any trouble swallowing, or with your breathing?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing is fine, breathing is fine.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies? Penicillin in particular.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I've had penicillin before, no reaction.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes his blood pressure pill every morning, amlodipine, five milligrams. I pack the pill box.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, high blood pressure, about eight years. That's the only thing. Panados since Friday, no other tablets, and I'm not on blood thinners.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Eight years, ja, I'm putting that in. Sorry, the cursor jumped. Is it just this tooth, or the others as well?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Just that crowned one, top right. The others are fine, no pain there.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Open for me. Right cheek is swollen and tender when I press, and the gum around that crowned molar is red and puffy. I don't see any pus, and you open the jaw fully.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, it looks fatter in the morning. I was saying, the bakkie's battery nearly packed up, and the cricket was on, but I couldn't even watch.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He did the whole innings recap in the waiting room anyway. Bavuma this, Maharaj that. I just wanted a coffee.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): You have to admit that catch was lekker. And it's meant to be cooler by the weekend, if you believe the forecast. Eish.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mhm. I'm not with the cricket, this note won't save. This is an infection around the tooth that was crowned. The swelling is your body fighting the infection, fluid and immune cells in the tissue, that's why the cheek blows up, it's not the crown moving into your face.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late, doctor. The bus sat behind a lorry for ages and then I came in the wrong door.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, Mrs Keane. Catch your breath. We've got time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): My neighbour collared me on the path. She says bin the tablets, her sister had a funny turn on blood thinners and now she won't touch them.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. We'll leave the neighbour's sister out of it. What's worrying you today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, um, I'm worried about my warfarin. The chemist phoned yesterday and said my blood's too thin.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Worried about the warfarin, and they told you the blood's too thin. I'll bring the number up.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): I was awake half the night. Is it dangerous? Am I going to bleed?
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's not jump. You're on it for the atrial fibrillation, aren't you. What dose do you actually take?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, 4, no, it's 5 milligrams. Every evening, with my tea. I don't miss days.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So 5 mg each evening, taken regularly. This morning's INR is 4.6. We aim for between 2 and 3 with the fibrillation, so 4.6 is higher than we want.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): 4.6? That's awful, isn't it. Will I have a stroke if you cut it, or a bleed if you don't?
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair questions, and we'll get there. Any nosebleeds, black stools, or blood in the urine?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No nosebleeds, nothing black, and the wee looks normal.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bruising, or bleeding when you brush your teeth?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, a few bruises on my left arm this past week, where I caught the door. Gums don't bleed.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Two small bruises on the left forearm, superficial. Nothing that looks like a big bleed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): So I'm not bleeding inside? You'd tell me, wouldn't you.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): I would. I'm not going to conclude there's an internal bleed from two door bruises. A few ordinary things can send an INR up, and I'm not settling on one yet.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): They started me on an antibiotic. The out of hours doctor, for a chesty cough. Clarithromicin, I think that's how you say it.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Clarithromycin. What strength, and are you still on it?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): 500 milligrams, twice a day. Started Saturday. I've got two days left. The cough's nearly gone, just a tickle now.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. 500 mg twice daily, two days to go. That one can push the INR up. Have you changed what you eat, the green leafy things especially?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. My neighbour said spinach and broccoli stop the warfarin working, so I cut them out about a fortnight ago. I used to have greens most days.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the greens have been out for about a fortnight. Less of that vitamin K usually sends the INR up, same way the antibiotic does.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Last time at the clinic, maybe a month back, they said the INR was borderline. I can't remember the figure, just borderline. Is that the same as this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline then, and 4.6 now, so it's moved. I can't use a number you don't remember, so we'll stick with today's result.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): So what is it then? My liver? The flutter getting worse? Tell me straight.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not pinning this on your liver, and I'm not saying the fibrillation has got worse. Working impression only, the INR is up because of the clarithromycin and cutting out the greens.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): If it's the antibiotic, should I stop it? I don't want the cough back. And if you lower the warfarin, will I clot?
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Finish the antibiotic, it's only two days and the cough is settling. We won't stop the warfarin. Miss tonight and tomorrow, then take 4 mg every evening instead of 5.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): 4 milligrams, from Thursday? And the greens, do I start them again or keep off? I don't want to get it wrong.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): From Thursday, yes, 4 mg with your tea. Put the greens back the way you used to, most days. Not a huge plate all at once, and not none at all.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): What if I see more bruises, or my nose starts? Do I ring you or go to hospital? And when do you check the blood again?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): A small bruise, just note it. If the nose won't stop, or the stool goes black, or you feel faint, go to A&E. We'll repeat the INR in a week, and I want you back here the same day so we look at it together.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): A week. Alright. You'll write the 4 mg down, won't you? I get muddled when I'm nervous.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll write it down. Miss tonight and tomorrow, 4 mg every evening from Thursday, finish the clarithromycin, greens back to your old habit, and the INR with a review in a week.

[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. Pulse seventy-two. Weight fifty-two kilograms. Last time in March you were sixty-eight. Temperature thirty-eight point three.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The weight was intentional. I changed my diet after March, and I am not concerned about it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): That's what the thermometer reads, thirty-eight point three, so I'll chart it. Doctor won't be long.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello. Come through, both of you, that's quite all right. What brings you in today?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you for seeing me. I have come about a pain in my jaw when I chew. It has become rather troublesome.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain on chewing. Um, how long has it been, and where exactly do you feel it?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about three weeks. Well, actually it has been three weeks. It is an ache just in front of the ear, and the jaw clicks when I open. It is worse when I am stressed.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grinds his teeth as well. I hear it at night, most nights, for two or three weeks. He only half believes me.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I do believe you. I simply was not aware of the grinding until it was pointed out. I am sorry it disturbs you.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Pain with chewing, a click, grinding at night. I'm thinking this sits in the jaw joint rather than a tooth, err, the grinding loads the joint and the stress clamps the muscle. Does that match what you feel?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is a fair description. I have had no trouble with the teeth themselves.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Have you felt properly unwell? Any swelling you've noticed?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not had a fever, I have not felt unwell, and I have not noticed any swelling.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it lock at all, or is it only the click? Any earache, or a change in your hearing?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): It does not lock. I can open fully, it merely clicks. No earache, and my hearing is normal.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your chest, just briefly. Any cough, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing of that kind. My breathing is perfectly fine.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you taking for it? Any regular medicines?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Only paracetemol. One gram, um, four times a day, for the past week, for the jaw. I take nothing else regularly.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His sister keeps on about biotin. She takes high strength biotin herself, for her hair, and she wants him on it. I said no.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I have not taken her biotin, and I would not start it without your advice.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Quite right, that's hers, not yours, and it won't touch a jaw joint. Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no allergies that I am aware of.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me feel the joint. Open slowly for me... and again. Mm. There is a click in the left joint on opening. The muscle here is tender. I can't feel any swelling.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That is the tender place. It is uncomfortable, though I can bear it.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, the click, the pain on chewing, the grinding your partner hears and the tender muscle, and you don't feel ill. The chart says thirty-eight point three, a little warm, but there's no swelling and it isn't behaving like an abscess. My working impression is a temporomandibular joint problem driven by the grinding.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So you're not giving antibiotics? Does he need a scan?
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): No antibiotics. We might do a scan of the joint if it does not settle. I wouldn't book one today.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like a soft diet for a fortnight, no crusty bread, no chewing gum, and a soft mouth guard at night. The chemist will have one. It just cushions the grinding.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight, yes. Would soup and pasta be acceptable? I shall obtain the mouth guard today, if that is suitable.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Soup, yoghurt, pasta, eggs, all fine. Steer clear of steak. Guard at night only, not in the daytime.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I should mention that work is heavy at present. I am an accountant, and it is year-end, so avoiding stress is not straightforward. I will do my best.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): The stress will keep feeding the grinding, which is why the guard matters more than another tablet. Let's see you in two weeks, and we'll go from there.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. We will return in two weeks. I am grateful for the clear explanation.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure the guard actually gets worn. And no parcels of biotin from his sister.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ha. Leave the biotin with her. If the pain suddenly blows up, or you can't open the jaw at all, come back sooner, otherwise two weeks. Mind how you go.

[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): It's my knee. The right one. It's gone all swollen and, um... it just won't go down.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swollen right knee. How long has it been like that?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): About three weeks? Maybe a bit more. I noticed it after games, then it just stayed.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): After games, so you play sport?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Football. For school, and a Sunday team. Well, I did. I haven't, since it got bad.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Does it hurt, or is it mainly the swelling?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): It aches. Sort of a dull... it's worse when I go down the stairs.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): So a dull ache that's worse on the stairs. Anything in the mornings?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): It's really stiff when I wake up. Takes ages, like an hour, before I can bend it properly.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): An hour of stiffness. Does it ease as the day goes on?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, mostly. Then by evening it's sort of... tight again.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Have you noticed yourself limping?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit. My mum says I walk funny. I didn't really... I hadn't noticed.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's helpful, thank you. Any particular injury before it started? A fall, a twist?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I've been thinking about it and, no.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any fevers, or feeling hot and shivery?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. Just tired. Really tired, actually, which I thought was revision.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tired, yes, I'll note that. Have you had any redness or pain in your eyes?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No, my eyes are fine.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any tummy trouble? Loose stools, belly pain, blood?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing there. It's all normal.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. What medicines do you take?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 400 mg, when the knee's bad. Mum gave me it. And, um... the cetirizine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): The cetirizine, what's that for, and what dose?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): For my hay fever. 10 mg, once a day, in the spring and summer.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. And how often is the ibuprofen?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Most days now. Two, maybe, trailing off... it takes the edge off.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Do you have any allergies, to medicines or food?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Peanuts. My lips went puffy and itchy once, so now I just avoid them.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Peanuts, with puffy, itchy lips. I'll put that on your record. What else is in your medical history?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Eczema, since I was little. And acne, which is annoying. Um... and I get migraines.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Eczema, acne and migraines, plus the hay fever. Have you had any operations?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Tonsils out when I was six. And my appendix, two years ago.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Does anyone in the family have joint or skin conditions?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): My dad's got psoriasis. On his elbows, mostly. I don't think it's... I don't know if that's connected.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): It might well be useful to know, so thank you. Tell me about your day-to-day. School?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm in Year 12. Doing sciences. I'm trying to keep up but the knee gets in the way.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): And who do you live with, and what do you eat?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Mum and my little brother. And I'm vegetarian, have been since last year.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Great. Hop up on the couch, and I'll look at that knee.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your right knee is swollen and warm compared with the left. It bends only part of the way, and it's tender along the inner side.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now your numbers. Blood pressure is 112 over 68, and pulse is 78.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature is 37.4 degrees, oxygen is 99 percent, and weight is 62 kilograms.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all fine? I'm sorry, I always worry about the... yeah.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): No need to apologise. The numbers are fine, apart from the slightly warm temperature.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): So what is it? Is it something really bad?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me explain. This looks most like an inflammatory arthritis, where the lining of the joint gets irritated.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Arthritis? Like old people have?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Young people get it too. I can't rule out an infection in the joint yet, which is why we test.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): An infection? That sounds scary.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's less likely, given the lack of fever. But we check, to be safe.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. What tests?
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to order blood tests for inflammation, an ultrasound scan of the knee, and an X-ray as well.
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ultrasound is painless. And I'll arrange an eye check with our eye clinic, because this type of arthritis can quietly affect the eyes.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks with the results, and we'll decide treatment then.
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay. Can I keep taking the ibuprofen until then?
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, take it with food, and no more than you have been. We'll talk about the football after the tests.
[SEG0061] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry for not saying much.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): You've told me everything I needed, Imani. Take care, and say hello to your mum.

[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): So you had three doses, but no certificate. When, roughly? ~
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): In 2014, I think. The first, then a month later, then six months after. ~
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the right schedule. Have you had any symptoms, anything that's made you think of the liver?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Not exactly. I've been tired for about two weeks, but I've also been working nights, so, I can't say it means anything.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit of nausea last week, after a takeaway. It settled by itself.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the nausea has gone. Anything else you want to mention before we go on? ~
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really, I just want the form sorted, I'm that sort of person. ~

[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Latex, as a child. I got a rash on my hands from balloons. I haven't had it since, but I always wear nitrile now.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very useful, thank you. Any other health problems?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Eczema, mild.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you do at the moment?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a healthcare assistant, nights. I've been doing it for four years.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): A glass of wine on Fridays.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me check you. Pulse 68, blood pressure 114 over 70, temperature 36.5, oxygen 99 percent, breathing 14, weight 64 kilos.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Normal? ~
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): All normal. Look up for me.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): The whites of your eyes are a normal colour, no yellowing.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Good. ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now I'll press your tummy. Tell me if it's tender.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): It's fine. ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your abdomen is soft and not tender, and I can't feel an enlarged liver.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): That's reassuring. ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, no sign of any liver trouble. The tiredness is most likely the night shifts.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): That's what I thought. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me repeat the plan back. You had three doses in 2014, there's no certificate, and the form needs proof. The way to get it is a blood test. ~
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange a hepatitis B surface antibody blood test, and while we're at it, liver function tests.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the antibody is low? ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we'll discuss a booster. We'll decide on that when the results are back. ~
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): That makes sense. When will the result be ready? ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually within a week. Reception will text you. ~
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Perfect. Will I need to fast? ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, you can eat normally. ~
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Brilliant. ~
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in a week to go through the results and sign your form.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): That works. Monday's my start date, so it's tight, but fine. ~
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll put it on the form that the result is pending. ~
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. You've been very clear. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late. The garage was packed and that elevator just sat there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, I was behind too. Have a seat.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): I already grabbed his vitals if you want them.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yeah, go ahead.
[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Blood pressure one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse seventy two, oxygen ninety six percent. Weight a hundred and seventy four pounds.
[SEG0006] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother got diagnosed with emphysema last month. That's honestly why I booked this. It scared me.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll get to your brother. First, what's been going on with you?
[SEG0008] person_4 (PATIENT): Cough.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the cough been around?
[SEG0010] person_4 (PATIENT): Years.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Every morning he—
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, let him answer. Is it every morning?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does phlegm come up, or is it dry?
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Brown stuff.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Brown. Only mornings, or through the day?
[SEG0017] person_4 (PATIENT): Mornings.
[SEG0018] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It can hang on till lunch, but the bad part is the morning. Been like that since he smoked.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you quit?
[SEG0020] person_4 (PATIENT): Last year.
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): March, last year. Pack a day for about thirty years before that.
[SEG0022] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Umm, former smoker, about a thirty pack-year history, quit last March. I'm leaning toward chronic bronchitis, but I don't want to call COPD yet. Any chest pain?
[SEG0024] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever? You been feeling hot?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He never lets me check a temperature, I've tried—
[SEG0027] person_4 (PATIENT): Uh. Sometimes warm. Not really.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you been losing any?
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He eats like a horse. I cook a full dinner every night.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. Long morning cough, brown phlegm, weight steady, no chest pain, and the fever bit is muddy. You get short of breath?
[SEG0032] person_4 (PATIENT): Some.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Stairs, mostly. On the flat he's alright, he just slows down.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking? Any inhalers?
[SEG0035] person_4 (PATIENT): Purple one.
[SEG0036] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The purple inhaler, that's the Advair, morning and night. Plus the blue one when he's tight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Advair twice a day, and the blue rescue inhaler, that's albuterol, as needed. How often is the blue one?
[SEG0038] person_4 (PATIENT): Rarely.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Maybe once a week. And there's the little white pill, lisnopril, ten milligrams every morning, for his blood pressure. He's had high blood pressure for years.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Known high blood pressure, lisinopril ten milligrams daily. Let me listen.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a wheeze on the right. No crackles. Heart's regular, I don't hear a murmur.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Working impression is chronic bronchitis. COPD is still possible, the test will sort that. I'm ordering spirometry.
[SEG0043] person_3 (NURSE): Thursday morning is open for the breathing test if that works.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Book Thursday. Then I want you back in about three weeks to go over it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We can do Thursday.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay quit, that's the biggest thing you already did. You should also get the flu shot and the pneumonia vaccine, with this history. Pharmacy downstairs can give both.
[SEG0047] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he actually goes.
[SEG0048] person_4 (PATIENT): Fine.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): The brown phlegm in the morning fits that old smoker airway irritation, even a year after quitting. Err, not an emergency, but we shouldn't ignore it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His brother keeps telling him to try some tea thing. I told him no.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skip the tea. We'll let the spirometry talk. See you in three weeks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, I've got your obs. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse is 74. Your partner was filling me in out there while you were in the loo.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh she does that, she'll have told you the whole saga. We went round the block twice, the parking here is a nightmare. I nearly just went home.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grab a seat. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my jaw. It hurts when I chew, like a deep ache, and it clicks. Right side mostly.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok. When did the click start?
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, she got in first out there. She told me the clicking's been about three months, and that you've been getting headaches with it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months? No. Umm, the click started about three weeks ago, after that stupid deadline. And I haven't had headaches, she's the one with the migraines, she gets mixed up.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so I'm hearing three weeks from you and three months from her. I'll park the click as somewhere between three weeks and three months. You don't go along with the headache.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. The chewing pain, that's more like a fortnight. Toast is the worst, and it's heaps worse when I'm stressed, like this stocktake at the bookshop. On the weekend when I'm pottering it's milder.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the grinding, is that you noticing it or just her?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): She hears it at night, wakes her up. I'll give her that one, I do grind. I don't hear it myself, obviously.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and she keeps waving her metformin at me. Metforman, err, whatever, for her sugar, telling me to lay off the biscuits. I don't take any of her tablets.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's hers, we'll leave it right out of this. The stress and the clenching, that actually fits what the jaw joint does.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's been mad. We watched this terrible renovation show on the weekend too, I don't know why we bother with it. Anyway.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature, I feel fine in myself.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight shifted at all lately?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't think so. Maybe I've been snacking a bit more, hard to say, the jeans still fit. I wouldn't call it a change. Or maybe a tiny bit, I dunno.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing chesty. Lungs are good.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you been using for the pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nurofen. Four hundred milligrams when it's bad, maybe two or three times in a week, by mouth with food. My sister's mad on biotin gummies for her hair and she keeps offering them. I had one once to shut her up, did nothing, they're hers.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): So nurofen four hundred as you need it, not the biotin. Let me feel the joint.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Open slowly... yep, there's a click right over the joint on the right when you open, and the muscle here is tender. Left side is quiet, no click there.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the spot. Ow, sorry. She reckons I should give up crusty bread forever, she's dramatic.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this is the jaw joint, the temporomandibular joint, stirred up by the clenching and the grinding. The click is the little disc in there slipping a bit as you open. I don't reckon it's an infection, not without a fever. That's a working impression, I haven't proved it on a picture.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I need a scan then? My uncle waited ages for a knee scan, totally different, I know, he still brings it up at Christmas.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't scan this now, a picture wouldn't change the first step. Soft foods for a couple of weeks, nothing chewy, and a mouth guard at night. Start with one from the chemist. If you want a fitted one later your dentist can make it, but I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Soft food, soup and eggs, I can do that. Will the guard make me dribble? Sorry, dumb question.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most people settle with it after a few nights. Keep the nurofen as you have been, with food, and don't go over the packet dose. Try not to chew gum or pen lids, that loads the joint.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I do chew pen lids. Caught. Ok I'll stop.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back if it's not settling in about four weeks. Sooner if you can't open properly, or the pain goes sharp and constant.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks, yep. If I can't open I'll come in. Tell her the headaches were a false alarm, she'll hate being wrong.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you back out. I think she's still in the waiting room.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): And just so my note's straight, the click we're calling roughly three weeks to three months, and no headache as far as you're concerned. Look after the jaw.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late, doc. The robot by the Spar was out, and then the parking machine wouldn't take my card, so my wife had to dash back to the bakkie for coins.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Shame, it's been hectic this whole week with the school holidays. The N2 was bumper to bumper even at half past nine, and we just sat there.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, I know that feeling. So, what brings you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, it's the hand, really. The left one. It's still a bit weak, three months after that mild stroke, and I keep dropping things.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more about the weakness.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's not terrible, hey. I can still hold a cup of coffee, but buttons are a mission, and when I try to... um, when I try to open a jar my wife has to finish it. [SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the walking?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Walking is okay. I go to the shops most mornings, a bit slower than before, no stick, and I haven't fallen. My wife walks with me on the weekends down by the promenade, which is nice except when the wind...
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): ...comes off the sea and it's freezing. But ja, the legs feel steady enough for that.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about your speech? Any slurring, or words getting stuck?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Speech is fine now. For about ten days after the stroke I was slurring a bit, my brother said I sounded drunk, which was embarrassing at the braai, but that cleared. I don't slur anymore.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any headaches?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no headaches.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I'm not short of breath, even up the stairs at home. We live in a double storey in Plumstead, so the stairs are there every day, and I manage them fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the medicines, what are you actually taking?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Aspirin, a hundred milligrams, one in the morning with breakfast, the little cardio one from the chemist. Then atorvastin, sorry atorvastatin, forty milligrams at night for the cholesterol. And the blood pressure tablet, amlodopine, five milligrams, also in the morning.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine five milligrams every morning, and the statin at night. Any misses?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I miss them. My wife sets them out in one of those weekly boxes, Monday to Sunday, so if I forget she...
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): ...she notices before I leave for my walk. So pretty much every day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any other operations, or is the stroke the main thing in the history?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty two, that's the only operation. And the high blood pressure has been there for, ag, years and years, they picked it up at a work medical before I retired from the railways.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family side, anyone with strokes or heart trouble?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My older brother, Piet, he had a heart attack at fifty eight. He's fine now, lives in George. My dad died of old age, nothing like this.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink much?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped smoking in two thousand and ten, used to be about ten a day. Now I have a glass of red wine with supper, maybe four nights a week, not more. My wife is stricter than the doctor was, hey.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me just take your blood pressure while we talk. Arm out for me.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): This arm? The right one is easier, the left still feels funny when you squeeze it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, right arm is perfect. Sit quiet a second.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I was saying to my wife in the waiting room, the magazines are all from last year, and the sister at reception was so kind, she...
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's one thirty six over eighty two. Pulse is seventy four.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright? Last time at the clinic it was higher, like one fifty something, but that was when I was stressed after the hospital.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Today's reading is fine for where we are. Let me check the hand. Squeeze my fingers.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? I can do it but it feels softer on the left.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, left grip is a little weaker than the right. No droop of the face, and your speech sounds clear to me sitting here.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, because I keep worrying it's starting again, especially when I drop the teaspoon in the morning.

[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): So I don't need to panic every time I fumble a button.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Keep doing the hand exercises the physio showed you, little and often, and keep walking like you are.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): She said squeeze a soft ball, twenty times, three times a day. I've been a bit slack on the evenings if I'm watching the rugby, I'll be honest, the Stormers game just runs on.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try not to skip those. I'll book a cholesterol blood test, the lipids, so we can see if the 40 milligrams is enough.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): At the lab downstairs, or do I go to PathCare?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception will book it with PathCare, this week if they can. And we might do a scan of the head if the hand does not settle by the time I see you again.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): A scan. Like the one in the hospital? That machine was so loud I nearly...
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only if it hasn't improved. I'm not ordering it today. Come back and see me in six weeks, we'll look at the hand and the bloods together.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Should I bring my wife in next time? She remembers the dates better than I do, and she wanted to ask about...
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's welcome. If the weakness suddenly gets worse, or the speech goes funny again, or you can't walk properly, don't wait for that appointment, go to casualty.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Casualty at Groote Schuur, ja. I'll tell her. Thanks, doc, I feel a bit less wound up than when I walked in.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. See you in six weeks, Mr Dlamini. Drive safe.
