[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, the corridor is very noisy today, sorry about the wait.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ya, I can't hear myself think out there. And now I've got a frog in my throat, just nerves, it's nothing.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Shoes off please, we'll do the weight and the pressure.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Weight will be up only. I've overdone it with the laddoos at home, that's all, not a big problem.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Today you are 74.5 kilograms, height 158 centimetres. The file says 68 from last year, I'm not using that figure.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): See, sweets. It's fine, don't look so serious.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 122 over 78, pulse 84. Doctor will see you now.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm Dr. Mehta. Your mother fixed the visit, but what is actually bothering you?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing much. Pimples on the face, and the periods are a bit off. She fussed, I didn't want to come.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the periods off, exactly?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): They come every two months, sometimes three. Since two years. Normal for me only, I don't care.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the spots, how long now?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): From first year college, so three years. Cheeks and chin. Just spots, I'm not crying over them.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any coarse hair on the chin or the upper lip?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): A little on the chin. I thread it. Every girl has some, why the fuss?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): The weight, over how long has it climbed?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't say when it started. Sometime in college. Clothes are tight, so what. I've overdone the eating, finished.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Energy wise, any other feeling in the body?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): By evening I feel like a wet rag. And if I stand too long in the lab my feet feel dead. Ignore both, everyone gets that.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think aloud. Spots, late cycles, chin hair, weight up. This can be a polycystic ovary pattern, but I am not confirming it sitting here.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't make pimples into a disease, doctor.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): The ovary can put out a little extra male-type hormone, so acne, hair and irregular menses travel as a set. Tests decide it, not my guess.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. From my side it's still nothing.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): When the period does come, is the bleeding heavy, clots, soaking through pads?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Late, that's all. Not heavy.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about thirst, or passing urine much more than before?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll leave that fuzzy. On the tummy side, loose motions, constipation, pain as a regular thing?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Tummy is fine. Nothing like that.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you yourself have diabetes, or a thyroid problem?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only my mother has sugar, tablets for many years. I'm healthy.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Her diabetes still counts. With this weight I can't rule out an early sugar issue in you, even if you feel well. That sits separate from the ovary thought.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): She takes the medicine. I don't. Please, no tablets for me.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tablets or creams just now?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, adapaline gel last year, for two months, then I left it. Face was peeling. Nothing now.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so that gel is stopped, and I am not starting any hormone pill today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): My friend eats some pill for her skin. I don't want that.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): A combined pill, drospirenone with ethinylestradiol, can settle cycles and help acne. If these reports fit, we might start it at the next visit. Not now.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): We'll see. Maybe never.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Inflamed spots and blackheads on the cheeks and chin, and a few coarse hairs along the chin. May I check the abdomen?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Go ahead. You won't find anything.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft, no mass. So my working impression is possible polycystic ovary syndrome, and I still can't exclude a glucose problem with the gain and your mother's sugar.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Possible only. Don't write it in big letters on the file.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): For this ovary pattern, and to check the sugar side, I'll book fasting bloods, glucose, HbA1c, TSH, testosterone, LH and FSH, plus a pelvic ultrasound. Both are arranged, not a maybe.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles and a scan for pimples. If you insist.
[SEG0046] person_1 (NURSE): Fasting blood form is with you, and the scan is Thursday at eight in the morning. Come empty stomach, bloods that same morning. The slot is already booked.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday I have a practical. Does it have to be then?
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Kindly come Thursday itself, the test is fixed. If you are a little late we will still take you.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut back the laddoos, steady only, not a crash diet. That part sits with you.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. No promises. The canteen is right there.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks with both reports, and we decide about the pill then. If you feel badly unwell before that, call us, don't sit on it.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. My class is starting, I can go, no?

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, my chest has gone all tight and I think it's the pollen. I've got hay fever, you see, and I'm frightened it's turned into something worse.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, deep breath, you're in the right place. Tell me about the tightness. When did it start?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sunday. So four days ago. I was watching my nephew at a cricket match, sitting on the grass, and I could feel it creeping in.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how would you describe it? A band, a weight, a pinch?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Like someone's pulled a seat belt tight across the front of me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good picture. Is it there all the time, or does it come and go?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Comes and goes. Worse in the afternoon, and when I'm outside, especially near the park.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does anything take the edge off?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Coming indoors and sitting down helps a bit. But then I sit there and worry, which doesn't help.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's very human. Is it actually painful, or just tight?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. Just tight. Is that better or worse?
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Better, as far as I'm concerned. Now, you mentioned hay fever. How long have you had that?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, years and years. It's the same every summer. I'm used to that part, it's this chest thing that's new.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right. Let me ask about the rest of you. How are your tummy and bowels?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Nothing to report there.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, I keep thinking it's my heart. I lie awake doing the maths on how long I've got.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said it out loud. Let's check things properly rather than leave you doing sums in the dark. Can I listen to your chest?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, please. Do I need to take my top off?
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just lift it at the back. Breathe in and out through your mouth, nice and steady.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your chest is clear all the way down, and your throat looks completely normal.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Really? Nothing at all?
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing worrying on the listening side. I'll clip this little sensor on your finger as well.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Oxygen is 98 per cent and your pulse is 76. Both sit right where I'd want them.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): So it's not my heart.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to put a name on it yet, and I'd rather not guess. Think of your airways as a smoke alarm. Sometimes it's too sensitive and goes off when you've only made toast.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): So the pollen is the toast.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Possibly, but we can test it instead of assuming. I'd like to arrange a breathing test, spirometry, which you blow into a tube and it measures how well the air moves.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it hurt?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. It's mostly puffing like you're blowing out birthday candles, as hard as you can, three times.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage a birthday cake. When would that be?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse next door can book it before you leave. I'm not starting any tablets or inhalers today, so you aren't taking anything you don't need.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, actually. I get nervous about new pills.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. Meanwhile, check the pollen forecast in the morning, keep your bedroom window shut on high days, and change your clothes when you come in from outside.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Change my clothes. I never thought of that.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pollen hitchhikes on your sleeves like a stowaway. Little things like that can make the days easier.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. And I'll try not to google it tonight.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good plan. Googling at midnight is like asking a stranger for directions in a language you don't speak.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Ha. Right. Thank you, doctor, I feel less like I'm drowning.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Off you go, and enjoy the cricket from a deckchair next time.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon. Sit. What did you come for?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, ja, hi. Sorry, I'm a bit all over the place. I came to ask if I can drive again.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last seizure?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Two years, hey. No fits since then. I'm thirty four, epilepsy since I was twenty two, on the kepra.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): There's more. Tell him properly.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, she's going to make a thing of it. It wasn't a fit.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember a blank spell. I was tired, that's all. It was not a seizure.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tablets. Still on levetiracetam?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, levetirasetam, by mouth, seven fifty milligrams twice a day. Been on it five years.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Missed any?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, when we travelled to Durban for the wedding the bottle was in the other bag. I did miss some evenings.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was two or three evenings, and some mornings when he's late for deliveries he skips it as well.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not the mornings. Maybe two evenings, maybe three, I honestly don't know. Not a regular thing.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever at all.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough, tight chest, trouble breathing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine, hey.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight gone up or down?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nurse left the vitals. Pressure one oh six over seventy seven.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She said one oh nine over seventy seven. I heard her read it.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja. Chart is one oh nine over seventy seven. I misread it. Pulse seventy two. Weight seventy one kilograms today. Last time in March you were sixty eight kilos, and your last pressure was one forty over eighty eight.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one oh nine ok? Does the March one mean I'm worse? Can I drive the bakkie for work if it's only short trips, like to the robot and back?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Today's pressure is fine. I am not signing you fit to drive.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Why? Two years is two years. My boss will lose it. Will the medical aid even pay for a letter? What if I drive slow?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): That spell might have been a small seizure, an absence, or you were just tired and zoned out. I can't tell which. Missed tablets make a seizure more likely. No driving.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I take an extra tablet to catch up? Is one miss enough to cause it? Am I going backwards with the epilepsy?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): No extra tablets. Same seven fifty twice a day, every day, including when you travel. Epilepsy is still the diagnosis. Don't double up.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok ok. Do I need bloods? Does the needle hurt, how many tubes, will medical aid pay or must I pay cash?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): One blood test, a levetiracetam level. I'll book it. Come back in three weeks for the result.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks is hectic. What if I blank out again at work before that? Can my sister bring me sooner?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you have another blank spell, come straight in. Otherwise three weeks. No driving till I say, not even a short one.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring him. He lives with me and his sister since that Durban trip.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I live with them. It's alright. Must I bring the pill bottle? The chemist label is half rubbed off.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the bottle next time. She drives. You don't.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): If the level is low will you put the dose up? And kepra is the same as levetirasetam, right? I read it makes people angry. Am I getting angry? Sorry, too many questions.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Same drug. I'm not changing the dose today. You haven't said you're irritable, so leave the internet. We see the level first.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp. And if the test is normal can I get the driving letter then? Just now, or only after three weeks?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today, and not automatically. Three weeks, we look, then we talk about the form. Reception books the bloods and the visit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Shame, thanks. I'll try not to panic. Eish.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): In you come. I'll do the checks before Dr Keane sees you. Have a seat there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope I am not inconveniently early.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): You're grand, sure. My sister had a wicked dose of back pain after her little lad was born, and she couldn't sit in the car for months. Different story to yours, mind. Cuff's going on.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Blood pressure is 132 over 78, pulse 74, oxygen 98 percent. That's all fine. He won't be long.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Keane. Sorry, the morning list ran over a bit. What brings you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. I have a pain in my lower back which shoots down my right leg, from the back past the knee into the calf. It has been three weeks. Sitting at my desk brings it to seven out of ten, and walking eases it a little.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the pain reach the foot?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It stops in the calf, and it does not go into the toes.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): How did it start? Was there a lift, or did it just arrive?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I lifted a box of files at the office. The ache began that evening. Well, actually, the shooting began the next morning.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Umm. Are you taking any tablets for the pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Ibuprofin, four hundred milligrams, three times a day, by mouth, with food, for the past two weeks.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ibuprofen, four hundred milligrams three times a day for the pain. Grand.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That is correct.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has someone been at you about exercises?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A colleague at the office showed me some stretches. I have been doing them in the evenings, as she advised.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do they help at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I would not wish to say they have made a difference.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not had a fever.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any trouble passing water, or with the bowels, or numbness where you sit?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I have not weighed myself, so I cannot say.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you had the back imaged before, an x-ray or a scan?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): About two years ago they did an x-ray of the lower back. They said it was borderline, a bit of wear and tear. I was not given a figure.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Err, a borderline remark on an old x-ray isn't something I'd hang a diagnosis on. Lie back there. I'm going to lift the leg, a straight leg raise.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right leg, the pain comes on at about forty degrees. Left side is clear to seventy degrees, no pain. Tender over the lower lumbar spine, and no weakness in the foot that I can find.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I think is happening, thinking out loud, is the disc is irritating the nerve going down the right leg. Sitting tugs on that nerve, which is why it shoots. Your body isn't fighting an infection here, and the bone isn't the main event.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you for explaining it so carefully. Would a scan be required?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not for now. I won't order an MRI yet. If it hasn't settled with the physio, we might do a lumbar MRI then. I'll refer you to physiotherapy, and I'll see you back in six weeks.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep moving, don't sit for hours, carry on with the ibuprofen with food, and only do those stretches if they don't stir the pain. If the leg gets weak, or you cannot pass water, don't wait the six weeks, come straight in.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly, doctor. I shall follow that, and I will not ignore a change of that kind.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll send the physio form from the desk. Mind the step. My sister swears by her physio, but that's her own business.

[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah it's nothing really. The heel's a bit sore first thing, that's all. I'm only here because herself booked it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's making little of it. Every morning he's hobbling on the right heel, and I've seen it swollen.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): There's no swelling. It's not swollen. It's a sting for a few steps and then I'm walking like normal. I've just overdone it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Overdone it how? Tell me a bit more, in your own words.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Like there's a pebble stuck under the heel when I get out of the bed. Two steps of that and it's gone. It's two months, maybe. I couldn't tell you the date, sometime after the new year or before it, I've no notion.

[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he's still out running on it, which is pure mad, three times a week.

[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): New shoes in the mix at all?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeh, new runners. Fierce stiff. Got them, ah, I don't know when, a while back.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or pain shooting up the leg, or a sore back with it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I can't hear myself think in the shop some days but that's the radio blasting, not me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or did you twist it or stand on something?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no twist. I'm on my feet in the hardware shop all day, that's the job.

[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A pint at the weekend, that's it.

[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I had a bad do with penicillin myself years ago, but sure that's me, not him.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): What I think this is, is plantar fasciitis. The strong band under the sole tightens while you're asleep, so those first steps are you tugging on a bit of tissue that's irritated. It's the foot complaining about the load, not an infection and not a break.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through and sit yourself down. Sock and trainer off the sore foot if you can manage.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Cheers. It's the left ankle. I twisted it yesterday playing football.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Talk me through it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, five-a-side after college, I'm on a sports course, I'm 19. Pitch was soaking, I turned, foot stuck, and there was a pop. Not a crack. Dave thought it was hilarious till I started limping, typical.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight on it right after?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yeah, I limped off. I can still walk on it, it just hurts, quite bad when I walk. Bus was a nightmare, two changes.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has it swollen?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Came up last night, puffy on the outside. My sister said to strap it. She takes biotin for her hair and thinks she's a pharmacist. Honestly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave your sister's biotin. Any numbness in the toes?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bruising?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Not a proper bruise.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever, or feeling shivery?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I feel fine. Had a huge pizza after, which was probably stupid.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Notes say asthma. Still a problem?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Had it five-ish years. Blue inhaler's salbutermol, well, salbutamol, two puffs when I need it. Brown one's beclomethazone, no, beclometasone, two hundred micrograms twice a day.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does wheeze wake you at night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I've been training in the cold. Not most nights.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough with it?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain today?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never had one.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Taken anything for the ankle?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two tablets, five hundred milligrams each, this morning. My mum's on metformin for her diabetes, that's her, not me.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Couldn't, with the asthma, and coach would lose it. We train three times a week usually.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Tender over the outside ligament, not on the bone. Moderate swelling, and I can't see a proper bruise.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah the bone pressing is alright. Ow, front outside, that's the bit. I can feel your finger.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Foot pulses are good, toes pink, and sensation's intact where I'm touching. Pulse at the wrist is seventy-eight. Temperature's thirty-six point six degrees.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Is seventy-eight bad? I was sprinting in the warm-up, heart going mad, but that was before. And my uncle broke his ankle last year, they X-rayed him straight away.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Seventy-eight is a normal resting pulse. Your uncle's break is a different beast.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I know, I'm not him. Go on.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ottawa rules, thinking aloud. You've got malleolar-area pain. I'd want an X-ray if there was bone tenderness at the back or the tip of the lateral or medial malleolus, or if you couldn't take four steps both then and now. You're tender on the ligament, not the bone, and you walked in.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Four steps is easy. It throbs after, that's all. I walked from the waiting room fine, slowly.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I don't think this is a fracture. Working impression is a sprain of the lateral ligament, provisional.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): So I dodge the X-ray queue?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No X-ray today. If it worsens, if you can't weight bear, or the pain starts climbing, then we arrange an ankle X-ray.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Fair. What do I actually do with it, then? Saturday's a cup match, I'm on the wing, Dave will be unbearable if I cry off.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rest, elevate it when you sit, ice in a tea towel for about ten minutes a few times a day. No football this weekend, and no training until you're walking without a limp, a week at least. Paracetamol, up to two tablets four times a day. If you need more, ibuprofen four hundred milligrams with food up to three times a day.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ice, feet up, no wing wizardry, got it. Keep the inhalers going even if I'm not running?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, salbutamol when you need it, beclometasone twice a day, don't stop them. If it's not clearly better in a week, book back in.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, uh, that's been fine.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Neurologically, anything strange?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing odd there.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I mean, it's metoprolol, 50 milligrams, twice a day, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, how long has that been going on?
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): About two months. I mean, she takes glibenclamide, 5 milligrams, before breakfast. It's ramipril, 5 milligrams, every morning for my blood pressure, doctor.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I, I had amlodipine at one point, but I'm off it now.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Just my tonsils removed, as a teenager.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll have a glass of wine with dinner.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): How are your meals?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I grab fast food at lunch most days.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there someone at home?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband and I live above the shop.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No known allergies.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Actually, uh, I remember she had some kind of reaction to erythromycin before. I couldn't swear to it.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, maybe, but I don't recall it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, I'll note both of those. Are there any illnesses in your family?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had breast cancer. Let me think, my brother has epilepsy.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you have any chronic illnesses?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, heart failure. Diabetes, for nearly five years. Yes, high blood pressure. My family kept telling me to get it checked. I wasn't sure whether to come in at all, to be honest. I've got gout.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm, okay. Yes, heart failure and gout are known to us, good to have that clear.
[SEG0055] person_4 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 136 over 72, oxygen saturation is 94 percent, temperature 37.4, pulse is 94 beats a minute.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold that for a second.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): There is dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds at the right base.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, you can sit up again. From what you've told me and what I found, this is probably a pleural effusion needing a cause. We shouldn't forget a tumour. [SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any scans or blood work done already?
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): I did have a CT scan of the chest done last month, but the paper's at home.

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please don't wait if the symptoms get worse. That's when to be seen urgently. Let's review you after the scan. Anything else on your mind before you go?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): That's clear, thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): hey, come on back. weight today is 52 pounds. doctor will be right with you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): thanks. I'm her mom. parking was awful, we looped the garage forever.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): hi there. what's going on?
[SEG0004] person_4 (PATIENT): Bloating.
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): yeah, bloating and loose stools. umm three months, well actually more like four or five. not every day. mostly after milk and ice cream.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): uh, does the tummy hurt, or does it just feel puffy?
[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): Hurts.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): any weight loss? clothes getting loose?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no. she's eating, weight hasn't budged.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): throwing up? any fever?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no throwing up. no fever.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): okay. thinking out loud, this could be lactose intolerance, super common, or celiac disease if gluten is in the picture, or just a sensitive gut. I am not gonna pin it on one yet.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): did you try taking dairy out?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): we did, for a week. the bloating eased off. then ice cream at a birthday and it came right back.
[SEG0015] person_4 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): mm. so what I was gonna do is skip the labs, keep her off dairy for a month, maybe a lactase chew when she wants a treat.
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): well actually, hang on. my sister has celiac. and she gets loose stools after pasta too, not just milk. spaghetti, like twice.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): spaghetti bothers you?
[SEG0019] person_4 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): oh. err, that changes it. I'm not comfortable just calling this lactose and sending you home. I want a blood test for celiac, the tTG IgA and a total IgA. no need to fast. she has to keep eating some gluten or the test won't mean anything.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): so bread stays?
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): yes, normal amounts of gluten until the draw. she can skip the ice cream if it wrecks her stomach. and I want a diet diary for two weeks, foods and when the bloating or loose stools hit. bring it in.
[SEG0023] person_1 (NURSE): lab can draw her on the way out. today work?
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): yeah, book it today. I'll see you back in about three weeks, results and the diary.
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): three weeks. oh she's on a kids multivitamin, one gummy a day. we stopped those gas drops.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): keep the vitamin. which drops were they?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): umm symethicone. didn't help, so we quit.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): right. let me feel. belly's soft, no tenderness.
[SEG0029] person_4 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0030] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): her school play is friday, that's why I'm a little rushed.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll be quick. one small tube, she'll be fine.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. What brings you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's nothing much, I almost cancelled. After milk or ice cream my stomach gets bloated and the motions become loose.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, many months. Maybe four five months. Not daily, only when I take those. Very minor.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss over these months?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No no. Weight is the same only. People at work even say I have put on a bit from the canteen.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or blood in the stool?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, the chocolate ice cream from the parlour near my office is the worst. Half a cup and by evening I am bloated.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): I heard that about the ice cream. I was asking if you get fever, or any blood in the motions.
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, no fever, no blood also. Just loose, two three times, then it settles. Been like this these four five months, nothing serious.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cramping pain with it?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): A little mild cramp, that's all. I don't take anything for it, I just carry on.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you try keeping off the milk and ice cream?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Ya, for these four five months, one week I stopped both. Stomach was much better. Then Sunday I had kulfi at my cousin's and by night it was back. So I can manage, see.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, better that one week without dairy, and kulfi brought it back. Does roti or wheat trouble you?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Roti every day, no problem. Only the milk things. Curd a little also, but ice cream is the main one.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting with these episodes?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Never. I eat fine otherwise.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do the loose motions wake you at night?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Daytime only. Sleep is perfectly okay, I am not bothered.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking nowadays?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Only pantoprazol, the panto 40, one tablet in the morning, for my acidity since long. If the motions are more I take some ORS, not every day. Nothing else.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): So pantoprazole 40 milligrams each morning for the acidity, ORS only when the motions are worse. On pressing, the tummy is soft, a little distended, no tenderness. This may be trouble handling the lactose in milk and ice cream, though I can't rule out coeliac, even with roti sitting fine and no weight loss.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Coeliac sounds too big, doctor. I told you it's nothing only.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still, I'll book a blood test for coeliac today. Kindly keep eating your wheat till that test, don't cut the roti. And keep a diet diary for two weeks, what you eat and when the bloating or loose motions come.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): A diary and all. Okay, if you insist. Two weeks is long but I'll try.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks with the report and the diary. Till then keep the milk and ice cream low, and continue the pantoprazole the way you are taking it.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on through. What's going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, so, it's a mole on my back. My husband swears the color changed, like one side went darker, and he's been pointing at it every night, and I finally came in because I can't twist around and see it myself.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which side?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Left upper back, right by the shoulder blade. He noticed it after the lake, err, that trip was three weeks ago Saturday. It used to be just a flat brown freckle we'd ignored for years, or at least that's what he tells me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bleed?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, one time. Last Tuesday in the shower there was a little smear on the towel, I dabbed it with a tissue, it stopped in like a minute, and it has not bled since.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hurt?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crust on it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Itch?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really. I notice it when my shirt rubs in the truck, but I can't say if that's an itch or just me worrying at it.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other moles changing, or anything else on the skin?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else. I went over my arms, my chest, even my legs with a hand mirror last night, and it all looks the same as always to me.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bad sunburns as a kid?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, constantly. Every July at the shore I'd blister across both shoulders and peel for a week, and my mom thought sunscreen was optional, so I just cooked out there from breakfast until dark.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ongoing illnesses?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Hypertension. About eight years now. I take lisinopral, uh, lisinopril, twenty milligrams once a day for it. I almost said ten, but they raised it, it's been the twenty the whole last two years.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Penicillin, sulfa, I've had both for dental stuff, no rash, no swelling, nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Not on the job either, and I'm a landscaper, so I'm hauling mulch and stone all day.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leg swelling? Dizziness?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. And dizziness, not that either. No... well, sometimes, if I stand up too fast, the room goes a little gray for a second and then it's gone.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shirt up. I'll look.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Sorry about the pen circle, my husband did that this morning so I wouldn't point you at the wrong spot, and the ink might've smeared on the drive.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left upper back. About 8 millimeters. Asymmetric, border irregular, brown and black. No bleed and no ulcer today.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. My dad had a melanoma cut off his forearm at sixty-two, and ever since my husband said the color shifted I've been up at night reading about that, which I know isn't helpful.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can't settle it in this room. Atypical mole, and melanoma stays on the list with the color change, the one bleed, and that burn history.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Do you take it off today? I cleared the afternoon, though I didn't exactly tell the crew, they're mid-job and short a guy.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. I'm referring you to dermatology. They'll book the visit.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it bleeds in the shower again while I'm waiting on them? I don't want to just sit on it if the towel's pink.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. if it bleeds again before dermatology sees you, come back. We might do a skin biopsy then, only if that happens.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I'll leave it alone and I'll go when they call. Thanks.

[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): The car was hot. And I don't like those chairs.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's this been going?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Six weeks. It faded for a couple of days, then came straight back.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): It wakes me up. I scratch and scratch. Will I have to have a needle? Is that bad?

[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Mostly just dry and she picks at it.

[SEG0017] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough. Breathing's been fine, she was tearing around the park yesterday.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anyone at home with asthma, or eczema?
[SEG0019] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her dad's had asthma since he was a kid. I get a bit of hay fever in spring, nothing else.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): So will I get daddy's asthma? Is the itchy thing forever?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not automatically, sweetheart. They can run in families, but lots of kids only get the skin part. What creams have you been using?
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A big white tub a few times a day, and a little yellow tube at night that the chemist gave us. I can never remember the names, we just go by the colour.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know if the yellow one was a steroid?
[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, someone said hydrocortazone, the one percent one, but I wouldn't swear to it. Might be wrong.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): The yellow one stings a bit. Do I have to keep using it? What if it stings worse?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): We can stop anything that stings. Any allergies to creams or medicines?
[SEG0027] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that. She's never reacted to a medicine.
[SEG0028] person_4 (NURSE): She was picking at both elbows in the waiting room. I left the skin alone, didn't put anything on.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good to know. Mia, can I have a look at your knees and elbows? I won't do anything that hurts.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. But will it hurt? I don't want it to hurt.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Just eyes, no poking. Skin behind both knees and both elbow creases is dry and a bit thickened, with scratch marks. No weeping, and it's not hot.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I look weird? Are they gonna laugh at me at kindy?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): You don't look weird at all. From those dry itchy patches in the creases, I'd call this eczema, atopic dermatitis. That's my working impression, not a final stamp.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. So do we chuck the yellow tube? And is the white tub even doing anything? Google's been no help.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the yellow tube, and stop the white tub too, we don't know what's in it. I'll prescribe methylprednisolone aceponate ointment, zero point one percent, that's Advantan, a thin layer once a day on the patches only, for two weeks. And QV cream, the plain moisturiser, at least three times a day, plus straight after a bath. Steroid first, give it a minute, then the QV.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Three times? That's heaps. Will the new cream sting me?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ointment's usually kinder on cracked skin than a cream is. Thin smear only. If a patch gets redder, or hot, or starts weeping, stop and ring the clinic.
[SEG0038] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Baths though? A mum at playgroup reckons no soap and oats in the water. Is that actually right?

[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still swim? What if the pool makes it bad?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swimming's fine. Rinse the chlorine off and put the moisturiser on after, or the skin will dry out.
[SEG0042] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should we do a blood test, or those allergy pricks? Her cousin had the whole lot.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the patches aren't settling after the two weeks of ointment, we can look at allergy testing then. No pricks this visit.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And follow up, do we come back only if it's worse?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks either way so I can check the skin. Reception will book it as you leave.
[SEG0046] person_4 (NURSE): I'll walk you out and get that two week review in the book. You were brave, Mia.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Ok. Bye. It still itches.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the jaw. It clicks, and it aches when I chew. Been about two months. But it's not bad.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): You said about two months. Can you place it any tighter than that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Work's mad. I'm an accountant, tax season, everyone's shouting. I just clench.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eish, that sounds heavy. Coming back to the jaw though, when did the ache actually begin?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, I can't say the day. I had a few weeks in my head. Well actually no, more like two months, when the audits kicked off. I just ignored it.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the click there all the time, or mainly with food?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly when I chew. Steak's a write-off, I just leave it. Left side, I think. Minor stuff.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And does stress make it worse?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, deadlines make it tighter. But everyone's stressed. It's not a thing.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does your partner notice anything at night?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): She says I grind my teeth, keeps her up. I don't feel a thing, so maybe she's exaggerating.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you felt hot and unwell with this?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The click's louder in the morning, then it eases off. That's all.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Louder in the morning. I did ask about fever though. Have you had one?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I'm not ill.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Pain in the ear?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. Ear's fine. People make a fuss.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Panado. I take four, wait no, two, when it's annoying, which is hardly ever. Chemist also sold me those yellow muscle tablets, can't remember what they're called. Took like three, they made me dozy, so I stopped.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything you take every day? Pressure tablets, that sort of thing?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't do chronic pills. I'm healthy.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry folks, I still need his obs. I got pulled away earlier.
[SEG0030] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature is 36.4, blood pressure 128 over 76, pulse 74. All decent.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Click on the left as you open, and the muscle just in front of the ear is sore when I press. No swelling, and you open fully, no problem.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I reckon is the little disc in the jaw joint slips when you chew or clench, that's your click, and the muscles are overworking from the grinding. Your body's not fighting an infection, the joint's just overloaded.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): It's not dangerous, but it is real. Soft foods for a few weeks, hey, no steak, no biltong, cut everything small. And a mouth guard at night so the teeth stop grinding on each other.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): A thin one from the dentist, just while you sleep. I'll write them a note today. Also skip chewing gum, and when you catch yourself clenching at the desk, just let the jaw hang.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the guard and the soft food haven't sorted it in six weeks, we might do an x-ray of the jaw. I won't book that now.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks anyway, whether or not, so we know where we stand. Reception will book it on your way out.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Fine. And the Panado?
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Panado's fine, two tablets when you need them, don't go over eight tablets in a day. Leave those yellow ones, we don't know what they are.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sharp. I'll tell her she was half right. Cheers.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, sorry we're late. The robot by Checkers packed up and we sat in the queue for ages.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ag, that's fine, you're here now. Have a seat, both of you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm shattered. I hardly slept.
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been grumpy the whole morning, shame. Sorry about the mood.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): No stress. What brings you in today?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): My cheek's all swollen and the tooth won't stop throbbing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which side, and how long's that been going?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Right bottom one. Three days. It's the tooth with the crown.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And when did they put the crown on?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. I honestly don't know.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her dentist's away in Durban this whole week, so we couldn't get seen there.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. The pain, is it a throb or a sharp jab?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Throbbing. The whole time. It's bad. Keeps me awake.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the swelling got bigger since yesterday?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not sure then, we'll leave that. Any bad taste, like pus coming out?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. I can't say.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you felt feverish?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja. A bit warm since yesterday. Mild, nothing hectic.
[SEG0020] person_4 (NURSE): Obs are in, doctor. Temperature 37.8, pulse 96, blood pressure 128 over 82, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta. Any trouble swallowing?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Swallowing's fine.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): And breathing, any difficulty there?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine. I'm just sore and irritable, can we move on.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, wheeze, other chest stuff?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for the pain?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Panado. Paracetamol. Two of the 500 milligram tablets every six hours. Takes the edge off, only a little.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had a Brufen as well, yesterday.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, one 400 milligram ibuprofen, then my stomach burned, so I stopped. Not again.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, penicillin, anything?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diabetes, high blood pressure, heart problems, anything ongoing?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She teaches grade four at the primary, she had to phone them this morning.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, I'm a teacher. I should be in class. Can we just get on with it, I'm exhausted.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja. Let me look. Open slowly for me.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Ow. That's the one.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right cheek is swollen, warm, tender when I press. No pointing abscess. Mouth opening is limited. Throat is clear and the airway looks fine. There's a gland up under the right jaw.
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Well it hurts if you press it, obviously.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, this is a dental infection, probably an early abscess around that crowned tooth. That's my working impression. Swelling plus the mild fever fits, though I can't lock it down without a dental x-ray.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): Dentist's not even in town. So now what?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll prescribe amoxicillin, by mouth, 500 mg, three times a day, for five days.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Amoxacillin. Okay. Does that actually fix it?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): It should settle the infection in the cheek. It won't sort the tooth. See the dentist the day he's back.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the paracetamol, same dose you've been using. Don't restart the ibuprofen, your stomach didn't like it.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Warm salt water rinses, gently, a few times a day. Soft food, and don't poke at the gum.
[SEG0049] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What if it gets worse in the night, though?
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If swallowing becomes difficult, or you battle to breathe, or the swelling jumps, go to casualty. Don't wait.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back if you're not better by Friday.
[SEG0052] person_4 (NURSE): I'll get the script printed at reception so you can fetch it on the way out.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Good. I need to lie down. This has wiped me out.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Obs are done. Blood pressure is 142 over 86, pulse 78, oxygen sat 96 percent. Weight today is 81 kilos.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. In you come. What's the problem?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. The cough.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Every morning there's this brown phlegm and it's been going forever and I'm worried sick about it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Dad had the lung cancer. I keep thinking that's me. Is it cancer?
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): One thing at a time. The cough, every morning?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Soon as I'm awake. Err I hack away for about ten minutes.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the phlegm's brown?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Brown. Like tea. Not blood. I check it every time.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in it at all?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No blood.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain. That's the one thing I haven't got.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight dropping?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Weight's steady.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did this cough start?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm I can't pin a date. Years. Maybe five, maybe longer. I don't know.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): I quit last year, in March. Before that thirty years, twenty cigarettes a day.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still off them?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Not one since.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): True. No smokes in the house. I drive him in and I sort the tablets.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which tablets?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Omprazole twenty milligrams every morning for the reflux. Mizartan 40 mg once a day for the pressure. And Metformine for the sugar, the diabetes.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dose of the Metformine?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): 500 milligrams, twice a day. Morning and with tea.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He misses the evening Metformine though. Half the time it's still in the blister.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not. Well. Sometimes. Umm maybe I miss a few.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stopped any?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): The Seretide, purple puffer. I stopped it in March when I quit the smokes. They wanted atorvastatin as well but I never took that one.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bowels alright? Any change?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No. They're fine.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fevers? Night sweats?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Neither of those.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Is brown phlegm always cancer? Do I need the scan today? What if it's already spread?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. I'll listen to the chest.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Expiratory wheeze both sides. No crackles. Rest of the chest is clear.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Wheeze means COPD, doesn't it. Am I heading for oxygen? How worried should I be?
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): I reckon chronic bronchitis from the smoking. Can't rule out COPD till we measure it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Spirometry next Tuesday arvo to check for the COPD. That's booked. Nurse takes bloods Thursday morning at eight, fasting. Full blood count and kidney function.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, the alpha-1. If the cough does not settle, a scan.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): The alpha-1. What's that. Is that the cancer marker?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. It's a blood test for a rare cause of lung trouble. Only if the other two come back borderline.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Fast from midnight or what? Do I take the Mizartan? And the Omprazole? Will the Metformine wreck the numbers?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fast from midnight. Take the Mizartan and the Omprazole with a sip. Hold the Metformine till after the bloods.
[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): And the vaccines. Should I get them? Which ones? Will they stir the cough up?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Flu jab and the pneumonia one. Get both at the chemist.
[SEG0048] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll book the chemist on the way. Freeway was a shocker, mind you, forty minutes from Parramatta, and his grandson's cricket grand final is Saturday if the weather holds.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Little Jack bowls leg spin. Only nine. We were up early on the forecast. Meant to be sunny all weekend, he'll be filthy if it rains.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. I'll see you in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If I cough up blood before that, is it emergency or do I ring here? And can the wheeze just suddenly get worse?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood, straight to emergency. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday morning, eight o'clock, fasting. I'll slot you in. Right.
[SEG0054] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry about the hundred questions.
[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of.

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit queasy with the metronidazole, but I take it with food and that helps. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab a pressure and a pulse before you go in, just sit easy there.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I will of course, I've been sitting out there an age, the radio was going and some fella talking about the hurling, I wasn't even following it, my mind was on the legs.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Grand so. Blood pressure is one forty two over eighty six, pulse is seventy eight, and your oxygen is ninety seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the oxygen the important bit? Years ago in the hospital with the flu they said a different number but that was a whole other story, I was in a ward with six of us.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Mm. That's only today's. Doctor's ready for you now.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): In you come. How are you keeping these days?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure I'm not bad in myself at all, doctor, it's the legs that have me in.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go on so, tell me about the legs.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): It's cramps in the two calves, at night. I'm two months at it, nearly every night, and they wake me out of the sleep.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It begins with a little twitch, err, and then the calf just locks, like someone has a fist in there, and I'm out on the landing walking up and down, and then I put the kettle on even though I won't drink the tea.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): What eases it when that happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The walking eases it, and if I rub the calf hard with my hand. The hot water bottle was useless, I gave up on that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you get any swelling in the ankles or the legs?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling at all. I check them in the morning and they're ordinary, no puff in them.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or are you getting breathless walking on the flat?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort. Down to the shop and back I'm grand, the breathing doesn't bother me, it's purely the nights.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): How are the waterworks and the bowels, any change?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No change, they're as they always were. I go regular enough and there's no burning or anything like that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And what tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Well there's a few. Amlodipine five milligrams with the breakfast, that's for the pressure. I've a long history with that tablet but you don't need the whole saga.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the water tablet, forty milligrams, every morning, the little white one. On the box the chemist has frusemide, but everyone at home calls it the water tablet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): At night I take the cholesterol one, atorvastin twenty milligrams, for the cholesterol. And my sugar tablets are metformin, five hundred milligrams in the morning and again with the tea, for the sugar.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and only the magnesium from the shop as well. I got it in the chemist on Patrick Street, two hundred milligrams, one at bedtime, for these cramps. I'm about three weeks taking that.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you getting all of those in, the way they're supposed to be taken?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The prescription ones, yes, they're in a box by the kettle and I don't miss them. The magnesium, umm, I forget it. Maybe four nights in the week I actually take it, I couldn't swear to which nights.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about fluids, how much are you drinking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Very little water, doctor, I'll admit it. Two small cups of tea in the day and that's the height of it. With the water tablet I'm afraid of being up half the night, and the bathroom window doesn't even close properly, there's a draught.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): I follow you. May I have a look at the legs?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): You may of course. Don't mind the hole in the left sock, I've been saying I'll mend it since Christmas and I haven't.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Calves are soft, no tenderness there. Pulses are present in both feet. The ankles are a bit puffy, both sides.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Are they now. Well actually, by the evening they do puff up. The shoes get tight and the elastic of the socks leaves a mark, the two ankles, and that's been a few weeks. They're grand again in the morning so I put it out of my head.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. So they swell by evening and settle overnight.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it exactly. Just the ankles, not up the leg.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working thought is these night cramps are linked with the water tablet and how little you're drinking, because the potassium can drop on frusemide. I don't want to call it for certain until the bloods are back.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'm booking blood tests, the kidney function and the potassium, and the magnesium too while you're on the shop one.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put you down for Thursday morning in the clinic. No fasting for those.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday is fine, I have bowls but I'll skip the start. The half eight bus is reliable, Mrs Kearney from two doors down gets it as well, she talks the whole way.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, stretch the calves before bed. Both of them, hold it about half a minute, and do a few on each side.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Half a minute, a few each side, I can do that in the kitchen. Should I stay on the magnesium?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay on the same two hundred at bedtime for now. Try and sip a bit more water through the day, nice and steady, not buckets of it. And don't start any other bits from the shop.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't, no. There was an ayurvedic powder sitting on the shelf and I looked at it twice, but I never bought it and I certainly never took any.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in two weeks, whether the results are in or not.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, I'll write it on the calendar beside the bins day. Am I to keep the water tablet going the same?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep it the same, forty milligrams in the morning. Don't stop it yourself.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): And say the cramp is desperate on a given night, would you give me something for the pain of it?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't add a painkiller today. Let's see what the tests say before we add anything.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Your blood form will be at the desk, so Thursday is booked.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Lovely, thanks very much. I'll start the stretches tonight so.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Itchy.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Itchy dry patches behind the knees and in the elbows, worse at night. How long's that been going?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, I was gonna say three weeks. No, hang on, his birthday was six weeks back, so it's six weeks.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks. Does it hurt as well, mate, or just itch?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Itchy.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Any fever with it? And is he eating normally?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. Eating's fine. He's just not sleeping, up scratching for half the night.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the skin weeping at all, or any pus?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No weeping and no pus. Just dry and flaky. It bleeds a tiny bit sometimes where he scratches.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you putting on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. The white cream for the itchy bits. The yellow one at night for the dry skin. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. White cream for the itch, yellow cream at night for the dryness, Ayurvedic powder in the morning. Mum, what are the actual doses?
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The white one is the hydrocortizone. I nearly said nought point five percent, no, it's the one percent, a pea-sized amount twice a day. The yellow tube is QV, just a thick layer at night. He's had eczema since he was a bub, that's what we use the white one for.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the powder, do you know which one?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know the proper name. It's just an Ayurvedic powder from the grocer. He has a pinch by mouth in his milk every morning. I doubt it does much.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. We'll park that as an unnamed powder. Anyone in the family with asthma?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma, yeah. Been on a puffer for years.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Daddy's puffer is purple.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's your dad's, not yours. Any cough or wheeze in this little one?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough, no wheeze. He runs around fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about his tummy or his waterworks, anything there?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. All fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Behind both knees and both elbow creases the skin's dry and thickened, scratch marks, no pus. Couple of small soft glands in the neck.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, breathing's easy, and his tummy's soft.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry he wriggles. Err, we were late, the carpark was a shocker.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. So, six weeks of itchy dry patches in the creases, worse at night, scratching, not infected. Hydrocortisone one percent twice a day, QV at night, and a pinch of that powder each morning. I think this is an eczema flare.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll change the steroid. Stop the hydrocortisone, start Advantan fatty ointment nought point one percent, a thin layer once a day on the patches only, for seven days, then stop it.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the nurse to take bloods Thursday morning, a full blood count and an IgE. No fasting, breakfast is fine, just have him here around 8.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, a RAST panel. Not ordering that today. And if the neck glands do not settle, we'll organise an ultrasound.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Will the needle hurt?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Quick pinch, then it's done. I'll see you back in two weeks for a skin check and those results.
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday for the bloods, back in two weeks. We'll grab the Advantan from the chemist. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Room three is open whenever you're ready. Umm, sorry for the wait, the lot was jammed with that paving on Maple.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. The interstate was quite slow as well, so I gave myself extra time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Oh I know. I sat through three lights by the mall. They keep saying the work wraps up Friday if it doesn't rain.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I do hope the forecast holds. It has made the mornings rather trying.
[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Hey, I'll grab vitals before Dr. Shah comes in. I'm his sister, I work this clinic on Thursdays. Blood pressure is 132 over 78, pulse 118, respirations 16, oxygen 99 percent, temperature 36.9 Celsius.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. I'm Dr. Shah. Tell me what made you come in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. I am 29. I have been losing weight, and my heart races even when I am sitting quietly.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. How much weight have you dropped, and any sweating, shaky hands, or eating more or less?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): About twelve pounds, I would say. I sweat more than before, my hands shake, and I am eating more than usual.
[SEG0010] person_3 (NURSE): It's been three months of this. And he barely sleeps, I've watched it at the house.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): If I may, the weight loss is closer to six weeks, not three months. And I do sleep, only more lightly than I used to. I would not say I barely sleep.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so err, somewhere between six weeks and three months, and the sleep is lighter rather than gone. Let me think this through. When the thyroid puts out too much hormone it revs up metabolism, so you can lose weight even while eating more, and it drives the heart faster and makes the hands tremble. I'm wondering about an overactive thyroid.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister does have thyroid disease, doctor. The symptoms themselves are what brought me in, though.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): Yeah, they told me Graves back in college. My little boy tries to sneak the white pill like it's a mint, which is its own headache at home.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Useful context, but we'll go by your labs, not hers. Any ongoing medical problems of your own?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I have asthma. I have had it since I was a child. I use an albuteral inhaler, two puffs when I need it.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever with all this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): And with the asthma, have you been wheezing?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, if I hurry on the stairs.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, sometimes on the stairs, not constant. Uh, let me look. Fine tremor in both hands, yeah that fits. Thyroid feels a little full, rhythm is regular, and the lungs are clear with no wheeze right now.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Do you think it is serious?
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't say for certain today. My working impression is hyperthyroidism, provisional, from the weight loss, the fast heart, the sweating, the tremor, eating more, and your sister's thyroid disease. We'll get a TSH and a free T4, and an EKG while you're here.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Is there anything I should do in the meantime?
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ease off the caffeine, coffee and those energy drinks, until we know more. Keep the albuterol if you wheeze. I'll see you back in one week to go over the results. If you faint or get real chest pain, go to the emergency room.
[SEG0030] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book the EKG down the hall and the blood draw right after, and I'll put that one-week visit on the schedule.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I appreciate all of your help. Thank you.

[SEG0007] person_4 (PATIENT): Itchy.

[SEG0009] person_4 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been sleeping on the couch instead of playing. And his eyes went pink yesterday.
[SEG0011] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah, and he keeps scratching his belly. Dana stays with us on school nights, so she's seen more of this than I have.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Leo, have you been coughing at all?
[SEG0013] person_4 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mm. Oh, his dinosaur backpack is still in the car, I'll grab it after. Sorry.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about his stomach. Any vomiting, or loose stools?
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. He didn't throw up. He had one loose stool this morning, I don't know if that even counts.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And ears or throat, anything going on there?
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing. No ear pain, and he's been eating popsicles, no sore throat.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has he been on any medicine for this?

[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, and my sister would not stop texting me to give him benedryl. We never gave it. Not once.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about, medicines or anything else?
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing he's reacted to.

[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a red blotchy rash on his face, chest, and both arms. Eyes are a little bloodshot on both sides. Throat's mildly pink, no pus. I don't see any Koplik spots inside the cheeks. Lungs are clear.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in one week either way, so we can go over those bloods. Keep him home, no school and no playdates, through Thursday, that's four days after the rash started. If he gets worse before the blood draw, call us, don't wait.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll notify the health department today about a suspected case. My working read is possible measles, but it could still be some other viral rash. I can't lock it in until the bloods come back. Leo, you were brave.

[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're here now. What's the problem?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, for the last four days I have had a burning when I pass water. I am going very often, and there is an ache across my lower back.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Every time you pass water?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. It is quite sharp, umm, particularly at the finish.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): How often?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): About every hour in the daytime. At night I am up, uh, three times... no, twice.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any discharge?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blood in the urine?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I have seen. No.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Feverish?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mildly, yes. Yesterday evening I felt warm. The thermometer at home read thirty seven point eight.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sick? Vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Been abroad lately?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not travelled.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): The ache, one side?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, both sides, low down. A dull ache.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Shooting down the leg?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Background conditions?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, for five-ish years. I take amladipine, five milligrams, every morning for it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Operations?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Err, they did kidney bloods at some stage. They said it was borderline. I could not tell you the date.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I come out in a rash.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take your observations. My sister had a kidney infection last winter, two nights in hospital, she was in bits.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I am sorry to hear that. I hope she is well.
[SEG0031] person_1 (NURSE): She's grand now. Right. Blood pressure one forty two over eighty six, pulse seventy eight, temperature thirty seven point six.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, in the evenings. Not severe.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest or breathing trouble?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The chest is fine.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I never have.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the couch. I'll feel your tummy and your back.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Abdomen soft, not tender. A little tenderness across the lower back. Loins are not sore.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It is more a dull ache than anything sharp, doctor, if that is useful.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): The burning is germs irritating the lining of the water pipe. Track up towards the kidney and you get the back ache. The temperature is your body fighting the infection.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think it's a urine infection, possibly starting towards the kidney. Provisional. We'll see what the sample says.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. What happens next?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll have the urine dipped and sent to the lab today. If it shows infection I'll start ciprofloxacin, five hundred milligrams twice a day for seven days. Nothing until we see it.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be from the chemist, then?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only if we ring you. Plenty of water in the meantime, and don't hold on. I'll see you back here in a week.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the pain goes sharp on one side or you start vomiting, come back sooner. Don't wait the week.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you out in that on Sunday for the match?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was, up in the stand, soaked through. Dublin were poor in the second half, I thought they'd never score.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, well, um, it's the hands. They go numb at night.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which fingers, and is it the two hands?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Mostly the right. The thumb, the index and the middle one. I do be waking with it and I have to shake the hand to get the feeling back.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, I haven't a clue of the date. A few months anyway. Maybe since the spring, I'm not sure.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how are they in the daytime?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Daytime they're mostly grand, but I've started dropping cups. Dropped a mug of tea yesterday, all over the kitchen floor.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): Sorry for barging in. I'll just do the blood pressure. My own sister had the numb fingers last year, shaking her hands out at breakfast, her husband was driven demented.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): God, was she alright? Am I going to lose the use of the hand? I keep panicking.
[SEG0016] person_3 (NURSE): She was grand after. Yours is 138 over 86, and the pulse is 74. I'll leave ye to it.

[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or pins and needles in the feet?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No, the legs are fine, and there's nothing in the feet. Uh, is this a stroke? I was reading things at half two and I frightened the life out of myself.

[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): If I'm right, the median nerve is getting pinched in the little tunnel at the wrist. That nerve looks after those three fingers, so they go dead, and the little finger is usually spared because a different nerve minds it.
