[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The tram sat at Richmond for ages and then I got the wrong lift.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries. Take a second, we've still got time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Bit warm out, I legged it from the stop.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. What brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's nothing, honestly. I nearly didn't come. Just the heel.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The heel. Tell me about it, even if you reckon it's minor.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right one. First thing, those first steps, it nips, then it walks off. Not a big deal.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, six weeks. No, hang on, it started before the long weekend, so closer to two months.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So two months, right heel, worst on the first steps, then it settles. Have I got that straight?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can still do a full shift though.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What sort of shift is it?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hardware shop. On my feet the whole day, up and down the aisles. I run three times a week as well, nothing flash.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have new shoes been part of this?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, umm, yeah. New joggers about a month ago. Flat as. Thought they'd be fine.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the running stir the heel up?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit after, maybe. Morning's worse than the running. I'm not giving it up.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling or redness that you've seen?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah. Looks normal. My boss reckons I limp, but I don't.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles in the foot?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your breathing when you run?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Lungs are good.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any tablets, even the odd one?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. Neurofen if it annoys me. Two hundred mils, nah, the tablets are four hundred. Just one.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how often would that be?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Couple of times a week. I forget half the time. Not worth fussing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, neurofen included?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the heel been scanned before?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Ultrasound, ages ago. Couldn't tell you when, last year or maybe before. They said the fascia was borderline thick. I left it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): An old ultrasound, called borderline thick, no actual figure, and you didn't chase it. Mind if I have a feel?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on. You won't find much.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tender just in front of the right heel pad. No swelling, the skin isn't red, and the calf feels tight.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): See. Hardly a thing.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely plantar fasciitis. The morning first-step pain and that tender spot fit, and we don't need a scan today.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): So I just put up with it then?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stretch the calf and the sole before you get out of bed, morning and night. Grab some cushioned insoles from the chemist, and give those flat joggers a rest on the long shifts. If it's still niggling in six weeks, come back and see me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Stretches and insoles. Heaps of fuss for a small niggle.

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): About... well, one week.

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): My partner and our baby. I walk the dog every morning. I grab fast food at lunch most days.

[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, nickel. I get a rash on my skin.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What do you take on a normal day?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, it's something called dicl... diclofenac, 50 milligrams, maybe, when needed.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you happen to bring the box or the paperwork?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): So, no, it's at home. Okay, so I take paracetamol, when needed.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you know the dose?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): It's 1 gram.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you have any chronic illnesses?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, I have arthritis in my knees, for about a year.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any joint swelling, fever or weight loss at all?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't had joint swelling, fever or weight loss, no.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, has there been any rash?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): No rash, thankfully.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any change in your bowel habit or your stomach generally?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing unusual, no.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your skin, any changes there?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): No rashes.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me quickly check your readings.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you in a second, make yourself comfortable.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stay as you are for a moment.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your joints are not swollen and you are tender over many muscle points.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed to check. Okay, so my impression is this: My working impression is fibromyalgia. Polymyalgia is still possible.

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's book blood tests to look into widespread pain. You'll be taking amitriptyline, 10 milligrams, at night, long term. You take it by mouth. That's for pain and sleep. It's a commonly used medicine and most people tolerate it well.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I carry on if I feel better?

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm, okay. The pain clinic would be the right next step, I'll refer you. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): I know what to watch for.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's review you in six weeks. That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have a good day.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, I've been getting these awful sweats first thing, and the shakes, and I'm frightened if I'm honest.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sweats and shaking, in the morning. How long has that been happening?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, a few weeks. Maybe three weeks. It started after I began missing breakfast, I just can't face food that early.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): And my daughter was staying over, she said one morning I was all confused, not making sense, just for a few minutes. Just the once. I came round after a cup of tea.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, sweating and shakiness for about three weeks when you skip breakfast, and one brief muddled spell that settled with tea.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that's it. I've had type 2 for, err, about fifteen years. Is this a hypo? My neighbour had one and ended up in hospital and I've been worrying myself sick.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): It may be a low sugar, with the gliclazide and no breakfast, but I'd rather not call it that until we've been through the detail. What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin, 500 milligrams, twice a day, with my lunch and with my tea, for the diabetes. And the gliklazide in the morning. Is the metformin the one that hurts your kidneys? I read something.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come to the kidneys. The repeat list the nurse updated last month says gliclazide 80 mg each morning. Is that the dose you take?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's wrong. I take 40. One 40 milligram tablet. She must have put 80 by mistake. I've always been on 40.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so the record says 80 and you say 40. I'll leave the dose unset until we see the box. Don't change anything today.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Shall I bring the packet? My daughter can read the label, my eyes aren't brilliant. What if I've been on the wrong dose all this time?
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, bring the box next time, that would settle it. And the metformin, 500 mg twice a day, you're sure of that one?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, definitely 500, twice a day. I stopped the atorvastin though, back in March, the cholesterol tablet, my legs were aching. And at the hospital they talked about insulin but I never took it, I said no.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Atorvastatin stopped in March, insulin never started. With these morning episodes, have you had any fever?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. I just go clammy and shaky.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted at all?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't know really. My daughter says my trousers are looser but I haven't been on the scales, and they still do up, so maybe not. I'm not sure.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the weight. Any problems passing urine, burning, or going more often?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No, waterworks are fine. Why do you ask? Is that the metformin?
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, so I'd like a blood test for kidney function, and an HbA1c for the diabetes overall. Not because I think your kidneys are failing today.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): HbA1c, that's the average one, isn't it? Will it show these morning hypos? And if it's high will you put me on insulin? I don't want injections.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): It shows the average over about three months, so it won't catch a single low. I'm not starting insulin. Let me check you. Blood pressure today is 136 over 78, pulse 72.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Is 136 alright at 74? I get ever so anxious about numbers. And am I safe on my own in the mornings?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): 136 over 78 is acceptable. You're not sweaty just now and there's no tremor while you're sitting. My working impression is morning hypos, the gliclazide on an empty stomach, but that's provisional until the bloods are back.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): So if I eat something it might stop? What do I eat? If I feel it coming, do I take sugar? My daughter doesn't live with me, I'm scared I'll black out and no one will know.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have some toast, or anything, before or with the gliclazide. If you go sweaty and shaky, take a sugary drink and sit down, and let your daughter know what to watch for. Don't drive until this has settled.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Toast, sugary drink, no driving. Right. Will you cut the gliclazide now, or is that dangerous too?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll wait. I won't change the dose while the two figures disagree. The blood test is booked, the receptionist will give you the form, this week if you can manage it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): This week. Ok. And do I come back? What if the shakes carry on even when I eat?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight regardless, and we'll go through the results. If an episode is severe, or you become confused again, don't sit on it, get help the same day.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Sorry, I know I've asked a lot. I tie myself in knots.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's fine. Putting it together: sweats and shakes for about three weeks when you skip breakfast, one short confused spell, metformin 500 twice daily, gliclazide dose still to confirm, statin stopped in March, bloods this week, and I'll see you in two weeks.

[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hello, Mr Fitzgerald. It's the back, isn't it, and the leg?

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Sitting, mostly. And coughing, or sneezing, that sends a jolt down.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or weakness in the foot?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit of tingling in the toes. But the foot's strong. No weakness.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your bladder or bowels, or numbness in your groin? ~
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): None whatsoever. ~
[SEG0013] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor, here's his list. ~
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, GrÃ¡inne. Mr Fitzgerald, let's go through the medicines.
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Naproxen, 500 mg twice a day, with food. And paracetamol, 1 gram, four times a day.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is that helping? ~
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Takes the edge off. Not the leg. ~
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure, and my knees.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped a few years back, ten a day, for forty years.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Would you like me to take his blood pressure, doctor? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today, thanks, GrÃ¡inne. Mr Fitzgerald, I'll check your leg. Lift it straight. ~
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow. That's the one.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's reproduced the pain when I raise the left leg, and your ankle reflex is a bit reduced on that side, but your strength is normal. ~
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that a disc? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): It sounds like sciatica, which is a pinched nerve at the lower back, often from a slipped disc. ~
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need surgery? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people improve without it, over six to twelve weeks. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Could I keep working? ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, gentle activity, but no heavy lifting. Staying in bed is worse.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): How will I lift the sacks? ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ask for help, and bend your knees. ~
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll get my son. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the naproxen with food, and the paracetamol regularly.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): And hot water bottles, doctor? ~
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heat helps, yes. If you develop numbness between your legs, can't control your bladder or bowels, or your foot becomes weak, go to the emergency department right away.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Otherwise, if it's not better in six weeks, come back and I'll arrange a scan and a physiotherapy referral.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks a million, doctor. ~

[SEG0004] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll take your blood pressure and weight while you talk to the doctor. ~
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Do you have any family history of diabetes?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had it. He was on tablets.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight, or have blurred vision?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't lost weight. My vision's fine.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take at the moment?

[SEG0015] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Blood pressure 142 over 88, weight 94 kilograms.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. A bit up on the pressure. I'll check your blood sugar with a finger prick now.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, of course.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): The finger-prick sugar is 14.2, which is high.
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that diabetes? ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): It strongly suggests it, but I need a proper blood test to confirm.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Will it need insulin? ~
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not necessarily. Many people start with tablets, diet and exercise. Let's get the tests first. ~
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): What tests? ~
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): I will arrange a blood test for HbA1c, kidney function and cholesterol, and a urine test.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take the blood today, and I'd like to see you again in a week with the results.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Until then, drink water rather than sugary drinks, and try to cut back on sweet foods.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I will. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you start vomiting, feel very drowsy, or become short of breath, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thanks, doctor. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): sorry the wait ran long. i'm just getting vitals before dr. okonkwo comes in, arm straight please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah well i've been sitting out there forever and i didn't even want to come. just do it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): blood pressure is one twenty-eight over eighty-two. pulse is 76.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. fine.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): med list says diciclomine ten milligrams three times a day. you still on that?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): uh no. ten did nothing, i take twenty. three times a day, yeah, but twenty not ten.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): okay, i'll flag the dose. she should be right in.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): hi, i'm dr. okonkwo. sounds like a long morning. what brought you in today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): these cramps, and my bowels are all over the place. i'm exhausted.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): okay. how long has it been, and what are the stools actually doing?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): a year. maybe a bit more, but basically a year. cramps come on and if i pass stool they ease off, and i'm bloated like six months pregnant by the afternoon, which i'm not. and it flips, constipated one day, loose and urgent the next, sorry.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): no apology needed. so cramps that ease after a bowel movement, bloating, and the habit swinging between constipation and loose stool, for a year. did i get that?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah. that's it. and work is making me crazy on top.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): any blood in the stool, on the paper or mixed in?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): no. i looked. there's no blood.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): and weight, have you lost any without trying?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): no. i wish. if anything my pants are tight from the bloat. can we skip the twenty questions, i'm wiped.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): i'll keep it short. how often do the cramps hit, anything set them off?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): most days. worse when a deadline's on fire, and after lunch. um, nights are okay once i've gone.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): any family stuff, bowel disease, diabetes, blood pressure?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my sister has pressure but no sugar. she's on biotin for her hair, that's hers. and my husband takes metformin for his diabetes, don't put that on my list.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): understood, none of those medicines are yours. what about work, and the day to day, food, exercise, drinking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): i'm a project coordinator at a freight company, and the hours are brutal, like 55, sixty hours most weeks. diet is mostly a desk salad if i remember and takeout at nine. exercise, ha, i walk from the parking garage and that's it. alcohol, a glass of wine maybe two nights a week, not more, and i don't smoke, never did.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): project coordinator, 55 to 60 hours, salad if you remember otherwise late takeout, walking just from the garage, wine a couple of nights, never smoked. and the gut picture we said, a year, better after stool, no blood, no weight loss.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah. don't get on me about the wine, it's not the problem.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): i'm not. alright if i feel your abdomen?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): fine. don't jab though, it hurts.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): soft. tender over the left lower side, no guarding, no masses that i can feel.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): see. told you.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): that pattern, the cramp easing when you pass stool, the bloating, constipation trading off with loose stool, fits a working impression of irritable bowel. i'm not calling it final until the labs are back.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): i'm ordering bloodwork today, a blood count, a crp, and a celiac panel. they can draw it before you go.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): more needles. great. will that even explain why i'm this tired?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): it can pick up anemia or inflammation if one of those is sitting there. it won't measure the work stress, but it keeps us from missing something else.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah the work stress isn't in a test tube. i know. i'm just tired of all of it.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): right. for food, smaller meals when you can, don't save the whole day of eating for nine o'clock, add some fiber like oats on the constipated days, and cut back on the greasy takeout. that's advice, not a speech.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): oats. sure. if i remember.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): i want to see you back in four weeks with the results. if the cramps or the stools get a lot worse before then, call the office.
[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): i can walk you to the lab for the blood draw now.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): err, yeah let's just get it over with.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll go through the numbers together when you're back.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The tiredness, mostly. I'm snapping at my flatmate over nothing. And yeah the stairs, one flight and I'm gasping.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I keep eating ice. Like proper cubes out of the freezer, all evening. It's ridiculous, I know.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, I haven't a notion of the exact day. A couple of months, anyway. It just crept up.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the gasping on the stairs, did that come on around the same time?

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any cough with it?

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you had a fever?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): They're normal. Why, did someone say they weren't? Every twenty eight days, five days, not heavy, same as always.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nobody said a word. I'm only asking because heavy periods can leave you drained. The ice, then, how long have you been at that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks. Err, maybe three. I go through a whole tray a night. My flatmate thinks I've lost the plot.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you eat meat or fish at all?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing else. And I'm not starting them again, they were brutal.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Can you not just ring me?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd rather see you. Two weeks, here, and we'll go through the numbers properly. If you feel faint, or the breathing gets markedly worse before that, don't sit on it, come back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Two weeks. And the tea thing.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Food first, and no new tablet from me today. If the ferritin is low we can talk about a gentler iron then, but I'm not starting one now.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'm going before I fall asleep on this chair.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Get the bloods done on your way out, and mind yourself on those stairs.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. I heard you the first time.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Up on the chair for me and I'll grab a temperature and a blood pressure before you go in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm grand. Sure it's nothing, I nearly didn't bother coming.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He said that the whole weekend. I was blue in the face trying to get him into the car.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature is thirty seven point eight. Pulse eighty eight. Pressure one thirty two over seventy eight. Grand, the doctor won't be long.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Doctor Keane. What brought you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a small bit of burning when I pass water. Nothing to write home about.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pass water. How long is that going on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm a week... no, four days. Since Monday. I'm grand in myself mostly.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you going to the toilet more often?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah. Up a couple of times in the night. It's not desperate or anything.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any ache in the back or down the side?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh lower back, a small ache. I put it down to the van, the seat is brutal.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any discharge at all?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you been away anywhere lately, abroad or even a weekend off?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No travel. Just the usual driving for work.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was shivering a small bit Tuesday night. He told me he was only warm.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): So there was a temperature in it as well, even if mild. Any pain in the tummy, or blood in the urine?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood. Tummy's fine. The fever is barely there, I wouldn't even call it one.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the bowels, any change?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels are grand.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, I'll have a feel of your tummy and your back. Soft tummy. Tender just over the bladder, and a bit tender in the left loin. No guarding.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you on any tablets at the minute?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, two point five... no, five milligrams, once in the morning, for the blood pressure. And paracetamol if the back is at me.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): How much paracetamol are you taking?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): A thousand milligrams, the odd time. Not every day.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They gave him omeprasole in the spring and he stopped it in March. And the statin, atorvastatin, he never even started that. The box is still sitting in the press.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): So ramipril five milligrams every morning, paracetamol now and again, omeprazole stopped back in March, and the atorvastatin was never taken. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family with kidney trouble, or diabetes, that sort of thing?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Err my father had diabetes in his fifties, my mother did not, umm my sister has the pressure but no sugar, and my brother had a kidney stone a few years back. That's the lot really.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): And day to day, the work, the hours, food, exercise, drink?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a delivery driver for a builders' merchant, on the road six till three most days. Diet is sandwiches and a takeaway more evenings than not. I walk the dog around the block, that's the exercise. Alcohol is three or four pints of a Saturday. That's me.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me put that back to you. Four days of burning when you pass water, going more often, a lower back ache, a mild temperature, no discharge and no travel. I'd say this is most likely a urine infection, possibly tracking towards the kidney, but I want the sample before I commit to it.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Sure if you say so. I still think it's a whole lot of fuss.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll send a urine sample today for microscopy and culture. The nurse can take it before you leave, dip and all.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Yeah I can do the dip now and bottle the rest for the lab.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): And bloods Thursday morning with the nurse here, half eight. Kidney function and a full blood count. No need to fast. Take your usual ramipril before you come.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): If those bloods are borderline we'll add a CRP, that would be the third test. And if this does not settle we'll organise a kidney scan. I'm not booking the scan today.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the urine confirms a lower infection I'll start trimethoprim, two hundred milligrams twice a day for seven days. I won't issue it until the result is back.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah whatever you think. I'm not pushed.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks with the results, antibiotic or no antibiotic.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here. He'll say he's grand and forget.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the burning gets worse, or you start vomiting or the shakes come back, don't wait the two weeks. Come straight back or go to the emergency department.

[SEG0001] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good morning. Before we start, can I just check your name? Is it Mr Desmond Achterberg?
[SEG0002] person_1 (PATIENT): That's me. Desmond is fine, though. Nobody calls me Mr Achterberg except the bank.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Desmond it is. Your GP asked me to take a look. What's your own understanding of why you're here?
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Honestly? It's my left foot, and it's probably nothing. My daughter nagged me into coming.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Daughters usually have good instincts. Has anything stopped you doing what you normally do?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. I still walk the dog every morning. I just wanted her to stop going on about it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good for you. Now, a few questions about the nerves. Do you have any weakness in the leg?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): No weakness. It has never given way on me or anything.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about your balance? Have you had any falls lately?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't fallen. I'm steady enough, thanks.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last of the nerve questions. Any trouble with your bladder or bowels?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, those are the ones I worry about most. Do you have any other health conditions?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Type 2 diabetes. Diet only so far, the GP keeps an eye on it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does anybody else in the family have diabetes?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): My father did. He had diabetes for years before he passed.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks for telling me. Do you smoke?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): About ten cigarettes a day. I know, I know.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to nag, your daughter has that covered. What about alcohol?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): A couple of pints on a Saturday at the club. That's my lot.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair. And are you taking any tablets at the moment?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Not a thing. I keep away from them where I can.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): None that I know of.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'm going to check your blood pressure and pulse, then test the feeling in your feet.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Is this going to hurt?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all. Blood pressure is 136 over 84, and your pulse is 72.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pretty reasonable. Now close your eyes and say yes each time you feel this wisp of cotton wool touch your foot.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Yes. Hang on. Was that the toes? I couldn't tell.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. The feeling is reduced in the toes of your left foot, compared with the right.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah. Well. Is it serious?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me explain it plainly. Nerves are like electrical cables, and years of high sugar can wear away the insulation, so the signal gets fuzzy. It looks like early nerve damage from the diabetes.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Can it be fixed?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can be slowed down a lot. Step one is bloods. I'd like to order blood tests, for your sugar control and your vitamin B12, since a low B12 can do something similar.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Today?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): The nurse can take them on your way out. Then I'd like to see you in two weeks, to go through the results together.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Right. I'll bring my daughter, she'll want to hear it for herself.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please do. And look after those feet in the meantime. Check them every evening, and wear slippers indoors.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Understood. Thank you, doctor.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take care, Desmond. Give the dog my regards.

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Sharp, right at the base of the thumb side, worse if I try to turn the hand over.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you move your fingers? ~
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, I can wiggle them. ~
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling?

[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medical conditions I should know about?

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't say without an X-ray. But with this kind of fall and pain on the thumb side, I think it's possibly a fracture of the wrist.

[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. And in the meantime? ~

[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll ask the nurse. ~

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in and we'll get the weight and that done. Shoes off if you don't mind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Sorry, the bus was all over the place, I'm a bit flustered.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Not a bother. You're seventy two point four kilos. Blood pressure is one thirty six over eighty four, and the pulse is seventy two.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that ok? I never know with those numbers.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): It's fine for me to record. Doctor will be in now. Were you waiting long?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah a few minutes. I was watching the hurling on the phone, so.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Who was playing?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Kilkenny. I don't know, I only half watched it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Dr Brennan. Take a seat. What brought you in?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the bloating, doctor, and loose stools. Comes on after milk and ice cream.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Did you try leaving the dairy off, or are you still having it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I did, for a week... well actually it was five days. Then ice cream at my sister's and it all came back. I don't know if those five days helped, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has the bloating been going on, before that?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, three months... no, that's not right. It's been since before Christmas, so six months I'd say.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the stools, watery or just soft?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Soft and urgent, two or three goes, not every day, only after the ice cream or cereal with loads of milk. Maybe an hour later. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your sister, has she the same trouble? You mentioned her there.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, she's grand. She takes biotin for her hair, that's her thing. And my husband is on metformin for his sugar, but that's him, not me.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ok, not you. What are you taking yourself?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, five milligrams... no, they put it up, ten milligrams in the morning. The cholesterol one at night, atorvastin... atorvastatin, twenty, sorry, forty milligrams. And sugar tablets, gliclazide, eighty milligrams with the breakfast.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shop stuff, herbs, that kind of thing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. A teaspoon, from the health shop. I don't know the name of it, doctor.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Any blood in the stool at all?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting? A temperature? Pain apart from the bloating?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting, no fever. There is a bit of cramp low down when the bloating is bad.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think so. Same as I remember, near enough.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through. The timing after milk and ice cream makes me wonder about the lactose. But coeliac, the gluten problem, can look the same, bloating and loose stools, and I wouldn't want to miss it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it the bread? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't come off the bread yet. If the gluten is out of the diet before the blood test, the test can look normal even if coeliac is there. Keep eating as you usually do until we have the result.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): And what about the milk?
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can ease off the milk and the ice cream if that settles the symptoms, that's a separate thing. A diet diary for a couple of weeks would help me, just what you ate and what the bowels did.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. I'm hopeless at writing things down, but I'll have a go.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rough notes are grand. I'll book a coeliac screen, bloods, the tTG and the IgA.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to starve for it?
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it's not a fasting test. The nurse can take it before you leave.
[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): I can, yeah. No bother at all.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks, we'll go through the result and the diary. If the stools go black, or the pain gets severe, don't sit on it, come in or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks... I don't know, doctor, is that long enough?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): The lab is usually back inside that. Two weeks, yes.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): Sleeve up whenever you're ready and we'll fill the bottle.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, hello, doctor. Gosh, it's the scar, you see, it's been months and it still hurts, and it's right where my skirt rubs, and I told my daughter, she's getting married in June, a lovely lad, a plumber...
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Congratulations to her. Which scar, Margaret, remind me? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): The hip. The new hip, four months ago, on the left. The pain around the scar, it's like a burning, and a bit numb on the side.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has the burning been there?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Since about a month after the operation, so, three months, nearly? Though I had the tingling in January too.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the numb patch, is that the same area?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, just on the outside of the thigh. Oh, and the hip itself is stiff in the mornings, I can't get my tights on.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever or sweats?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no fever at all. I took my temperature, I've got that thermometer you put in your ear.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any discharge, any weeping from the scar?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Nothing like that, it's dry as a bone.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you taking at the moment?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Tramadol, 50 mg, twice a day. Paracetamol, 1 gram, four times. Lansoprazole, 30 mg, in the morning, for my stomach, and levothyroxine, 75 micrograms, first thing.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Any allergies?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Iodine. I react, they put it on my wristband at the hospital, but I can never remember what it does to me.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, we'll note iodine. What conditions do you have?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Underactive thyroid, acid reflux, and the thin bones, osteoporosis.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations apart from the hip?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): The hip, four months ago, and my cataract in 2019, the left eye.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bone problems in the family?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): My mother broke her hip when she was eighty.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): What did you do for work?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): I was a nurse, retired now. Thirty-five years on the wards.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Where do you live?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): A second-floor flat, no lift, so the stairs are a battle.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And have you been doing the exercises?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): The physio ones, yes, every morning, apart from when it hurts too much.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me do your numbers. Pulse 72, blood pressure 138 over 84, temperature 36.8, oxygen 97 percent, breathing 16, weight 64 kilos.
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that all right? Oh, my daughter's fiancÃ© fixed our boiler last year, that's how they met. ~
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Let's look at the scar.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Mind the skirt. ~
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scar is healed and dry, with no redness or swelling. But the skin along it is very tender to light touch.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, that's the burning, even the sheet bothers me. ~
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any problem with your chest or breathing?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing, I'm fine in that department.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): The scar looks healed, and I think this is irritation of a small skin nerve, which is common after hip surgery, but I can't completely rule out a deep infection.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh dear, is it infected? ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I doubt it, but I'd like to check. I'd like to arrange an X-ray of the hip, and blood tests for inflammation and infection markers.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I carry on with the exercises? ~
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'd also like to do an ultrasound scan around the scar, and a bone density scan, since you have osteoporosis.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): When would that be? ~
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): The bone scan can wait a few weeks. I'd like to see you again in two weeks with the results.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. I'll put it on the fridge. ~

[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Say that again? No protection at all? The screen jumped.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): None. Five days a week, and a Saturday now and again if the line is behind. Eight till half four.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastin, twenty milligrams, every night after the news. Not the morning, the night.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's what I thought. It doesn't feel dirty, it feels stunned, from the machines I'd say.

[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, do you smoke?

[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Great, thank you for your help.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): See you soon.

[SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, I am so sorry we're late. Err, the garage was full, and then a school bus just sat on Maple Street forever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, truly. We still have the time. I'm Dr. Hale.
[SEG0003] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. I'm Carla, his mom. This is Owen. He just turned seven.
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Good afternoon, doctor. It is a pleasure to meet you.
[SEG0005] person_4 (NURSE): Chart's updated. Weight 23 kilograms, temp thirty six point eight celsius. Umm, my sister's little boy had a total meltdown in that same garage last Tuesday, made us late to his checkup. Our circus, not yours.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Dana. What brings you in?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): My skin has been itching quite a lot, doctor.
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He's got these dry rough patches behind both knees and in the creases of his elbows. He scratches them, especially at night, till they look raw.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dry rough patches behind the knees and in the elbow creases, itchy, scratched raw, worse at night. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, about six weeks, maybe a little longer. I can't pin the day it started.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Any oozing or crusting? Any wheezing?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. Nothing oozing. And he has not wheezed.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Good, that's reassuring. Anyone at home with asthma or eczema?
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma. He keeps a blue inhaler in his bag. I don't have either. Nobody's told me Owen had eczema before.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Father with asthma, noted. What have you been putting on his skin?
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The big white tub, we just call it the white cream, thick moisturizer, morning and night. A little pink tube, the steroid Dr. Patel gave last year, she said once a day, but uh I forget a lot of nights so it's more like a few times a week, and I cannot remember the real name of that pink one. And sometimes the blue lotion from the drugstore, just a plain moisturizer, if the white tub is upstairs.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. White moisturizer twice a day, an unnamed pink steroid that was supposed to be daily but often gets skipped, and a blue plain lotion now and then. Owen, may I look? Sleeves and pant legs up, please.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Certainly.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both elbow creases and the skin behind both knees have dry, slightly scaly patches. No honey-colored crust. The skin is not warm to the touch.
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He scratches in his sleep too. I find little spots of blood on the sheets some mornings.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): The itch comes from a leaky skin barrier. Water slips out, and the small nerves in the skin fire off, especially when he is warm under the blankets at night. That part is not an infection.
[SEG0022] person_4 (NURSE): Right. My own hands split every winter from the dish soap at my place. Drives me crazy. That's me, though, not Owen.
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, that hail yesterday, did you see it? We pulled over by the ball field after school and just watched, little white pellets bouncing, and the coach was dragging a tarp over the bases like it was game seven.
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): I counted forty hailstones, doctor, before mother said we ought to leave.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. I got caught between the lot and the door. My shoes are still damp.
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the traffic after was ridiculous, everybody creeping along. We spent the whole ride on his class turtle. His name is Pickle. He will only eat the fancy lettuce, not the cheap kind.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pickle. Alright. Coming back to the skin.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Putting this together, I think this is eczema, atopic dermatitis. That's my working read. I'm not proving it with a test today, and I don't think it's infected.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay. So do we keep using the pink tube?
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to stop that unnamed pink steroid. We'll switch to triamcinalone zero point one percent cream, a thin layer on the patches only, twice a day for seven days, then stop.
[SEG0031] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day for a week, patches only. Got it. What about the white cream and the blue one?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the white cream, but use it all over at least three times a day, especially within a few minutes after a short lukewarm bath. The blue lotion is fine as a backup when the white tub isn't around. Mild soap, pat dry, don't rub.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cotton pajamas if you have them, and keep his nails short so the scratching does less harm. Steroid stays off the face, and off any spot that's openly bleeding. Just moisturize those.
[SEG0034] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): White cream three times a day after lukewarm baths, blue one only as backup, triamcinalone on the patches twice a day for a week, stop the pink tube, short nails, no steroid on the face. Did I miss a piece?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the whole plan. Yes.
[SEG0036] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What if it doesn't settle?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in three weeks either way, so I can recheck it. If the patches get hot, or there's pus, or he gets a fever before then, call and we'll see him sooner.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I appreciate your help.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll pick it up at the pharmacy. Thanks for squeezing us in after we were late.
[SEG0040] person_4 (NURSE): I'll send the triamcinalone to the pharmacy now.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sounds good. See you in three weeks, Owen.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm grand, doctor, really. It was only Bridget here who insisted I come in for the check on the leg after the tablets.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good on Bridget, then. This is the second time it's flared up on that shin, so I'd sooner look than guess. Bridget, you're with him at home?
[SEG0003] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I am, I'm his live-in carer, five days a week. He'd never tell you if it was bad, so I tell you for him.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): There's nothing to tell.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, we'll see. Is it all right if the healthcare assistant takes down the dressing first?
[SEG0006] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Hello Mr Doyle. I'll unwrap the leg and have the dressing pack ready for the doctor, it won't take a minute.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, don't be making a fuss.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): While she does that, a couple of questions. Any fever or shivers since I last saw you?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any pain in the leg, or is it just a bit tender?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain. Nothing worth mentioning.
[SEG0012] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He doesn't complain, that's the problem. But I'll say he's been walking the garden path every day without limping.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful to hear from you, thank you. Now, the tablets. Which antibiotic are you finishing?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): The doxycycline, 100 mg, twice a day. I've two days left.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. And you're taking that because of the penicillin trouble, aren't you?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): I am. Penicillin gave me hives years ago. They told me never again.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, penicillin allergy with hives, I'll make sure that's on the front of your notes. Any other tablets I should know about?
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There's the water tablet for the swelling, the furosemide. It's in the morning. I think it's maybe 20 mg? I'd have to check the box.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Maybe 20 mg, we'll confirm it against the pharmacy list. Mr Doyle, do you remember?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): I take what Bridget puts in my hand.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair. Anything long-term behind the swollen legs?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): The heart failure. It's well managed. And I had the hip replaced about ten years ago.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart failure and the hip replacement, thank you. Let's have a look at the leg.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Temperature is 36.8 degrees, and your pulse is 76. Now I'm looking at the shin. The redness has faded to a pale pink, and there's no warmth over the skin where it was.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that good or bad?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. It looks like the cellulitis has cleared, which is what we wanted from this course.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I told you it was nothing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): You did, and I'm still glad we checked. Now let me give you the choices for keeping it from coming back a third time.
[SEG0029] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Please do. I'm tired of the carpet being covered in cotton wool.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): First option, compression stockings in the daytime, which helps the swelling that sets the skin up for infection. Second, moisturise the skin twice a day so it doesn't crack. Third, keep your feet up when you're sitting.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): The stockings are a divil to get on.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): They are. Bridget or the community nurse can help with that. Which of the three would you actually do?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): The moisturiser. I'd do that.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And I'll do the feet up, if I have to tie him to the stool.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then moisturiser every day, feet up when sitting, and finish the doxycycline. We can talk about the stockings another day.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand. Will that be everything?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's everything for today. You look well, Mr Doyle.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll put a light dressing back on, and a clean sock over it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks, love.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring him in for a cup of tea first, we passed a lovely bakery.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Enjoy it. Take care, both of you.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Good day, doctor.

[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fatty meals. How long does a spell last before it—
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hours.

[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Once.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Once only. Has it come back?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And any fever with these?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): After chips.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chips, I'll add that to the fatty food. I meant fever. Any temperature?

[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Ok.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book bloods, liver tests and a full blood count, plus an ultrasound of the tummy. Ease off the fatty food, keep the two Mylanta tablets when it starts, and come back in two weeks for the results.

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): It's my stomach. The cramps. That's why I'm here.

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Stomach cramps. Down low. They ease up after I pass stool.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she's bloated. Pants get unbuttoned by like three every day.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Bloated. All the time. It's annoying.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long's this been going on?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. About a year. Maybe longer. I don't know, call it a year.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): A year. What about the stools themselves?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): They flip flop. I'll be constipated for days, then it goes loose, then back.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And work is a mess. New boss, deadlines every night. She gets home and just crashes on the couch.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, thanks. But yeah, work's been stressful. Can we stay on the stomach.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. The bowels. Constipation and then loose. Say it one more time so I get it in the note.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Alternating. Constipation and loose stools. The whole year.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the stool?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I wish. Nothing's coming off, the clothes are tight from the bloat.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No nausea. I don't throw up.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had bloodwork though. They told her the iron was borderline.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Like six months ago. They said it was borderline. Then nothing.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Borderline iron, okay, typing it. What medicines are you on?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Omprazole. Twenty milligrams every morning, for the heartburn.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Err, I put ten. What's the dose again?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Twenty. Not ten. Every morning.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She actually takes that one. Never skips it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else, a laxative, pain stuff?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Fiber gummies for a bit. I stopped. They just made me gassier.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stopped the fiber gummies. When?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Weeks ago. I'm not on them.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do certain foods set the cramps off?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I can't blame one food.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. Right. So no clear food trigger. Any fever?

[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah that's the spot. You done?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working thought is irritable bowel. Cramps that ease when you go, the bloating, bowels switching for about a year. I'm not calling it final till the bloods are back.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So it's not something awful? She was up googling.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I googled once. Drop it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): No confirmed diagnosis today. I'm ordering bloods, a CBC, a celiac panel, and an iron level since that old one was borderline.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): More needles. Wonderful.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Food wise, eat on a regular schedule, cut back the caffeine, and add fiber slowly instead of a pile of gummies. A food diary for two weeks would help me.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. I'll try. Don't expect perfection, I'm wiped.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in three weeks and we'll go over them. Front desk can book the blood draw for this week.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get her there for the bloods, don't worry.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): I can book my own blood draw. Are we finished.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. Three weeks. Bring the diary if you do it.

[SEG0001] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, I'm Marcus, Mr Delaney's carer. I'll be precise. Yesterday evening, around six, his face drooped on the right side, and his speech was slurred for about ten minutes. It's cleared now.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Marcus, that's very helpful. Mr Delaney, how are you now?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm fine now. Just a bit tired.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you describe what happened, as you remember it?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I was watching the news. My mouth felt strange, like it was numb. And I couldn't find my words.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His right cheek sagged, and his words came out garbled. His arm was fine, I tested it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the droop completely gone now, Marcus?
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Completely gone, the droop and the slurring. By seven it was normal.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in your arm or leg, or loss of vision, even for a moment?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): What medicines is he taking?
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine, 5 mg once a day, and a little blue tablet for his cholesterol, I can't name it, it's in a dosette box, and the pharmacist fills it.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll check the record for the blue one. Any allergies?
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No, none.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And his history?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): High blood pressure, for years.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does he smoke, or drink?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): I gave up smoking years ago. I take a small whisky in the evenings.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me check his face and arms. Mr Delaney, smile for me, raise your eyebrows. ~
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your face is symmetrical, your speech is clear, your arm strength and grip are normal, and your walking is steady.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): So he's all right? ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Today he looks normal, but what you describe sounds like a mini-stroke, a transient ischaemic attack, where the blood supply to part of the brain is briefly interrupted.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): A stroke? ~
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): A warning, not a stroke. These attacks, and their risk of a full stroke over the next days, need urgent attention. ~
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): What do we do? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to refer him today to the stroke clinic, where they'll see him within 24 hours.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Today? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I want you seen urgently, with a brain scan and heart tests. ~
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll take him. ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Until then, if the symptoms return, even for a moment, call 999 straight away, don't wait.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Understood. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): And please don't let him drive.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't drive any more, doctor. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'd like to see him again after the stroke clinic, next week.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll book it. ~

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): My own sister had numb fingers last year and she ended up with an operation on the wrist. She's fine, but that's her life, not yours.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been dropping cups at home. This morning she nearly smashed the mug I won at the braai.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I did drop it. Things just slip. It happens at work too, the small parts.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): The doctor's battling with his screen. He'll be here now now. I'll leave you the file.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, sorry. It froze again. Ok. What brings you in today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): My hands, doctor. At night they go numb, the thumb and the index and the middle finger, and I have to shake them to wake them up.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Say that again? I was still clicking.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Numb at night. Thumb, index, middle finger. Both hands, but the right is worse. I shake them until the feeling comes back.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this been happening?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, about three weeks, ag no, that's wrong. It's been closer to two months. I kept hoping it would pass.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm scared the factory will say I'm not coping. It's packaging work, the same movements all day, and some shifts are twelve hours.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. Is there pain, or only the numbness?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): There's an ache in the wrists as well, mostly at night. Not terrible. The right one is worse.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the feeling run up the arm? Any pain in the neck?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing in the neck. It doesn't go up the arm, it stays in the hand. Sometimes those fingers tingle too.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And in the daytime, numb then as well, or only at night?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly at night. Daytime they're alright unless I've been on the line for hours, then they tingle. Is that a stroke? My uncle had a stroke.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I've been so worried I can't sleep properly. Do I need a scan? Am I going to lose the use of my hands? I have to work tomorrow.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hold on, err, blank screen again. You said a stroke?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her uncle, her mother's brother, had a stroke at sixty. She's been on her phone half the night about it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it a stroke, doctor? Please. Someone at work had a hand operation and she was off for ages. Is that where this is going?
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): This pattern, the thumb and those two fingers, waking you and shaking the hand, that is the median nerve getting pinched in the carpal tunnel at the wrist. The tunnel gets tight and the nerve can't send proper signals, especially when the wrist is bent at night. It is not a stroke.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): So the nerve is squashed in the wrist? Will I need the operation? How long would I be booked off? Can I still do my shifts?
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not an operation today. What I want is a neutral wrist splint at night, so the wrist stays straight and that nerve isn't kinked. Wear it every night for the next few weeks.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, a brace from the pharmacy? Do I wear it on the factory line? What if I can't fall asleep with it on? Will the numbness stop completely?
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nights only, not on the line. Don't strap it so tight your fingers go blue. If it bugs you, loosen it, but try to keep it on.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the tablets, Thandi.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, ibuprofin, I mean ibuprofen. I thought the dose was four hundred milligrams, but no, the box is six hundred, twice a day, with food, for the ache.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): The dose again? I only half caught it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Six hundred milligrams, not four hundred. Twice a day.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Six hundred twice a day. Any tummy trouble with it, ulcers, heartburn?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My stomach is fine. No heartburn. Can I carry on with it together with the splint, or must I stop?
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the ibuprofen for now if the stomach stays happy. Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no allergies. Nothing. Could diabetes be doing this to the nerve? I don't think I have it. Do I need bloods?
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you already have diabetes, thyroid trouble, arthritis?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No diabetes, no thyroid thing. I don't think it's arthritis. I had my gallbladder out about five years ago. Is that connected, sorry, I know that's a lot of questions.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Gallbladder's not connected, no. Do you smoke? What about drinking?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I've never smoked. A glass of wine on a Friday, that's all, we're not big drinkers. If the splint doesn't fix it, then what happens?
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the numbness hasn't settled once you've properly used the splint, we might send you for a nerve conduction test, to check how the median nerve is conducting. I'm not booking that test today.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Does that nerve test hurt, is it needles? Will medical aid cover it, and would I need a sick note to miss a shift? And when do I see you again?
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Wires on the skin, mostly, more uncomfortable than sore. Come back and see me in six weeks so we can judge the splint. Reception will book it. If it gets properly worse before then, phone the rooms.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Splint from the pharmacy, nights only, back in six weeks. Thank you, doctor. Sorry I talked so much.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ag, you're fine. See you in six weeks.

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not with me. I'll bring it next time.

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): I walk the dog every morning.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you got any known allergies?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, um, what was I saying, yes, trimethoprim, it gives me itching.

[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, my father has Parkinson's disease. My uncle has high cholesterol.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): What operations have you had, if any?

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other things?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, gout. Work has been very busy so I kept ignoring it. I have heart disease. I have anxiety, for about ten years. I'd rather know what's going on than keep guessing.

[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): No, you know, not a single one.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll note both what you've said and what you've noticed. Any muscle or joint problems besides this?
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): I move fine otherwise.
[SEG0046] person_5 (NURSE): Okay, so the vitals from earlier. Pulse is 100 beats a minute, blood pressure 124 over 68, saturation 97 percent. Temperature 38.4.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's move on to the examination.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.

[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, you can get dressed.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me tell you where I've got to. The most likely explanation is a quinsy, a peritonsillar abscess. I'd also keep severe tonsillitis in mind. Let me just check I've got this right. You've had a muffled voice, yesterday, and no cough.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Exactly.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to arrange an urgent ENT drainage for peritonsillar abscess. Let's book blood tests to look into abscess.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, what was I saying, where would I go for that?
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm going to put you on benzylpenicillin, 1.2 grams, now, single dose. That's for peritonsillar abscess.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I collect it from my own pharmacy?
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): You need to be seen by ENT today to drain it. And please bring the latest prescription or the medicine boxes to the next visit, so we can settle the dose. Have I covered everything you wanted?
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, thank you, doctor, goodbye.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Goodbye for now.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit him up there. What's the problem today?

[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long is this spell?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sure he's had the dry skin since he was a baby. This bad bit is about six weeks. Umm, maybe a bit more.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking with it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He wakes himself scratching. The sheets are a state in the morning.
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): And then in the morning I feel like a wet rag, all floppy and heavy, because I was scratching all night and I didn't really sleep, and school is hard when I'm sleepy, but the itchy bits are why we came, not the school, the school is grand mostly.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any oozing? Yellow crusts?
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No crusts. Just dry and red.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. He's grand in himself, apart from the itch.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wheeze? Any trouble with the breathing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, not a bother with the breathing. Himself, his dad, has the asthma. Finn doesn't.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tummy pain? Runny eyes?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. My tummy is fine, I had porridge and it was grand. I can't hear myself think when the telly is loud in the kitchen but that's just the telly, not a sore thing. And my eyes don't run, they just blink normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What creams are on him?
[SEG0018] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A grand big white tub, no smell on it, the label's worn off so I couldn't tell you the name. And a little pink tube for the sore patches.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Name or strength on the pink one?
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know it. The chemist just said use the pink one. We put it on the elbows and the backs of the knees.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): The white one is cold, I do it myself sometimes, two squirts, and I rub and rub till it's all gone in, and the pink one is only a tiny dot, mam does that because she says I've overdone it if I squeeze too much out.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often, the white tub?
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most days. Well, when I remember. Some mornings we're out the door and it doesn't get done.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the pink tube?
[SEG0025] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pink tube, once a night on the patches, these last few weeks. Not every single night, if I'm honest.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything by mouth for the itch?
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We had cetirizene. I think it was 10 mg, no, he's small, it was the 5 mg, one at night. I stopped it in March. It made him dopey for school.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else you were given and didn't use?
[SEG0029] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, they gave us fucidin last winter for a spot on his chin and I never opened it. Never gave it to him.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies? Medicines or creams?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Nothing that I know of.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Elbows up. Let me see.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dry thickened patches, both elbow creases and the backs of both knees. No ooze. Skin's not hot. No infection that I can see.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): They look like maps, all pinky and wrinkly, and when you press them it doesn't really hurt, it just itches after, like the ants come straight back, and the left knee is the worse one I think, or maybe the right, I forget which I scratch more.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): This is his eczema flaring. I'm changing the steroid.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the pink tube. I'll give you clobetasone, 0.05 percent, a thin layer twice a day on the patches only, for seven days, then stop it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day, seven days, then stop. Grand.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep a plain moisturiser, lots of it, all over, three or four times a day. The white tub is fine if it's a plain one. Steroid on first, wait twenty minutes, then the moisturiser.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No soap in the bath. Nails short. Cotton at night.
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ok. No soap, short nails, cotton.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Can I still have the blue bubbles? I like a big pile of them and then my skin goes all tight after, and mam says that's why the patches get cross with me, but the bubbles are the best bit of the bath.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No bubbles. They dry the skin.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll live. And if the seven days doesn't clear it?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it's not settling, or if it starts to weep, we might swab it then. Not today.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see him back in three weeks anyway.
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks. Do I book that at the desk?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Reception will put the three weeks in. If it weeps before that, ring us.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Will the ants go if I do the new cream and I don't scratch, because I try not to but then I forget and I do it in my sleep and I wake up and the skin is sore from me, and I don't mean to, it just happens.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): The itch should ease. Hands off it if you can.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks, doctor. Seven days of the new one, the white tub, and back in three weeks.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. Off you go.
