[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 148 over 92. Pulse is 76. Oxygen is 98 percent. Have a seat, he's just finishing next door.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We were stuck on the M50 forty minutes. Some eejit with a trailer sideways at the Red Cow, and the rain bucketing.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I told you to leave earlier. Don't start with me.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Your man on the radio said it's the worst August in years. Then Sean rang, the under twelves hurling is off, the pitch is a swamp. He wanted his grandad in the stand.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Next week so. If the pitch dries.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, sorry about the wait. I'm Dr Brennan. What has you in today?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): The hands. They go dead on me in the night, the thumb and the index and the middle finger. Both hands, the right is worse. Pins and needles, like, and I have to shake them out to wake them up.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): And shaking them brings the feeling back?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Give it a minute. It's driving me up the wall.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's dropping things as well. Dropped a cup of tea on Tuesday, all over the kitchen floor.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): One cup. Don't be making a show of me.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the job hard on the hands?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm on the packing line all day, gripping boxes. That's not helping, sure.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. About three months. Maybe a bit less.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ah no, Pat. It was on you before Christmas. Five months, easy.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not five months. I'd have said.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. You don't agree, so I'll note it as roughly three to five months and we won't fight the date.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is there pain in the hands, or is it just the numbness?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit of an ache in the right wrist in the morning. Not much. It eases once I'm up and moving.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the neck, or pain shooting down from the neck?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's grand.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in the legs, or stumbling?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I'm just tired from being woke up.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks, the bowels, all ticking over?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. Yeah. Grand. No bother there.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on at the minute?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Mizartan for the pressure. Forty milligrams I think, at night. And Omprazole twenty mg every morning for the heartburn.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The Mizartan isn't forty. I did the box on Sunday. It's 80.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it. I don't look. Whatever the chemist hands me. I miss it on the late shift, I'll say that.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the dose of the Mizartan isn't agreed and I won't guess it. The Omprazole twenty, that's every morning?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Every morning.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the hands now. Sensation is duller on the right thumb and index than on the little finger. There's no wasting of the muscles. Tinel's, tapping the right wrist, brings that tingle into the fingers, and the left is milder. Grip is a little down on the right. The neck moves freely and there's no pain when I press.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the exact night tingle. Ow. Can we move this on, I've a shift at two.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): So, to say it back. Both hands, the right worse, numb with pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle at night, you shake them awake, a morning ache in the right wrist, you dropped a cup, somewhere between three and five months. Mizartan for the pressure, dose not settled, missed on the late shifts, Omprazole twenty each morning for the heartburn. No neck pain, no chest pain, no weakness in the legs. Pressure today was 148 over 92.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. Yeah.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): I could reel off three or four things that do this pattern. I'm not going to pick one out today. Let's see what the tests say before anyone puts a name on it.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Get a wrist splint from the chemist, the right one at least, and wear it at night while you sleep. And ease off the heavy gripping on the line if they'll allow it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): They won't love that. Fine. The splint, whatever.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bloods on Thursday morning. Niamh will take a fasting glucose and a thyroid check. Nothing to eat or drink but water from midnight on Wednesday.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday, half eight, you're on my list. Fasting, water only.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks with those results.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it has not settled with the splint by then, we'll book a nerve conduction test. If those bloods are borderline, we'll add a B12. Not today.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get the splint in the chemist on the way home. Come on, Pat, before that rain gets any worse.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Thursday, then two weeks. I just want a night's sleep.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. Mind yourselves out there.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late. The bus was a pure mess and I'm wrecked already.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand, not a bother. Sit yourself down there.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I did tell him to leave earlier. The quays were desperate, bumper to bumper.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): Look, can we leave the bus out of it. I'm not in form for a chat.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of course. What has you in today?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): It's this ringing in me right ear. It's doing me head in.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ringing in the right ear. How long, and is it there all the time?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, two weeks. No, wait, it's a month. A full month. It's there the whole time, worse when it's quiet, and the radio takes the edge off a small bit.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That radio is on half the night. And the ear defenders I bought him are still sitting in the hall.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): You work around loud machinery, do you?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Aye. The plant. Err, machinery roaring the whole shift. They don't give us proper protection so I don't bother with it.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is the hearing itself affected, or is it just the ringing?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hearing's fine. I can hear you grand.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the ear, any discharge, any spinning, any fever?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No pain, no muck coming out, no spinning, no fever. It's the noise, that's all.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Ringing in the right ear for a month, worse in the quiet, loud machinery at work with no ear protection, no pain, no discharge, no spinning, no fever. And you're sure the hearing on that side is normal?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. The right side is muffled. Like cotton wool in it. I have to turn me head to catch the telly.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Any trouble with your breathing or your chest at all?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is grand. I'm not here about that.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had a bad reaction to a medicine?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I came out in a rash all over and me lips swelled up. Years back. They told me never take it again.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what medicines are you on now?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Just the blood pressure one. Lisnopril, five milligrams... no, ten milligrams, once a day. I've high blood pressure for years.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'll have a look in both ears and check the pressure while you're here.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): The right eardrum is intact, a bit dull, no redness and no fluid behind it. The left ear is clear. Blood pressure is 136 over 84, pulse 76.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely noise-related tinnitus from the machinery. I can't rule out a hearing loss on the right until we test it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll refer you to audiology for a hearing test, that'll be booked in. And please wear ear protection on every shift, even if the plant is lax.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Whatever. Just get the test done. I'm sick of the noise in me head.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in six weeks with the result. And if the ringing suddenly gets much worse, or you get discharge or real spinning, don't wait, come straight back.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll make sure he actually wears the defenders. And I'll get him here for the six weeks.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's great. We'll leave the penicillin well alone, nothing in that family from me.

[SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. Dr Shah will see you in a minute. I'll just pop the cuff on for your blood pressure, alright?

[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Have a seat. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my skin. I've got this awful itchy rash between my fingers and round my waist, where the waistband rubs. It's been about three weeks, maybe a bit longer, and it's driving me mad.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. When you say three weeks, has it been there the whole time?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, yes, the whole time. I kept thinking I've overdone it at the cafe with all the hand washing, but this isn't just dry skin.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): And is there a time of day it's worse?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights. After tea I'm climbing the walls. It's like something's crawling under the skin between my fingers, and there's a bit on the inside of my wrists now too. I barely sleep.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Can you see spots, or is it only the itch?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Little bumps, and I've scratched it raw in places. Same along the waist.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is anyone else in the house itching?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. My partner Tom is scratching his wrists. And our little boy, he's four, he's itchy at bedtime as well. I'm frightened I've given it to them. We keep the place clean, honestly.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hmm, let me think this through. Fingers, waist, wrists, worse at night, and the people you live with itching too. That is very likely scabies. The mite sits in the skin, which is that crawling feeling.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh god. Does that mean we're dirty? I hoover every single day.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it doesn't mean that at all. It spreads by close skin contact, and tidy houses get it just the same.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still work? I'm in a cafe, hands on everything. And can he go to nursery, or do I have to keep him off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): After the cream has gone on, you can be back at work the next day, and he can be back at nursery the next day. We'll go through it step by step so it isn't a muddle.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Is it that permetrin cream I read about? How do I even put it on?
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, often sold as Lyclear. You apply it from the neck downwards, all over, and leave it on for eight to twelve hours.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not my face? What about under my nails, I bite them. And, umm, down below, do I have to?
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave the face unless it's itchy there. Do go under the nails, between the fingers, the soles, the groin and the bottom. Is your scalp itchy?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Scalp's fine. Face isn't itchy either. It's the hands and the waist.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Have a shower, dry off, then put the cream on cool skin. Leave it overnight and wash it off in the morning. Everybody at home should do it on the same night.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Even a four year old, the same night? Is that safe? I've read scary things online.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, it's the treatment we use from two months of age. You or Tom put it on him, neck down. Then all of you repeat the exact same thing seven days later.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I miss a patch, say behind a knee? Does it all fail? And does it sting? I'm going to mess it up.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can tingle a little. Try not to miss hands, wrists, waist, feet and the groin. If you've been careful, you don't throw the whole thing out over one small gap.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the bedding? There's a mountain of it. I'm all over the place trying to think it through.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wash clothes and bedding from the last three days at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, bag it for seventy-two hours. Don't buy insecticide sprays for the sofa, they aren't needed.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two hours for his rabbit as well, the soft toy? And all the towels?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, bag the soft toy or hot wash it. Towels from those three days too. The mites die off the body quite quickly, so it isn't the whole house.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try Canesten from the chemist last week, the antifungal one. I thought it was a sweat rash. It did nothing at all.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's clotrimazole, so it was never going to clear this. You can stop it. Anything else you've put on the skin?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I put the yellow steroid cream on, the hydrocortisone, twice last week, then I stopped because it wasn't doing much. And I take my water tablet every morning, the bendro, two point five, for my blood pressure. Years, that's been.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the bendroflumethiazide as usual. Hydrocortisone might ease the itch a touch but it won't kill the mites. Any allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Oh, and last autumn they did a cholesterol blood test, and the nurse said it was borderline. They never started me on anything.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't go into that today, I haven't got a figure in front of me. Any fever while this has been going on? Any cough, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No cough. Breathing's alright actually. I just feel like a wet rag from not sleeping.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Yes, small burrows between the fingers, and scratch marks where the waistband sits. No sign of a spreading skin infection.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Are those little lines the burrows? If I'm still itching in a fortnight, has it failed? I can't keep going like this.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itch often carries on for two or three weeks after the mites are dead, so a fortnight doesn't mean it failed. If the rash is still spreading after the second treatment, or if you see pus, or you feel feverish, come back sooner. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. And Tom and our boy definitely treat the same night, even if his spots are tiny? How much cream do we get?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same night, all three of you, whether you can see much or not. I'll prescribe three tubes of permethrin five percent to start with. You repeat it on day seven, so check with the chemist whether you'll need more cream for that second go. Reception can book the four week visit.
[SEG0045] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pop out to me when you're done and I'll book the four weeks. The prescription usually hits the chemist next door within the hour.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry for firing questions. I'll write every step down so I don't lose them.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, I'm so worried. I've not wanted any food and I've lost weight, and I don't know what's happening to me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come and sit down, Mr Okonkwo. We'll look into it together. Who's with you today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Dee, I'm his carer. I come in each morning and evening. I brought him because I'm worried too.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you, Dee, that's helpful. Mr Okonkwo, let me check I have it right. You're not wanting food and you've lost weight.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Is it serious? Tell me the truth.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll tell you everything as I learn it. First, how long has the appetite been poor?
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): About three weeks. He leaves nearly the whole plate, and he used to love his stew.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Three weeks, yes, it sounds right. Though it feels longer.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the weight. When did you first notice that?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, I couldn't tell you. My trousers were loose one day and I couldn't say when it began.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all right. Dee, have you noticed a change?
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His belt's gone in two holes, but I only started keeping an eye on it recently, so I can't give a date either.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the weight loss has crept up and you can't pin down when. Fair enough.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): And I'm very tired, doctor. Very tired, all day, even after sleeping.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Very tired all day. Noted. Any vomiting?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And does it hurt when you swallow food?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no, swallowing's fine. I just don't fancy anything.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's helpful. Now, what tablets do you take?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): The one for my heart. Dee, what's it called?
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Bisoprolol. 2.5 mg, every morning. I give it to him myself.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bisoprolol, 2.5 mg every morning. Any other long-term problems?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): High blood pressure. Years and years.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Do you have any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh dear. I think I came out in something once, years ago, after an antibiotic. But I can't remember which one, or what happened.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): So a possible reaction to an antibiotic, but you're not sure which. We'll be careful, and I'll make a note.
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that bad? Should I be frightened?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at all, it's simply a precaution. Now, you live on your own, I believe?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, since my wife passed. The house is very quiet, you know.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry. Dee comes twice a day, and that's a great help. Let me check your observations.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure 108 over 64. Pulse 96. Temperature 36.9. Oxygen 97 percent. Breathing 16. And your weight is 58 kilos.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it very bad? Fifty-eight kilos is so low.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Those numbers are a little on the low side for blood pressure and a little fast for the pulse. Nothing frightening on its own.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, thank goodness.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Open your mouth for me, please, and stick your tongue out.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your mouth is rather dry. Now let me press your tummy. Tell me if it hurts.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Ooh, that's all right. Does it feel odd?
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your tummy is soft and not tender. That's a good sign.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): What do you think it is, doctor? Is it cancer?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I understand why you ask. I don't want to guess about that today. What I think most likely is that you're mildly dehydrated because you've hardly been eating or drinking.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Mildly dehydrated. And that makes me tired?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can. So we'll deal with it in steps. Today I'd like to order some blood tests, to check your kidneys, salts and blood count.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Can I take him down for those straight after?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, please do. I'd also like to arrange a chest X-ray at the same time, since we're checking everything.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): An X-ray too? Why the chest?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Because weight loss deserves a thorough look, and it's quick. It doesn't mean I've found anything.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): All right. If you think it's best.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I do. In the meantime, Dee, small sips of fluid through the day, and little snacks rather than big plates.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can do that. Soup, yoghurt, that sort of thing.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): And a nice cup of tea, perhaps?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tea counts. So, tests today, little and often with food and fluids. Does that make sense, Mr Okonkwo?
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Tests today, little and often. Thank you for being kind, doctor.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Come on, Mr Okonkwo, I'll walk you down.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): righto, shoes off for a sec. weight and blood pressure before the doctor.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah. that waiting room, i can't hear myself think with the telly and the kids.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): blood pressure's one twenty over eighty. uh the cuff slipped. it's one thirty two over seventy eight. pulse 74, weight 79 kilos.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): g'day, dr patel. sorry about the wait. you've brought someone.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): jess. support worker. i come so things actually get followed up.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): she acts like i'd do a runner. i'm fine, this is a waste of an arvo.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): what do you want sorted, then?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): nothing, really. spots on my face, and my periods are weird. mum kicked off so jess dragged me. spots and weird periods.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): weird in what way?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): they disappear for ages, then just show up. i've overdone it with night shifts at the cafe. end of story.
[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): there's weight gain as well, and dark hairs on her chin. she shaves before work.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): it's peach fuzz, relax. i have gotten heavier. i feel like a wet rag after a shift. so what.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): how long have the spots and the irregular periods been going?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): umm, six months. no, that's not right. year twelve was two years ago and it had started already. so two years.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): and the weight and the chin hair?
[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): the hair's been a good few months. weight since last summer, less than a year.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): if you say so. i'm not keeping score.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): let me see. inflamed spots along the jaw, coarse dark hairs on the chin. not loads, but they're there.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): any pain low in the tummy, or pain when you bleed?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): nah. no pain.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): could you be pregnant?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): no way. i'm not seeing anyone.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): bowels been okay?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): yeah, fine.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): what about your breathing, or chest pain?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): no. chest is fine, breathing's fine.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): thinking out loud, acne plus irregular cycles plus chin hair and the weight, that can be polycystic ovary syndrome. here's the plan. i'll start you on levlen, one combined pill a day, to settle the skin and the cycle, and we'll send you for bloods.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): i don't want tablets. my feet feel dead after a double shift. that's just standing all day, not something a pill fixes.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): fair. before i prescribe anything, any headaches, zigzags, sparkly vision?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): err, sometimes a headache and the edges go sparkly. i lie down, it passes. it's nothing.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): sparkly edges like that are an aura, so i'm changing the plan. no levlen, i don't start a combined pill with migraine aura. we'll do the tests and decide later, and nothing is started today.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): family wise, diabetes? i'd add glucose if there is.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): mum's got type two diabetes, years of it. not me though.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): okay. these are booked, not a wait and see. fasting glucose, hba1c, testosterone, lh and fsh, and a pelvic ultrasound to look at the ovaries.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): a scan. for pimples. sure.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): medicines in the last while, and any allergies?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): no allergies. i tried doxycyclin, fifty milligrams, no, a hundred milligrams once a day for two weeks, then i stopped. useless. nothing since.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): we'll leave that doxycycline off. do you smoke at all?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): never have. two or three beers on a saturday, max.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): jot down when you bleed. a brand new worst ever headache means emergency, not the clinic. otherwise i want you back in three weeks for these results, that's booked in.
[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): i'll make sure she comes. she lives with her mum, i'll text her.
[SEG0042] person_1 (NURSE): i'll lock in the bloods, the pelvic scan and the three week review out the front.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): ta. frog in my throat, your aircon's dry as. just need water, not a diagnosis.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): water's by the desk. see you in three weeks.

[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Two months now, doctor. Umm, almost every night. They wake me. Both calves, though the right is the worse one.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Leah, his daughter. I hear him from the passage when it starts. We were late, sorry, the robots were out.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No, doctor. None.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cough?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Not that either, doctor.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weight going up or down?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't really say, doctor. Um, I have not been keeping track.

[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): A water tablet, doctor. Furoseamide, uh, 40 milligrams, one every morning. I have had high blood pressure for many years, and the tablet is for that.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm not sure it's every morning, doctor. Some days the tablet is still sitting there when he leaves.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): I believe I take it as I was instructed, doctor. I do not mean to miss it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything from the chemist?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. Magnesium, which I bought myself at the chemist. I think the strength is 250 milligrams, one at night, for the cramps. Err, I have used it for a few weeks.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much water in a day?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Very little, I am afraid. Two cups of tea and perhaps one glass of water. That is about all.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I pack a bottle and it comes home still full. Every time.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): With the blood pressure, any headaches?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, doctor. A mild one, early in the morning. Not every day.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): While we're here, his grandson, my Kyle, made fifty at cricket on Saturday. You should have seen the boy's face.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): It was a lovely innings, yes. We sat in the sun the whole afternoon. The heat this week has been quite something, has it not?
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja. Storms building over the Highveld too. I caught the Proteas on the radio driving in, that last over.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The drive back from the ground was worse than the robots this morning. If the bonus comes through we'll get him new pads.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): He has his eye on a bat as well. Gray-Nicolls, I think. Quite dear.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Legs.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think these are night cramps from the water tablet and not drinking enough. I can't rule out a low potassium until the bloods are back.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll book bloods for the potassium and the kidney function. Stretch each calf before bed, hold it thirty seconds, both sides. Drink more water through the day. If the cramps have not settled we might do a scan of the legs, but not now.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall stretch, and I shall try to drink more. When ought I to come back?
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks with the results. Sister will sort the form.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take you down to the lab, Mr Pillay, they can draw it this morning. Watch the step by the door.

[SEG0001] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, this is Liam. Back from Thailand on Saturday, fever and a rash. His mam's with him. ~
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Niamh. Hello Liam, hello Mrs Doyle. What's been happening? ~
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Fever. Rash.
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's not a man for words, doctor. Let me say it. He's had the fever since he got back, and the rash came out the day after.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Liam, how long have you had the fever, in your own words?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Three days.
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not three days, it's a week. I took his temperature at the airport on the Saturday before last and it was up then.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, you say three days, your mother says closer to a week. I'll put that down as three to seven days, and we'll see if we can narrow it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Feels like three.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Where's the rash?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Chest, back. Bit on my arms.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's red spots, not itchy, he says.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding, from the gums or nose, or in the stool?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you allergic to any medicines, any allergies at all?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And are you taking anything at the moment?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Doxycycline, 100 mg once a day, for malaria. I took it all trip. Missed a couple.
[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has tablets left, I saw the packet. ~
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): What were you up to in Thailand? Any insect bites, rural areas, fresh water swimming?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Beaches. Island. Loads of mosquito bites.
[SEG0022] person_3 (NURSE): Doctor, his obs. ~
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Go on, Niamh. ~
[SEG0024] person_3 (NURSE): Temperature 38.6, pulse 104, blood pressure 118 over 70.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Liam, let me look at the rash. ~
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fine, flat red spots over the chest and back, and they blanch when I press them.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What does that mean? ~
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): It means the spots fade under pressure, which is a more reassuring sign. But with a fever and recent tropical travel, I can't take chances. ~
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): What is it? ~
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most likely a viral illness, such as dengue, picked up from the mosquitoes, but I need the experts to look at you today.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Today? ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. I'm going to refer you to the infectious diseases team at the hospital and ring them now, they'll see you this afternoon.
[SEG0034] person_3 (NURSE): I'll write out the letter, doctor. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please. Liam, take paracetamol only if you have to, and don't take ibuprofen or aspirin until they've seen you.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. ~
[SEG0037] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll drive him up. ~
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please do, and go straight there. ~

[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mizartan? Repeat that, the screen's changed it.

[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies? To medicines or anything else?

[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about Miso. Go on.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, our cat Miso scratched my left forearm about a month ago. It bled a little, I washed it, and it's healed now, just a faint line. I didn't think it linked to my neck, they're different spots, but mum's been reading things.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): When was the scratch? Sorry, an email popped up.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): About a month ago. Left forearm. Healed. The lump started after that, the three weeks, so the scratch was first.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. I was going to send you straight for a fine needle biopsy. With the cat scratch I'm changing that. Blood tests and an ultrasound of the neck, and we'll leave the biopsy.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. I had myself braced for a needle today, I even looked up whether you can drive after, which is silly because mum drove anyway.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me feel it. Chin up a bit. There's a soft lump on the left side of the neck, about two centimetres, it moves, it's not tender, and the skin over it looks normal. No other nodes that I can feel.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): About two centimetres, okay. I had one and a half on a sewing tape but I was squashing it in the bathroom mirror, so yours is the one that counts, I won't argue the half centimetre.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. I'm not naming it today. It could be a reactive lymph node, possibly from the cat scratch, but I can't exclude other causes till the tests are back.
[SEG0034] person_1 (NURSE): Want the bloods done now while she's here?
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Full blood count, CRP, and cat scratch serology today, and book the neck ultrasound for this week. Come back in a fortnight for the results. If it suddenly gets bigger or you spike a fever, go to emergency rather than waiting.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight works, I'll swap my Thursday close at the cafe, my manager's alright with notice. I'll bring the Mizartan box so you can see the spelling, and if the ultrasound is way out in the suburbs mum'll drive.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get her here. The vet thing for Miso is the week after, that's nothing to do with this.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Itchy as well. I want to scratch and then I stop myself. There's only a handful, five or six blisters, all on the left, none round the other side.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or pain when you breathe in, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's easy. No cough.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And otherwise, any problem with your tummy or your waterworks?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, tummy's fine, waterworks fine. Oh, but I've had a frog in my throat all week, all croaky. Probably the dust off those pots.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been croaky, yes. The chest is what we came about, though.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Croaky for a week, and the chest for two days. May I have a look at the rash?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Go on, then. Mind, my feet feel dead from that waiting room chair. That's just the chair, not my feet playing up.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll leave the chair out of it. On the left chest there's a band of red skin with a few small clear blisters, and it stops at the midline. It's tender where I press.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yes, that's the bit.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Did you have chickenpox as a child?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Lord, yes. I was about seven, covered in spots. Mum painted me in calamine and shut the curtains, and I haven't had it since.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): While we're on tablets, doctor, don't put her on biotin. Those gummies are my sister Claire's, for her hair. Mum nearly took one this morning, thinking it was the blood pressure pill.

[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's meant to take it every morning, but if she's out in the garden she skips it. I wouldn't swear she's had it every day this week.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol. Two five hundred milligram tablets, four times a day, since yesterday. It helps a bit, not loads.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol one gram, four times a day. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I come up in a rash, big red blotches. I stay right away from it.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Penicillin with a rash, thank you. Any pain in the eye, or spots creeping up near it?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing near the eye. Eyes are fine.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. My first thought was to swab those blisters and hold off the antivirals till the result came back, just some calamine on the skin meanwhile.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): But Claire's pregnant, and this only started two days ago. She was all over Mum yesterday.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want to pass anything on. Claire's never had chickenpox, she told me so.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): That changes it. Forget the swab, and forget waiting on a result. This is shingles, I think, herpes zoster on the left chest, with the one-sided burning, the blisters, and chickenpox as a child.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles. My neighbour had that and she was miserable for weeks, wouldn't even chat over the fence. Are you giving me something today, then?
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, today. I'll start you on valaciclovir, one gram by mouth, three times a day, for seven days. You're still inside the seventy two hours, so it's worth it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Vala-sicky-veer, is that how you say it? Will the chemist actually have it in?
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Valaciclovir, yes, and they should. Carry on with the paracetamol, up to four times a day, and try not to scratch.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): The other bit is Claire. Keep the rash covered, don't share towels, and no close contact with her until those blisters have crusted. If she's never had chickenpox she could catch it from you, and that's risky in pregnancy.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll text her to stay away. What about seeing Mum again?
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a week, to check the rash is crusting and the tablets suit you. If it spreads toward the eye, or you get feverish or muddled, ring the surgery the same day, don't wait for that appointment.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A week I can do. The garden can mind itself. I'll try not to start on the pots again.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll sort a blister pack so the amlodipine actually gets swallowed, and I'll take Claire's biotin back to mine.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Two days of burning on the left chest, a few blisters in a band, no fever, no breathlessness, chickenpox as a child, a penicillin rash, amlodipine and paracetamol. [SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): You've got the lot. Thanks, doctor. Come on, love, before I get going about those pots again.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame, you made it. I was stuck at the robot by the garage for twenty minutes, some bakkie just wouldn't move.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, we came the long way round. The radio had the cricket on, the Proteas, and I missed half an over with all the hooting.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They were something like 180 for 4, Rabada was bowling. We nearly had a fight in the car about whether that catch was clean. Lovely day for it though, not too hot.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, I only saw the score at lunch. Right. What have you come about today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my left hand, doctor. I'm 68, three months since the mild stroke, and it's still a bit weak, and I can't stop thinking it's going to happen again.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Show me what it actually does. Buttons, a cup, that sort of thing?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, buttons are a proper nightmare and the tea cup feels clumsy. It's not sore. The fingers just don't listen. Is that going to stay like this forever?
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a feel. Squeeze my fingers, both hands. Ja, the left grip is a little down compared with the right, nothing dramatic. How's the walking, are you still getting out?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, round the block most mornings. It takes me a bit longer than it used to, but I do it. Is slower walking a bad sign, or, uh, am I being silly?
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He does go most mornings. I go along if I'm not at the shops. He's not been on the ground or anything.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): My speech was funny right at the beginning. That's what scares me. Does that mean another one is coming?
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): How is the speech today, as we sit here?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): It's fine now. The slurring went after the first week or so. People understand me, hey.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Any fever in the last while, hot or shivery?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And a cough, or bringing anything up?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough at all.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the stomach and the bowels, anything not right?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No, tummy's normal and the bowels are regular.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight, has it gone up or down since the stroke?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, err, I don't actually know. Maybe a bit down, maybe the same. The scale at home is all over the place.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He still finishes his food. I wouldn't say he's wasting.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll park the weight, that scale isn't helping us. Let me take the pressure... 152 over 88.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? Too high? I take the amlodopine, the 5 milligram tablet, in the morning, for the blood pressure. Should you put it up?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): 152 over 88 is a touch above where I want it after a stroke, but I'm not changing the amlodipine today. You've had the high blood pressure for years, ja?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, years now. And every morning I take asprin, a hundred and fifty mg, and at night the atorvastin, 40 milligrams, the cholesterol one they started after the stroke.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay on all three, don't skip any. Aspirin 150 milligrams every morning, atorvastatin 40 at night, amlodipine 5 in the morning. If the hand is still the same in a couple of months, we might do a scan, but I'm not booking one today.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A brain scan? What are you looking for? And if it gets worse next week, do I wait? Can I still drive to the chemist?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the weakness suddenly worsens, or the speech goes again, or a side goes numb, you go to casualty, don't wait. Short drives are fine if that hand can hold the wheel, and from what I felt it can. I'll see you here in three months either way.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months feels long. What if I seize up from sitting? I get anxious just thinking about it.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We live together, so I'm around. I keep telling him the morning walk is plenty.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep that morning walk, don't add a big programme on top. What I'm seeing fits residual weakness from the mild stroke, not a new one today. Reception will book that three month visit as you leave.

[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I drove her. I come weekday mornings, I don't live with her.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): let me get a blood pressure before he comes in. arm out. try not to talk for a sec.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): that can't be right. at the kitchen table this morning it was 130 over 82, I wrote it down.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I watched her. it was 132 over 80. she ran it twice.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): hey, sorry, one second, this screen just froze. uh. okay. what brings you in?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): well, where do I even start, the left shoe, I bought those back in march, and now I can't even...
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): sorry, say that again? I clicked the wrong chart. what's the main thing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): my ankles are all swollen, and I'm running to the bathroom all day.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): swollen ankles. how long?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): about three weeks. I've had high blood pressure for years, that's not why I came, but the ankles started as a little sock ring in the evenings and now it's both of them all day, the left one more, and my shoes leave a dent.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): it got worse after they changed her blood pressure pill. I keep telling her that.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): right, the high blood pressure. which pill. hold on, the list is loading.
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): on the med list I have amlodipine five milligrams once a day, and hydrochlorothiazide.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): no, that's the old dose. they bumped the amlodipene to ten. the bottle says ten milligrams, one every morning with my coffee.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): can you repeat that dose? the cursor jumped.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): ten milligrams. one tablet every morning. I set the pill box up on mondays. the water pill is twenty-five.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): yes, hydrochlorthiazide, twenty-five milligrams, also in the morning, and then I pee and pee. sometimes eight or nine times before lunch, and I get up twice at night, even if I skip my tea.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): any pain or burning when you pee?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): no burning, no pain. just often. the stream seems fine, I mean I'm not measuring it or anything.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): any fever?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): tell him about the shoes not zipping, you were going on about that in the car.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): oh. no fever. I checked yesterday with that thermometer from the drugstore, it said 98.4.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): lungs wise, any cough, wheezing, shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): no, none of that. there was a little tickle last month from the neighbor's cat but that was nothing, no cough now.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): what about your weight, any change?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): umm I don't know. the scale sticks, sometimes it says I'm up a couple pounds, sometimes it doesn't, I really couldn't tell you.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): yeah, don't trust that scale. it jumped six pounds in one day. nonsense.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): mm. right. let me see the ankles. shoes off.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): the left is the stubborn one. I sleep with a pillow under my feet and in the morning it's a little better, then by dinner it's back, which is annoying when we have...
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): both ankles are puffy. it pits when I press. pulses in the feet are fine.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): see, I knew it wasn't just thick socks. I ordered those beige compression things and they roll down and leave a worse groove, so I quit wearing them.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think the swelling is from the amlodipine. that medicine does this pretty often.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): but then what about my pressure, the home numbers are decent and yours aren't, and if you stop it won't I just...
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): we're going to stop the amlodipine. I'll start losartan, fifty milligrams, once a day, in its place.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): what about the water pill? she can't be sprinting to the bathroom at the senior center, they have one stall.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): keep the hydrochlorothiazide, twenty-five milligrams, every morning. same as now. don't move it to nighttime.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): so the water one stays with breakfast. and losartan, is that the one that starts with an l, because my sister takes something and she never stops talking about it...
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): yes. losartan fifty milligrams once a day. I'm also ordering a basic metabolic panel today, kidneys and electrolytes.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): I can draw that before you leave. lab's still open.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): good. put your feet up in the afternoon. if you get dizzy, or the swelling suddenly gets a lot worse, call us.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): and the peeing, is that just my life now? eight times in a morning, I timed it, I was late to my hair appointment last tuesday and she gave my slot away.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): the water pill is doing that. morning is the right time. we'll see you back in two weeks and look again.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): two weeks. should I bring the notebook? I write the date, the top number, the bottom number, sometimes a little star if I felt funny.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): bring the notebook, yes. sorry, what was that home reading again? I never typed it.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): 132 over 80. this morning.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I had 130 over 82 in my head, but she was watching, so she's probably right.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): okay. we'll use today's clinic pressure for the chart. reception will book the two weeks.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): thank you. I'll try not to talk the poor girl's ear off during the blood draw, last time I got going about my tomatoes and the tube...

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on back. You look like the waiting room wore you out.

[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sure. What's the main problem today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach cramps. And my bowels are a mess.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me what the cramps do.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): They're low, more on the left. A grabby pain. When I pass stool they ease off. Been a year.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): The bowels, what's the mess exactly?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I go constipated for days, then it's loose, then constipated again. Whole year, same as the cramps. And I'm bloated most afternoons, worse when work goes crazy.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you do for work, if that's the trigger?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Project manager at a logistics firm. Stress is basically the job. It never turns off.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm 46 and I feel like my body just quit on me. Don't need a lecture, okay.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): No lecture. Let me say it back. Left-sided cramps that get better after a bowel movement, bloating most afternoons, constipation trading off with loose stool, all for a year, and work stress makes the bloating worse.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. You got it. Finally.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the toilet, or black stool?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I checked more than once. No blood.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. If anything I'm up a little from sitting at a desk. I have not lost weight.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fevers? Chills?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I don't know. I get hot sitting at my desk but the vents are broken, and I never stuck a thermometer in, so maybe, maybe not.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, fever's a maybe, we'll leave it. Have you vomited?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. I do get queasy when the cramp hits, but it passes.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Top of my list is a sensitive gut, irritable bowel, especially with the stress and the way the pain eases when you go. I will not put that down as final today. I also can't rule out celiac, or a thyroid problem, from the story alone.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Wonderful. So nobody knows. What now, more pills?
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe not more pills. What are you on already?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the pressure, five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Next?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The cholesterol one at night. It's simvastaten, twenty milligrams. And sugar tablets, metformin, five hundred milligrams twice a day.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): So amlodipine five in the morning for the pressure, simvastatin twenty at night, metformin five hundred twice a day. Any shop remedies, teas, powders?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. Half a teaspoon in water. Label's gone, I couldn't tell you the real name.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister dumped it on me. I take it so she'll stop texting. It's probably nothing.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the amlodipine, the simvastatin, and the metformin going just as you are. Hold the powder until we're clearer. I don't want a mystery mix in the background.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Easy. I didn't like the taste anyway.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm going to order bloods. A blood count, a metabolic panel, thyroid tests, and a celiac screen. The lab here can draw you on the way out. I'll put the order in now.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): All of that today? Ugh. Okay. Stick me and let me leave.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the food side, keep a plain diary for the next two weeks, what you eat and what your gut does. And cut back on the usual agitators.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I live on coffee. Four cups, easy, and a sad desk salad. That's lunch.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four cups is a lot. Try bringing coffee down to one or two a day, and eat smaller meals, and see if the cramps settle. Not a punishment, just a trial.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): One or two. I'll try. I'm not gonna be nice about it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's allowed. Come back in three weeks and we'll look at the labs and the diary together.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. What if this gets ugly before then?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you see blood, if you can't keep liquids down, or if the pain turns sharp and stays, don't sit on it. Urgent care or the ER. Otherwise three weeks is fine.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Got it. Blood, can't drink, pain that stays. ER. Thrilling.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): One quick look at your belly before you go, if you'll let me.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah yeah. Just don't poke the left side like you're mad at it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft belly. Tender over the left lower side where you said, no rebound, bowel sounds are present.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yep. That's the spot. Are we done?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): We're done for today. Labs on your way out, hold the powder, diary and less coffee, and I'll see you in three weeks.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks. If the diary is a mess of scribbles don't yell at me.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Scribbles are fine. As long as I can read the pattern. Take care, Ms. Hale.

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, repeat that, the vent is loud. Fever yes or no, and have you been coughing?

[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about your weight, up or down?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, love. You look a bit worn out. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Didn't want to come, if I'm honest. I'm tired, and it's these morning sweats and the shakes. That's the whole reason.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds miserable. Walk me through what a morning's like.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I wake up dripping. Hands shaking. Err, three weeks of it now. I feel rotten until I eat, if I even eat.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She doesn't eat, doctor. Mum's been skipping brekky most days.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh leave it. I'm not hungry at six. The trains were stuffed again, but that's not... anyway.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. So the sweating and the shaking are on you before any food. How often is that?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every morning. Some days worse. I'm over it.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And one morning last week she was confused. Couldn't sort the kettle, kept asking me what day it was.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not confused. I was half asleep. Well, actually, that once I wasn't making sense. It passed after a cup of tea.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. Settled after the tea. Any chest pain when this happens?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Don't add things.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. What about your breathing? Any cough, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is wiped by lunch though. Flat on our couch. She moved in with us last year, so I see all of it.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I'm knackered. Couch is lumpy, write that down if you like.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, lumpy couch. The diabetes has been with you a good while though, hasn't it. How long?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-odd years. Umm. Tablets, not the needles. Thank goodness.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets, and what doses are you on these days?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. The chemist does a Webster pack. Metforman and the other one. Ask her, I'm sick of the questions.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Gliclazide, eighty milligrams, every morning. Metformin, five hundred milligrams, morning and night. She does take them.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): And that gliclazide still goes down on the mornings with no brekky?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Swallow it with water, down the hatch. Food can wait.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, side note. My husband left his metformin in the car boot again. His are the one gram tablets, not Mum's. And he reckons Aunty Pam's biotin is why her nails grew. Rubbish.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Pam can keep the biotin. I'm not taking that.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave both of those alone. Any reactions to medicines? Anything you're allergic to?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I get a red rash all over and my lips swell up. Years ago. They told me never to have it again.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Penicillin, rash and swollen lips. We'll steer well clear of that. Mind if I check you over?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. Be quick, I want a lie down.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is seventy-six, nice and regular. Blood pressure's one forty-two over seventy-eight. Hands are cool and a bit clammy. Chest is clear, heart sounds normal, and the tummy's soft with nothing tender.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Cold hands. Story of my life.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I reckon these morning sweats and shakes are low sugars, hypos, from the gliclazide on an empty stomach. That muddled morning fits the same thing.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm not losing the plot. Good. I suppose.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not losing the plot. I do want bloods today, the HbA1c and a kidney check while you're on metformin. We'll book both.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The pathology on High Street, same as usual?
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, reception out the front will book it. Have some brekky with that gliclazide, even toast. If you get shaky, juice or a few jelly beans and sit yourself down. Come back and see me in two weeks with the results, I'm not changing the dose today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Toast. Fine. I'm done in.

[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Three point eight. Mm. That's a shade over the 2 to 3 we like. Come on in and sit yourself down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Traffic was desperate. I'm grand though, hardly worth the trip. They only rang about the bloods.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll go through it anyway. You're on the warfarin for the atrial fibrillation, yes?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, five-ish years now. The five milligram tablet, once a day. Not a bother.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't let him skip the rest, doctor. He's on Mizartan as well, forty milligrams, for the pressure.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): And the Omprazole, twenty milligram in the morning, for a bit of heartburn. Sure that's nothing.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Did someone start an antibiotic on you somewhere else?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Out of hours last week, for a cough. Clarithromycin, 500, twice a day, well actually twice a day, and two days left. Only a tickle, like.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was more than a tickle, he was barking at night. And just so it's not written on him, my mam, his wife, is on Metformine for her sugar.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't put her Metformine anywhere near his list. Umm. Any fever with all this?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Fever? No. Not a bit of one.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your weight shifted at all?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Same as ever.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the cough itself, is it still about?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Err. It's there and it isn't. Mostly gone. Nothing to be writing down.
[SEG0017] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's gone off the cabbage and the spinach this last fortnight. Leaves them on the plate.
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of wind, that's all. I just pushed them aside. It's grand.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right so, let me think it out. Clarithromycin can lift the INR, and easing off the greens takes the vitamin K down, so the warfarin works harder. I'm not surprised we're at three point eight.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): It's only a number. I'm not bleeding.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any bruising you've spotted, or blood in the urine, or black stools?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I keep telling ye I'm grand.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of. Let me see your arms. No bruising there. And the chest sounds clear enough.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): So my working impression is the INR is up from the antibiotic and the diet change, not from a bleed. Nothing surer than that until we repeat it.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Do I knock the warfarin on the head then? Seems an awful fuss.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, don't stop it. I'd drop you from five milligrams down to four milligrams once a day, starting this evening.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Will I put the cabbage back on the dinner?
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the greens steady, a similar portion most days. Don't binge on them and don't cut them out. And finish the clarithromycin, there's only the two days.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Four milligrams. If you say so. Still think I'm fine.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll repeat the INR in a week, and I'll see you back here in a week the same day.
[SEG0031] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll have him here. He'll pretend he doesn't need to come.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): I'll come. I'm not that contrary.
[SEG0033] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the bloods for this day week, first thing.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand. So that's four milligrams from tonight, INR in a week, and in to me after.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Sure look, a lot of talk over nothing.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you get a big bruise or any bleeding, don't sit on it, ring the surgery. The visit in a week stands either way.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, the chair by the desk is grand. What brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor I'm really worried. It's the cramps and the bloating, my bowels are all over the shop.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. How long has this been going on, and what actually happens?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A year, um, a full year. Some days I'm bunged up for ages and then it goes loose, the cramp eases once I pass a stool, and the stress in work sets the cramp off. Is that serious? Be honest with me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, playing that back, cramps that ease when you open the bowels, bloating, and the stool alternating between constipation and loose, for a year.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes that's it. And the stress in work is making it worse. Could it be cancer? I need you to tell me.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't dodge it, we'll get there. Any blood in the stool, red or black?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None. I check every time.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No weight loss. The jeans are tighter but that's the bloat, not weight.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I take buscapan as well, 10 milligrams when the cramp hits, usually twice a day. Is that making the loose stools? Should I stop it?
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Unlikely to be the cause of a whole year of this. Stay on the 10 milligrams for the cramps for now. Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Err, the nurse wrote sertraline fifty milligrams on the sheet this morning. Once a day, she said.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah no, that's not right. I'm on a hundred milligrams every morning. She has the old dose. It's for the anxiety, I've had the anxiety for years.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, two different doses on the table and I won't pick one. We'll check it with the chemist. The anxiety we know about. Tell me the family history, since you were fretting about cancer.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my brother is grand, and another sister has pressure but no sugar. No bowel cancer in the family, not that I know of anyway.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Father with the diabetes, your sister with pressure, and your mother did not have it. Day to day now, the job, the hours, what you eat, the exercise and the drink?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in the accounts office in the county council, 37 hours a week, mostly stuck at the desk. The diet is sandwiches and tea, I don't get any exercise, I don't walk or anything, and I'll have a glass of wine most nights and two glasses at the weekend.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a feel of the tummy. Soft, tender low on the left, no lumps that I can find.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): With that pattern over the year, the cramp settling after you go, no blood and no weight loss, my working impression is irritable bowel. I still can't rule out coeliac or some inflammation until the bloods are back.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): So not cancer? Will the bloods show if it is? When are they, I can't wait months, I'm not able for the worry.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing in the story screams cancer. Bloods won't prove or disprove a growth. I'll book them this week, full blood count, coeliac screen and a crp.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): And a scan? Please can I have a scan. I read about it online and I can't let it go.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might do a scan if it does not settle. I'm not arranging one today.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She'll only half hear the food advice, she's that wound up. Can you say it plain?
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smaller meals, a bit more fibre, ease off the white bread and the fizzy drinks, and keep the wine to a couple of nights rather than most nights. That's for you to try yourself.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): If I do all that does it actually settle? Do I come back? And what if I'm worse at the weekend, do I go to the hospital?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's see you in two weeks with the results. If you pass blood, or you can't keep fluids down, then you go to the hospital.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Ok. Umm, and the hundred milligrams, you're sure that's not wrecking the bowel?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't think the sertraline is behind this, whatever the dose turns out to be. You were right to come in.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): morning. she was chatting in the passage. naledi, what number did you tell me?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Eye.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): shame, doc, sticky red eye. the school wants a sick note, otherwise they won't have her tomorrow.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): okay. one eye or both, and how long?
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): left one first, about four days, thursday. then the right one started, umm, i actually can't say if that was yesterday or the day before. both are red now, stuck shut in the morning.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): this came after a cold?
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ja, last week. snotty nose and a bit of cough. the nose is pretty much gone, the cough still pitches up at night.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): naledi, does the eye hurt?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): itchy at all?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she rubs it the whole time though. and she sleeps badly, tossing for half the night.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): naledi, are you sleeping okay?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): hm. mom says half the night, you say you're fine. were you hot this morning?
[SEG0018] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ja, uh, i thought so. checked with our thermometer.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty eight.
[SEG0020] person_1 (NURSE): she did say thirty eight, that was the home reading. mine just now is 36.8. pulse 104. and she said nineteen, the scale comes out at 19.2 kilograms.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): so 36.8, the fever has settled. any problems with the tummy or the waterworks?
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no, all fine. she's eating.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): what medicine has she had?
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): panado syrup by mouth, the paracetomol. i give 7.5 ml three times a day when she's hot. gave it this morning still.
[SEG0025] person_1 (NURSE): the bottle in the bag, the sticker says 5 ml, not 7.5. i read it twice.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): the sister at the clinic said 7.5 for her weight. so i've been pouring 7.5.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): err, the sticker says one thing, the clinic sister another. i won't pin a dose down off that. does she take it every day?
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): except sundays. she will not take the tablets, ag no, the syrup, she spits it on sundays at her gran's.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Saturday.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): ag, saturday, not sunday. gran has her on saturdays. i mixed the days up.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): saturday, got it. any allergy to medicines or eye drops?
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no. nothing.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): chin up, let me look. mm, both whites are pink, left more than the right, with yellow crust on the lashes. the cornea is clear and the lids aren't really swollen. pupils are fine.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Itchy.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): ah, itchy. so it is itchy, even though you said no earlier. the rubbing fits with that.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): oh, and the graze on her knee, from the bike at school. healed in five days, just a mark, no oozing.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): five days, that's normal healing, not a slow healer. i'm thinking viral conjunctivitis after the cold, though i can't completely rule out a bacterial one. no pain, both eyes, clear cornea, so no antibiotic, and chloramphenicol ointment won't hurry a virus.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): no drops then? what about the school, they were quite sharp on the phone.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): no drops. wash hands, her own face cloth, wipe the crust with cooled boiled water, no sharing towels. i'll do the sick note, keep her home tomorrow, and she can go back the day after if the goo is less. come back if the eye gets sore, if the clear bit goes cloudy, if a lid swells, or if it's not settling in a week.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): okay. the parking was a nightmare, but thanks doc.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Bye.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): cheers naledi. sister will print the note at reception.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, I've popped the cuff on. Blood pressure is 138 over 84, pulse 72, oxygen 98. Doctor Okonkwo's just washing her hands.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ta love. Um, is 138 decent? Factory medical had me at one fifty over ninety odd, that's why they stuck me on the water tablet.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Today's one is fine. My sister's blood pressure went daft after her third, she's on three different tablets, but that's her not you.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Okonkwo. Come and sit. What's been the trouble?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's me hands. At night the thumb, the index and the middle finger go numb, both sides but the right is miles worse, and I have to shake them to wake them up. Feels like I've overdone it on the packing line.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on, and does it actually wake you?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, maybe six weeks, could be longer, I can't pin it. Wakes me two or three times a night. I flap the hand and it eases off after a minute or so. Daytime I'm mostly alright unless I'm gripping boxes.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been dropping things?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I've started dropping cups. Smashed my Blackpool mug last Tuesday, wife was furious. Nearly lost the kettle as well. Sorry, I'm rambling.
[SEG0010] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I've clocked it too. I come three mornings a week for his dad, I'm his dad's carer not his, and twice this month a cup's just gone out of his hand. My own wrists are fine, my daughter's a hairdresser and she's the one always on about her hands.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the numbness travel up the arm at all, or is there neck pain?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it stays in those three fingers. Neck's fine. Honestly I can't hear myself think on that line, the machines are brutal, but that's just noise, my hearing's alright.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the feet?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, feet are fine. Mornings though I feel like a wet rag, from the broken sleep I reckon. Once I've had a brew I'm alright.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any aching in the hand itself?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, yeah, more of an ache in the right wrist and palm at the end of a shift. I take a couple of Nurofen for it, the 200 milligram ones, not every day.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the water tablet, do you know the proper name and the dose?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, bendroflumethazide, the water tablet. 2.5 milligrams, one in the morning. Little white tablet. Been on it a couple of years for the blood pressure.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bendroflumethiazide 2.5 milligrams, yes. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just that and the odd Nurofen. I pack biscuits, been on that line fifteen years. Oh I used to smoke, packed it in when the factory went smoke free, years back now.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, plasters, anything?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations on the hands or wrists before?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Closest I've come is a splinter off a pallet. Daft, really.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I only catch the mornings. My sister had wrist trouble years ago and she still goes on about it, but that's her, nothing to do with him.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look at the hands. No wasting in the palm muscles. I'm going to tap over the wrist.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. That tap on the right sends a tingle into the thumb and middle finger. Left side doesn't. Grip on the right is a little weaker than the left.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah that tap was weird, like a little shock. Reminds me of the static off the shrink wrap, we have a laugh about it on shift.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I think is going on is carpal tunnel. The median nerve runs through a tight tunnel at the wrist, and at night when the wrist bends the pressure squashes the nerve, so those three fingers go numb. Shaking the hand eases it a bit. Working impression, not a definite label yet.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So I'm not falling apart. The lads at work said it was arthritis and I nearly had a panic in the canteen.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call it arthritis from what I can see. A neutral wrist splint at night, not a tight bandage, often settles this. Buy one at the chemist and wear it every night for the next few weeks.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Every night, even weekends? I sleep with my hands under the pillow. And the dog hogs the bed, useless animal.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, especially then, it stops the wrist curling under the pillow. If the splint hasn't helped, we might send you for nerve conduction tests to check the nerve. Not booking that today.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll nag him about the splint when I'm in with his dad. I forget my own tablets half the time, the blood pressure ones, so I'm a fine one to talk.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let's see you back in six weeks either way, and we'll check how the nights are.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, yeah. Should I ease off the Nurofen? They help the ache but I don't want to mess my stomach. Canteen curry is already a gamble.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short courses with food are fine if your stomach stays happy. Don't take them every day for weeks. If you get heartburn or black stools, stop and let us know.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Stomach's been fine, touch wood. I'll grab the splint on the way home. Cheers for not rushing me, I do go on.
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): Chemist on the corner usually has them. My boy wears a wrist support for his boxing, completely different, ignore me.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha, boxing. Right, I'll leave you in peace.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Take care, and do wear it nightly. See you in six weeks.
