[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Uh, what has you in today?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Warfarin.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, the wheel's caught on the— there now. I do the mornings with her.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're very welcome. So, the warfarin. Any bleeding, any bruising, any blood when you go to the toilet?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And nosebleeds?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): I grabbed the vitals outside. Pulse 92, a bit jumpy. Blood pressure 146 over 84.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely, thanks. Are you still on 5 milligrams of warfarin every evening for the fibrillation?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0014] person_4 (CAREGIVER): There's the antibiotic as well, out of hours, your man started her on—
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): On what, sorry, I cut across you.
[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Uh, clarithromicin, 500 twice a day, for the chest. Since Saturday.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right so. Is the cough still there?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Cough.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Umm, bringing up any phlegm, or a fever with it?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that cough been at you?
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She was at the bingo on Tuesday and then the—
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): A week.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): A week, ok. Any pain in the chest, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now the greens. Cabbage, kale, spinach, any change in that lately? It moves the INR around.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She's after dropping them altogether. Hardly a leaf of cabbage or kale. She just went off the notion.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): That'll push it up. Less vitamin K, and the clarithromycin does the same. I'm not a bit surprised the INR is 3.8, a bit high for the fibrillation.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness, or blackouts?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit about the family. Heart, sugar, pressure, whoever comes to mind.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties. Mother did not. Another sister has pressure but no sugar. The husband is on the metformin, that's his not mine, and my sister takes biotin for the hair, I don't take either.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted, none of those are your tablets. You still have the atrial fibrillation yourself?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Aye.
[SEG0037] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And bisoprolol, 2.5 in the morning, for the heart rate. I put it out with the tea.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other tablets of your own?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): What's the shape of the week for you, work, food, getting out, a drink, all that?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): I do the books for the son's garage still. Four mornings, about twenty hours. Dinner is potatoes and a bit of meat, not much veg these days, and I walk the dog to the end of the road. A glass of wine of a Sunday, and I don't smoke.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair play. I'll just have a listen, if you don't mind.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Heart's irregularly irregular, no murmur. Lungs are clear, which is reassuring with that cough.
[SEG0046] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Will she manage the bus after, we've the—
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): She will, sure, nothing heavy today. I'm going to ease the warfarin. I nearly said 3.5, err, actually we'll make it 4 milligrams every evening instead of the 5.
[SEG0048] person_3 (PATIENT): Four.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Four, yes. Finish the clarithromycin, don't leave it off early. Keep the greens the same small amount each day, no sudden big plate of cabbage.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll mind the cabbage so.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'll book the INR for a week from today, and I want you back in here the same day. A week, not an if.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0053] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put that INR in the book for next week.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Morning, doctor. Is this the right room?
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, take a seat. What can I do for you?
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh, morning, doctor. I'll stay and fill in anything that's missed.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, please do. Extra information is always welcome.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been having sudden severe breathlessness, doctor.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you tell me when it first started?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's been about four days, I'm fairly sure.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often do you get it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I'd say once or twice a day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other symptoms with it?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Being unable to lie flat goes along with it, most of the time.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): And the other thing I wanted to mention is that I can't really—
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell the doctor about the other thing, you know, that's what worries me.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I was getting to that! The being unable to lie flat? That's been for two months. I've been feeling very faint too.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): How much does it limit you?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, pretty mild, if I'm being honest.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Is there anything relevant on the family side?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): My grandmother had dementia. My son has asthma.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are there any allergies I should be aware of?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, plasters, it gives me a red itchy rash.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): What conditions have you been treated for in the past?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Depression, for two years.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other things?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had anxiety for five years now.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I follow.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I have migraines, for two years.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other things?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Arthritis in my knees, for about ten years.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, depression and anxiety are known to us, good to have that clear. How active are you?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I hardly move around during the day.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me your medicines, please. These questions might sound routine, but they matter.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm on sertraline, 50 milligrams, once a day for my mood. Actually, it's escitalopram, 10 milligrams, once a day for the anxiety.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She is supposed to take it once a day, but I can't say she always does.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): It's a... um, I can't remember what it's called. It's a small white one.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you remember what it's for?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): For my migraines, I believe. My daughter sets them out for me, I just take what I'm given. I'm on paracetamol, 650 milligrams, when needed.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any past operations I should know about?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Right, yes, I had an operation for a hernia, last spring. Sorry, I know I'm rambling a bit. I didn't want to bother you but it keeps coming back.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you get fever or leg swelling?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, no, no fever, no leg swelling. I did have sharp chest pain on one side at one point, but that went away on its own.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has there been any cough?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): I haven't noticed any cough.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): On the cardiac side, anything I should know?
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): No, that's been fine.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll do your observations first.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nearly done with the readings...
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay: oxygen saturation is 93 percent, BP is 121 over 84, temperature is 36.9 degrees, pulse is 89 beats a minute, respiratory rate 20.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shall I start the examination?
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Sure thing.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Take a deep breath for me.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Your windpipe is pushed to the right, there is no breath sound on the left, and your pressure is dropping.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the examination finished. Let me tell you where I've got to. It fits best with a collapsed lung under pressure. I'd also keep a heart attack in mind.
[SEG0053] person_1 (PATIENT): Do you think it's something serious?
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nothing I've seen today points to an emergency. It looks like a collapsed lung under pressure, but I'd like to confirm. Stop me if I've got anything wrong. You've had sudden severe breathlessness for about four days, and no cough or leg swelling.
[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): That's it, yes.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think a chest X-ray makes sense here, for chest pain. I'll request an urgent chest decompression, it'll help with tension pneumothorax. Stay sitting up, I need to relieve the pressure in your chest right now. Make sure you're drinking plenty of fluids, two to three litres a day if you can, and get proper rest. I think the emergency team should see you too. Come back or go to emergency straight away if the symptoms get worse.
[SEG0057] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, makes sense.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll catch up straight away.
[SEG0059] person_1 (PATIENT): I mean, I can manage that.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me what you've taken from all that, so I can fill in any gaps.
[SEG0061] person_1 (PATIENT): So, I come back straight away. Is that right?
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, exactly right. That's everything on my side. Anything you're unsure about?
[SEG0063] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, that makes sense. Thanks for explaining.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, see you soon.

[SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hey, come on in. I'm Dr. Ellison. Morning ran long, so thanks for waiting.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's fine. That TV out there is so loud I can't hear myself think. I'm, uh, pretty jumpy today, sorry.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're alright. What brought you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It burns when I pee. That's why I came. And I'm going constantly, like every hour, even when there's barely a trickle.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the burning and all that running to the bathroom been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Four days. It just showed up and it hasn't let go.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else riding along with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): My lower back aches, same four days. I keep thinking I've overdone it pulling orders at the warehouse, but sitting down isn't helping.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the warehouse is your job. What are you most worried this is?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): My kidney. Are you going to admit me? I can't miss a shift, rent's due, and I googled way too much last night.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not admitting you off this story. Burning and peeing all the time for four days, plus a backache, makes me think urine infection before kidney. Tell me the rest and then I'll look at you.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt warm last night, a little fever, not drenching the sheets. And I feel like a wet rag, just wiped out. Is a little fever already an emergency?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): A small fever can come with a bladder infection, and no, it isn't an automatic ER trip. Any discharge, any fluid coming from the penis?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. I checked because I was scared this was an STD. Be straight with me, is it?
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): No discharge makes an STD a lot less likely, though I won't swear to it without a test. Any cough, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Lungs feel normal. Could this move into my chest if we wait?
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would be a strange path, I don't see it. Have you lost any weight?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. Pants still fit, so, umm, I don't actually know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't put weight loss in as a yes or a no. How about the bowels, any diarrhea?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels are normal. My buddy got home from Mexico with the runs and I panicked, but that was him.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Did you travel yourself, anywhere recent?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't gone anywhere. Sorry, frog in my throat, that's just nerves, my throat isn't sore.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll ignore the throat then. Pop this under your tongue. 99.4. That's mild, not a big fever.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, 99.4. What if it climbs at 2 a.m.? Do I call you or just go in? I need the actual rule.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll give you the rule after I examine you, so it fits what I find. Belly's a little tender right over the pubic bone. I tap both flanks and you don't flinch, so nothing there is jumping out as an angry kidney.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The ache sits low, across the middle, and it's not a sharp stab. So the kidney's okay? You're sure?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Less likely it's the kidney. Sure would be overselling a two-minute exam. What medicines are you on?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, twice a day, these past four days, for the back. And lisinopril, 10 milligrams, every morning.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lisinopril for blood pressure? How long have you had that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. A couple of years. They tell me it's controlled. Should I stop it? Is that what's burning me?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop the lisinopril. Burning urine isn't how that pill usually misbehaves. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies at all. I just hate when pills make me sick. So what are you putting me on?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking through it, mild fever, burning, frequency, a quiet flank exam, blood pressure in the background. I was going to send urine today and start nitrofurantoin, 100 milligrams by mouth, twice a day, for five days, before you left.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Nitrofurantin? No, please. I took that last year for the same kind of burning and I threw up the whole next day, so I stopped after two doses. Will every antibiotic do that, and does my wife need a test too?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes it. Scratch the nitrofurantoin, I'm not handing you a medicine that made you vomit, and I'm not starting any antibiotic before the urine result.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): So I walk out with nothing? How long until you know? What if I get worse tonight while we're waiting?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll do a urinalysis and a urine culture before you leave today. If the test shows an infection, I'll call in an antibiotic that isn't nitrofurantoin. And if you're not better in three days, come back and see me.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): If I start shaking or puking, I shouldn't wait for that call, right? And can I work my shift tomorrow or am I done?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Shaking chills, vomiting, or you can't keep fluids down, go to the ER, don't wait on me. Drink water through the day, keep the ibuprofen if your stomach allows, and work is fine if a bathroom's close.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I keep thinking it's cancer, err, or my prostate, because some forum said so. I need you to say what you actually think.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working read is a lower urinary tract infection. I can't fully rule out some early prostate irritation, but nothing here screams cancer, and I want the urine back before I talk like it's settled.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm 46, does that make the prostate thing more likely? Also, um, sex. Should we hold off? I hate asking.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): 46 doesn't change the plan. Hold off on sex until the burning eases. Your wife doesn't need testing based on this visit.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Cup today, no script in my hand, you call only if I need a different antibiotic. Am I missing a piece?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the whole of it. Lab's down the hall on the left, they'll take the sample on your way out.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. I walked in sure you were keeping me overnight. One last thing, is coffee gonna make the burn worse?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee can poke at an irritated bladder, so skip it for a couple of days if you can stand to. Water's the better move.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Water, then the cup. Thanks for not rushing me out confused.

[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I'm not breathless. Just coughing.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which tablet is it, Gemma?

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): In and out. ~

[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Why not? ~
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to rule out other causes first. I'd like to arrange a chest X-ray, and some blood tests.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Usually it settles within a few weeks once the tablet is changed. ~
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief. ~
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the meantime, a spoonful of honey before bed can help soothe the tickle.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get some honey. ~
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd like to see you again in two weeks.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two weeks. Thank you, doctor. ~

[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr. Keller, I'm Doctor Shah. Sorry you got stuck out there. What brought you in today?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Like a hot iron sitting on the skin. It stays on the one side, doesn't jump across. Uh, if my shirt rubs it, forget it. And I feel wiped out.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Dana, I come by the house to help. He's been sleeping badly since this started, up half the night.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's right. I can't sleep with this thing.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry. Any fever with it, or chills?

[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about healing, do little cuts drag on for you or do they close up okay?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): It was fine. Healed. Can we get back to the burning, I'm tired of sitting here.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Of course. Way back, did you have chickenpox as a kid?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. I was maybe seven. Whole family had it. I remember the itching.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He takes a blood pressure pill too, lisinapril, ten milligrams. But he does not take the tablets on Sundays.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): It's lisinopril, not whatever you said. And it's not Sundays. Err, I skip Saturdays. Once a day the other days, by mouth.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Got it. Lisinopril ten milligrams once a day, and Saturday is the day you skip. How long's the blood pressure been a thing?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Years. Five-ish years. Don't ask me the month, I have no idea. It's still ongoing.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's okay, we don't need the exact month. Mind if I look at the rash? Shirt up just a little.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ugh. Yeah. Easy. It hurts when you touch near it.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): There's a small cluster of blisters on the left chest, kind of in a band, and it stops right at the midline. The skin around them is red. Lungs sound clear when I listen.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): So. What is it. Just say it.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Shingles. My neighbor had that. He complained for a month. Also his dog barked all night, not that you care.
[SEG0028] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Frank's daughter is pregnant. She's due in the spring, and she was planning to come over tomorrow.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then let's keep her away until the blisters crust over and dry up. The fluid can pass chickenpox to somebody who never had it, and we really don't want that in pregnancy. Wash your hands, don't share towels, keep the rash covered.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm seventy four and I don't get to see my own daughter. Fantastic.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Only for a short bit, till it crusts. I am going to start an antiviral today. Valacyclovir, a thousand milligrams by mouth, three times a day, for seven days. Better to start now.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times a day. I'll mess it up. I'm already lousy about Saturdays with the other pill.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): This one you shouldn't skip. Dana, if you can help him track the doses, that would be great.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll put an alarm on my phone. He's not gonna sleep though, the pain is bad.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): You can take acetaminophen by mouth for the pain, whatever the usual over the counter amount is on the bottle. I'm not adding a second prescription today.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Bottle dose. Sure. I just want the burning to stop.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): If it does not settle, we might do a scan, but I'm not ordering one today. Let's see you back in two weeks.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. And a scan if it doesn't. Okay I guess.
[SEG0039] person_4 (CAREGIVER): What if the blisters spread before then, do I call?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. If they spread quickly, or he gets short of breath, or the pain suddenly jumps, don't sit on it for two weeks. Call us or go to urgent care.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not sitting in an ER for a rash. I'm exhausted. We done?
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nearly. The valacyclovir will be waiting at the front desk, start it today. If it upsets your stomach, take it with a little food. And keep that rash covered if anyone stops by.
[SEG0043] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll tell his daughter not to come. I'll grab the prescription on the way out.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Tell her I'm not making it up. It actually burns.
[SEG0045] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the slip. Just so it's on the note, the blood pressure I got was 136 over 78.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I already said it was 152 over 90 at home. But sure, write your number.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Home numbers and office numbers don't always match, and that's okay. We'll use today's 136 over 78. Hope you get some rest, Mr. Keller.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Thanks. I guess.
[SEG0049] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Come on Frank, car's out front. We'll stop for the medicine.

[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, the Luas was stuck at Ranelagh and we were standing there like eejits.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I said we'd miss it if he kept checking the door was locked.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor, I always think I've left the iron on. Anyway.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a bother at all. How've you been keeping, apart from the rush in?
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ah we're fine. The dog ate a sock this morning, that's the real drama.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. So what has you in to see me?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the jaw. It's sore when I'm chewing.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more, however it comes to you.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): When I eat there's a pain, umm, and it clicks. Mostly the left side, I'd say.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It clicks every single time he opens, doctor, and he can't chew on the left at all. It's been three weeks.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): That's not it. I don't know, doctor, I can chew, it just hurts, and it doesn't click every time I open, only when I'm eating. And it's not three weeks, more like ten days.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Okay, so pain when you chew, somewhere between ten days and three weeks, a click with the eating, mostly the left. Not with every opening.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. The click might have been there longer. I don't know when that started.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): What makes the pain worse, would you say?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Stress. Work is manic. And chewing, toast especially. I don't know, doctor, crusty bread is brutal.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): And anything that eases it?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): If I stop eating it settles a bit. I don't know about anything else.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had a fever with this at all?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): The noise of the click is what gets me. First thing in the morning it's louder.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll keep the morning click in mind. Have you had a temperature, though?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No fever. I haven't felt hot.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grinds his teeth too. I hear it most nights, I'm lying there awake with it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I grind. I don't know, doctor, I'm asleep. She's making a big thing of it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): So she hears grinding and you wouldn't stand over it. We'll leave that as not agreed.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you on any tablets for the pain?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Paracetemol. Two of the 500 milligram ones, when it's bad.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every day, or just now and again?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Some days twice, some days I don't bother. I don't know, doctor, there's no routine to it.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines, from us or from the chemist?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Mornings are the worst for that click, like I said. Sorry.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. Any other medicines at all?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just the paracetemol.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A few pints of a Saturday, that's all.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the work you mentioned, what's that like day to day?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Accounts, err, up in the hospital. Deadlines every Friday. It's been like that a year. I don't know, doctor, it's just the job.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me have a feel of the jaw. Open slowly for me, there's no rush.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a click on the left as you open, and it's tender here, just in front of the ear. The right side is grand, no click.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's the bit. Ow.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry. No swelling that I can see, and the skin isn't hot.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd say this is the jaw joint, the TMJ, stirred up by clenching when you're under stress. The grinding your partner hears would fit that, though you two don't agree on it, so I'm not treating that bit as certain. It's a working impression.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Soft foods for the next while, nothing crusty, and get a mouth guard for the nights. The chemist has a boil-and-bite one, or your dentist can make a proper guard.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor, will a guard even stay in?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most people get used to them. Give the soft diet and the guard a proper go, and I'll see you back in four weeks to see where the pain is.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand. Four weeks. Thanks.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, come on through. I'll check your blood pressure before the doctor. Sorry if I seem a bit frazzled, my sister rang at breakfast about her little boy's school concert and I have not quite landed yet.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Please do not apologise. I am perfectly happy to wait.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Ta. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse 72, oxygen level 98 percent. Have a seat, the doctor will be with you shortly.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Nguyen. Come and sit down. What's brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. It is my right heel. For about two months the first steps in the morning have been really quite painful.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Tell me what a morning looks like. When your foot first—
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have to stand still. It is a sharp pain under the heel, then after a minute or two of walking it eases. By the arvo, on my feet at the shop, it grumbles again. I bought new work shoes just before it started, and I wonder if they are part of it.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you still in those shoes most days?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, I am. I have not found a replacement. My runners are about a year old, the ones I use for, umm—
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): For your running?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Three mornings a week, about five kilometres. I cut Thursday short and walked the last part home. I did not wish to aggravate it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the shop, what is the job exactly?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I manage a newsagency. Standing or walking the floor most of the day.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ongoing conditions I should know about?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I have asthma. I am forty-six, and it has been with me since my twenties. Generally it is well controlled.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you using for the asthma?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): simbicort, the 200/6, two puffs in the morning and two at night. Ventolin as well, two puffs when I need it, though that is rare. I also tried Nurofen for the heel, 400 milligrams twice a day for about a week, and then I stopped. It bothered my stomach.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Any swelling, or any redness there?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not really.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the heel feel warm?
[SEG0021] person_1 (NURSE): Oops, sorry, I left the cuff on the chair. I'll grab it and get out of your way.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. It is no warmer than the other foot.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, pins and needles?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Nothing of that sort.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): And pain in the calf, or in your back?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): My back is quite all right. The calf, err—
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It does not go up into the calf.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): With your asthma, any wheeze lately, or does it wake you at night?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes I wheeze if I have been rushing on the shop floor. It does not wake me.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, shoe off if you would. Tender on the inner heel where that band attaches, no swelling I can see, and the ankle moves freely. I reckon this is plantar fasciitis, the plantar fascia tightens overnight when it is irritated and those first steps yank on it, which is why mornings are the worst. New shoes can stir it up as well, and we do not need any scans.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll keep this simple. Stretch the calf and the sole before you get out of bed, and again after a run. Grab some cushioned insoles, or a gel heel cup, from the chemist, and ease the running for a couple of weeks, shorter and slower. If it is not settling in about a month, come back and see me.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall do that. I am grateful you explained it.

[SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Harlan, come on back. I'll grab vitals before Doctor Shah sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): About time. Uh, that waiting room chair is a joke and I'm not in the mood.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dad, please. Sorry, he's short on sleep. I'm Karen, his daughter.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Right. Arm loose for me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen 98 percent on room air. Doctor will be right in.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): 152. Wonderful. Exactly what I needed today.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr. Harlan. I'm Doctor Shah. Karen can stay if you want. What brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps. Both calves, every night. I can't sleep and I'm sick of it.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nighttime cramps in both calves. How long has that been?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Two months. Around when it got cold, I guess. Both of them, down in the calf.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every night, or just off and on?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much every night. Wakes me, I stand and walk it off. Couple minutes and I can lie down.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He paces the hall around two. I've caught it most nights I'm over there.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Both calves, nightly, about two months, and walking helps. Any pain in the legs when you walk during the day?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Walking's fine. Not painful then.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles? Redness or warmth in the calves?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Not that either.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you taking?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The water pill. Furosimide, forty milligrams, every morning. That's for my blood pressure.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide forty milligrams each morning for the pressure. So you've been told you have hypertension?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Years. They've called it hypertension the whole time. That's why the water pill.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hypertension, ongoing, on furosemide. Anything else, from us or from the store?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Magnesium. From the store, bottle says magnesium oxide, 400 milligrams. One at night for the cramps.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grabbed it off the shelf last month. I told him to ask you, but.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): How much water do you drink in a day?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The cramps are what I came for, not a lecture. They hit at like 2 or 3 and I'm up pacing. That's the thing.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll get to the cramps, I promise. The water, though, roughly how much?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup with the pill. Maybe one more if I remember. I hate drinking cause then I'm up peeing. Not much.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): A cup or two, on purpose. Were you ever given a potassium pill with the furosemide?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Those horse pills, uh, K-Dur, twenty milliequivalents. I stopped it in March. They made me queasy.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stopped the K-Dur twenty in March because of the queasiness. Did anyone ever give you quinine for the cramps?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Nobody gave me that. I never took it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, never took quinine. About the blood pressure. Any chest pain?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches? With hypertension, some folks get them.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. Mornings, behind the eyes. Not every day.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So not a flat no. Sometimes, morning headaches. Any dizziness, or a feeling you'll pass out?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not that either.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not asking if the hypertension is gone. You already said that's still there. Any blurry vision?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Pressure's still there, yeah. Vision, no. Not blurry.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And your stomach lately? Nausea, heartburn, any change in the bowels?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Stomach's fine now. Queasy was just those potassium pills, and I quit those.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me check the legs. Calves are soft, no tenderness, no redness, and I don't see swelling. Foot pulses are present, both sides.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Told you. Nothing in the daytime. Can we wrap this, I've had enough of sitting here.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Almost. Let me read it back. Nightly cramps, both calves, two months, you walk them off. No daytime walking pain, no swelling, no redness. Hypertension on furosemide forty each morning. K-Dur twenty stopped in March. Magnesium oxide 400 at night. A cup or two of water. Occasional morning headache. No chest pain, not really short of breath, no dizziness, vision's okay. Fair?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Don't tack anything else on.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he really does dodge the water. I've watched him slide the glass away.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Furosemide can lower your potassium, and not drinking much can feed cramps like this. I want a blood test for the potassium, a basic metabolic panel. It's ordered, and the lab will draw it before you leave today.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Just the needle, then I wanna go home. Don't hand me a jug in the lobby.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): No jug. Do drink more through the day, several glasses, not one cup. And stretch both calves before bed, hold it about thirty seconds each side.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over the panel. If the potassium is low we might talk about a supplement then, not today. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. Two weeks, alright, let's just get out of here.

[SEG0038] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll have the prescription at the desk for you, Mr Brennan, so you're not hanging about.

[SEG0010] person_1 (NURSE): Temp is 37.8, pulse ninety four, pressure 136 over 84, sats 98 percent. Respirations 16.

[SEG0016] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She was up half the night pacing. I nearly rang the out of hours, I didn't know whether...
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Breathing is fine. Not a bother. I'm wrecked and cranky, leave the pacing out of it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. What have you had for the pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Paracetamol from the chemist. Two tablets. Doesn't touch it.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): It's a gram, four times a day, I set them out. She missed the lunchtime one yesterday, and I'm not sure she took the evening one, she was dozing.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other regular tablets?

[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Metformin. Five hundred milligrams twice a day, for the diabetes. She's been on it years.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so the diabetes is ongoing. Anything else in the gut, or with the waterworks?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Can we get to the tooth.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking amoxacillin, five hundred three times a day for five days, and I'll see you in a fortnight. That should cover it.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Hang on, penicillin. I can't have penicillin.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): What happened when you had it?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Years ago, for a chest thing. A rash all over me and my lips swelled up. They told me never again.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The lips were bad that time. She's stayed away from it since.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, scrap that. No amoxicillin, nothing in that family. We'll use clindamicyn, three hundred milligrams four times a day for five days, by mouth.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Four times. I'm tired just hearing it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): I know. And a fortnight is wrong as well, err, now I'm thinking about the diabetes and the fever and the cheek still coming up.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She's been a bit higher on the sugars the last day or two too.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): That settles it. Nurse takes bloods Thursday morning, a full blood count and a CRP. No fasting, you can eat, just come at half eight.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Thursday half eight is free. I'll book her in.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'll see you here Friday morning, not in two weeks. We'll look at the swelling and the bloods.
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Friday. More waiting. That telly outside is brutal, cookery on a loop.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the swelling hasn't settled by Friday, or if you're worse, then we do a scan of the face. Not booking it now. If those bloods are borderline I'll add a swab of the gum, only if they're borderline.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And if she goes downhill before Friday?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): If swallowing gets hard, or the breathing gets difficult, or the swelling runs to the eye or down the neck, straight to the emergency department. Don't wait for me.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I hear you. I'm not deaf. I'm sore and I want the bed.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Soft food only. Keep the paracetamol going the way it's set out, and finish every dose of the clindamycin even when the tooth eases. Ring the dentist when they're back next week.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): Right. Fine.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Will the tablet fix the crown, or is the tooth gone?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Working read, it's an infection under the crown, a dental abscess, and the antibiotic should knock it back.
